title: Proposition 16.13.3 (Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom)
search_title: Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.3 (Strict compact stability with zero spectral bottom) . 7B9E16310EBB For every nonzero $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ the grim-reaper form satisfies \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\operatorname {sech}s\,  |(\phi \cosh s)'|^2ds>0.  \] Nevertheless its variational spectral bottom is \[  \inf _{0\ne \phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)} \frac{Q_ v(\phi )}{\int \phi ^2\cosh s\, ds}=0.  \] Proof Insert $w=\operatorname {sech}s$ in Proposition 14.14.6 to get the formula. Equality would make $\phi \cosh s$ constant; compact support forces that constant to be zero. To compute the infimum, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi $ equal to one on $[-1,1]$, supported in $[-2,2]$, and put $\phi _ R=w\chi (s/R)$. Then \[  Q_ v(\phi _ R)=R^{-2}\int \operatorname {sech}s\, |\chi '(s/R)|^2ds \le R^{-2}\| \chi '\| _\infty ^2\pi ,  \] while $\int \phi _ R^2\rho _ v\to \pi $ by dominated convergence. Stability gives the opposite bound zero. The null function $w$ in the weighted square-integrable kernel is not compactly supported, so there is no contradiction with strict positivity on compact tests. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.13.4 (A one-dimensional Schrödinger form)
search_title: A one-dimensional Schrödinger form
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.4 (A one-dimensional Schrödinger form) . 752E1E7B14D3 The substitution $\psi =\sqrt{\cosh s}\, \phi $ preserves the weighted $L^2$ norm and transforms the grim-reaper quadratic form into \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _{\mathbb R}\left[|\psi '|^2+ \left(\frac14-\frac34\operatorname {sech}^2s\right)\psi ^2\right]ds  \] for compactly supported smooth real tests. The weighted null field $\operatorname {sech}s$ becomes $\operatorname {sech}^{1/2}s$. Proof Writing $h=\log \cosh s$ gives $\phi =e^{-h/2}\psi $. Thus the weighted derivative energy is $\int (\psi '-h'\psi /2)^2$. Integrate the cross term by parts; its contribution is $h''\psi ^2/2$. The resulting potential for the full quadratic form is $h''/2+(h')^2/4-|A|^2$. Substituting $h''=\operatorname {sech}^2s$, $(h')^2=1-\operatorname {sech}^2s$ and $|A|^2=\operatorname {sech}^2s$ gives the formula. The norm identity and the transformed null field follow immediately from the substitution. No complete spectral resolution is asserted. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.13.5 (Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel)
search_title: Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Proposition 16.13.5 (Grim cylinders have a different square-integrable kernel) . 01561F6C5365 Let $M$ be the product of the complete unit grim reaper with $\mathbb R^ k$, $k\ge 1$, translating in its grim-reaper plane. It is weighted stable and has variational spectral bottom zero, but it has no nonzero smooth Jacobi field in $L^2(\rho _ vdA)$. Proof The metric is $ds^2+|dy|^2$, the weight is $\cosh s$, and the operator is the one in Proposition 16.13.1 plus $\Delta _ y$. The function $w(s,y)=\operatorname {sech}s$ is a positive Jacobi field, proving stability. It is not weighted square-integrable because its squared integral in $s$ is $\pi $ and the Euclidean factor has infinite volume. Lemma 14.14.10 therefore gives the zero kernel. For the spectral bottom, multiply the cutoff tests of Proposition 16.13.3 by $\eta (y/R)$, with nonzero smooth compactly supported $\eta $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Separation of variables makes the Rayleigh quotient the sum of the grim-reaper quotient and $R^{-2}\int |\nabla \eta |^2/\int \eta ^2$. Both tend to zero. This example has zero infimum without a nonzero weighted square-integrable null field; it does not require an assertion about the entire spectrum. $\square$

title: Example 16.13.6 (A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap)
search_title: A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap
section: 16.13 Weighted Jacobi fields on grim reapers and planes
text: Example 16.13.6 (A translating plane has a positive weighted gradient gap) . 84BE9F6FEFFB Let $P\cong \mathbb R^ n$ be an affine hyperplane and let $0\ne v$ be tangent to it. The image is stationary under translation by $v$, but its translator-weighted form has variational spectral bottom $|v|^2/4$. Its induced Euclidean metric is complete and its induced conformal translator metric is incomplete. Proof Since $A=0$, the Jacobi form equals the weighted gradient energy. For $\psi =e^{\langle x,v\rangle /2}\phi $, integration of the compactly supported cross term gives \[  Q_ v(\phi )=\int _ P\left(|\nabla \psi |^2+\frac{|v|^2}{4}\psi ^2\right)dA, \qquad \int _ P\phi ^2\rho _ v\, dA=\int _ P\psi ^2dA.  \] The lower bound is immediate. Taking $\psi _ R(x)=\eta ((x-p)/R)$ for a fixed nonzero compactly supported smooth $\eta $ makes its gradient Rayleigh quotient tend to zero, proving sharpness. Euclidean completeness is that of an affine plane. The ray $p-tv/|v|$ stays in $P$ and has finite conformal length by Proposition 14.15.1 , proving the final assertion. A tangential velocity changes this weighted functional even though it does not change the plane's image under the flow. $\square$

title: 5.7 Vector measures and the mass of a current
search_title: Vector measures and the mass of a current
section: 5.7 Vector measures and the mass of a current
text: The positive representation theorem extends to finite-dimensional vector-valued tests. We give the functional-analytic steps explicitly, including the passage from the comass of a form to the mass norm of a multivector. The source is [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 1, Theorem 5.14, printed pp. 37–38, and Chapter 6, Remark 2.7 and equations (2.8)–(2.10), printed pp. 160–161. Simon initially uses the Euclidean norm; the argument below works for an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm. Completeness of the real spaces $L^1$ and $L^2$, elementary integration, and finite-dimensional norm duality are background inputs. Lemma 5.7.1 (Representation of a bounded functional on a real Hilbert space) . 63273388A3B5 If $\mathcal H$ is a real Hilbert space and $L:\mathcal H\to \mathbb R$ is bounded and linear, there is a unique $z\in \mathcal H$ with $L(x)=\langle x,z\rangle $ for all $x$. Moreover $\| z\| =\| L\| $. Proof The case $L=0$ is immediate. Otherwise the closed affine set $A=\{ x:L(x)=1\} $ is nonempty and its distance $d$ from zero is positive, since $1\leq \| L\| \| x\| $ on $A$. Choose $x_ j\in A$ with $\| x_ j\| \to d$. Their midpoints belong to $A$, so the parallelogram identity gives \[  \| x_ j-x_ k\| ^2=2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4\left\| \frac{x_ j+x_ k}{2}\right\| ^2 \leq 2\| x_ j\| ^2+2\| x_ k\| ^2-4d^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] Completeness gives a minimizer $x_0\in A$. For $y\in \ker L$, minimizing $\| x_0+ty\| ^2$ in $t$ yields $\langle x_0,y\rangle =0$. As $x-L(x)x_0\in \ker L$, we get $L(x)=\langle x,x_0\rangle /\| x_0\| ^2$. Set $z=x_0/\| x_0\| ^2$. Testing differences against themselves proves uniqueness. Cauchy–Schwarz and testing $z/\| z\| $ give the norm identity. $\square$ Proposition 5.7.2 (The dual of a sigma-finite real integration space) . A1288D51AB95 Let $(X,\mu )$ be a sigma-finite measure space. Every bounded linear functional $L:L^1(\mu ;\mathbb R)\to \mathbb R$ has the form \[  L(f)=\int _ X f\eta \, d\mu ,\qquad \eta \in L^\infty (\mu ),\qquad \| \eta \| _\infty =\| L\| .  \] The density $\eta $ is unique up to a null set. Proof Choose measurable $E_ j\uparrow X$ with $\mu (E_ j)<\infty $. Extending by zero gives a bounded restriction of $L$ to $L^2(E_ j)$, because $\| f\| _1\leq \mu (E_ j)^{1/2}\| f\| _2$. Lemma 5.7.1 gives a density $\eta _ j\in L^2(E_ j)$. Write $C=\| L\| $. If $F=\{ |\eta _ j|>C+\varepsilon \} \subset E_ j$ had positive measure, the $L^2$ test $\operatorname {sign}(\eta _ j)1_ F$ would imply \[  (C+\varepsilon )\mu (F)<\int _ F|\eta _ j|\, d\mu =L(\operatorname {sign}(\eta _ j)1_ F)\leq C\mu (F),  \] a contradiction. Thus $|\eta _ j|\leq C$ almost everywhere. On $E_ i\subset E_ j$, all $L^2(E_ i)$ tests give the same integral for $\eta _ i$ and $\eta _ j$; testing their difference proves agreement. Discarding countably many null sets glues the densities to $\eta $ on $X$. Truncating both the domain to $E_ j$ and the values of an arbitrary $f\in L^1$ approximates it in $L^1$ by bounded functions supported in finite-measure sets. Continuity proves the formula for every $f$. The norm equality follows from $\| \eta \| _\infty \leq C$ and $|L(f)|\leq \| \eta \| _\infty \| f\| _1$. Uniqueness follows by testing the sign of the difference on finite-measure subsets where its absolute value is bounded below. $\square$ Lemma 5.7.3 (The positive variation functional) . A217FEC406E3 Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$ open, and $L:C_ c(U;E)\to \mathbb R$ linear. Suppose for each compact $K\subset U$ there is $C_ K<\infty $ with $|L(F)|\leq C_ K\| F\| _\infty $ whenever $\operatorname {spt}F\subset K$. For $g\in C_ c(U)$ with $g\geq 0$, put \[  \lambda (g)=\sup \{ |L(F)|:F\in C_ c(U;E),\  \| F(x)\| \leq g(x)\text{ for every }x\} .  \] Then $\lambda $ is additive and nonnegatively homogeneous on nonnegative functions. It extends uniquely to a positive linear functional on $C_ c(U)$. Proof The supremum is finite by the local bound and the support of $g$. Homogeneity is immediate. For additivity from below, choose almost maximizing tests for $g$ and $h$, reversing each sign so that its $L$-value is nonnegative. Their sum is admissible for $g+h$. For the reverse inequality, split any admissible $F$ as \[  F_1=\frac{g}{g+h}F,\qquad F_2=\frac{h}{g+h}F  \] where $g+h>0$, and set both fields to zero elsewhere. These extensions are continuous: $\| F_1\| \leq g$ and $\| F_2\| \leq h$ force continuity at every zero of $g+h$. Each is admissible for its corresponding function, so $|L(F)|\leq \lambda (g)+\lambda (h)$. This proves additivity. Define $\lambda (f)=\lambda (f^+)-\lambda (f^-)$; equality of two decompositions into differences of nonnegative functions follows by cross-adding and using additivity. Hence this extension is linear and positive. $\square$ Theorem 5.7.4 (Polar representation for finite-dimensional tests) . 458374FA534D Under the hypotheses of Lemma 5.7.3 , there are a Radon measure $\mu $ on $U$ and a measurable $\xi :U\to E^*$ such that \[  L(F)=\int _ U\langle F,\xi \rangle \, d\mu ,\qquad \| \xi \| _{E^*}=1\quad \mu \text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \lambda (g)=\int _ Ug\, d\mu \quad (g\in C_ c(U),\  g\geq 0).  \] The measure is determined by $\lambda $, and the field is unique $\mu $-almost everywhere for this measure. See [ Sim18 ] , Theorem 5.14; its Hilbert-space statement is the Euclidean-norm special case. Proof Theorem 2.3.7 applied to $\lambda $ gives $\mu $. In particular \[  |L(F)|\leq \lambda (\| F\| )=\int _ U\| F\| \, d\mu .  \] Choose a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ d$ of unit vectors of $E$. Each scalar functional $f\mapsto L(fe_ i)$ is bounded for the $L^1(\mu )$ norm. The density theorem 2.3.8 extends it uniquely from $C_ c(U)$ to $L^1(\mu )$. The measure is sigma-finite, since $U$ has a countable compact exhaustion and $\mu $ is finite on compacts. Proposition 5.7.2 gives coordinate densities $\eta _ i$. Define $\xi $ by $\langle e_ i,\xi \rangle =\eta _ i$. Finite linear expansion of $F$ proves the integral formula. For a fixed $q\in E$, the same domination applied to $fq$ and $L^1$ density give $|\langle q,\xi \rangle |\leq \| q\| $ almost everywhere. Take a countable dense subset of the unit ball and discard the union of the associated null sets. Continuity in $q$ then gives $\| \xi \| _{E^*}\leq 1$ almost everywhere. For every nonnegative $g\in C_ c(U)$, each admissible test in the definition of $\lambda (g)$ satisfies \[  |L(F)|\leq \int _ Ug\| \xi \| _{E^*}\, d\mu .  \] Taking the supremum yields \[  \int _ Ug\, d\mu =\lambda (g)\leq \int _ Ug\| \xi \| _{E^*}\, d\mu \leq \int _ Ug\, d\mu .  \] Consequently $\int g(1-\| \xi \| _{E^*})\, d\mu =0$ for every such $g$. Cutoffs equal to one on a compact exhaustion show that this nonnegative integrand vanishes almost everywhere. Positive Riesz uniqueness determines $\mu $, and scalar $L^1$ density determines each coordinate of $\xi $ uniquely. $\square$ Lemma 5.7.5 (Extending a finite-mass current to continuous forms) . CC6436C139E1 A current $T$ with locally finite mass on $U$ has a unique extension to compactly supported continuous $m$-forms that is bounded for uniform comass on each fixed compact support. For open $W\subset U$, its mass $\mathbf M_ W(T)$ is also the supremum of $|T(\omega )|$ over continuous compactly supported forms in $W$ of comass at most one. Proof Extend a continuous compactly supported form by zero and convolve its coefficients with smooth mollifiers of radii tending to zero. The resulting smooth forms converge uniformly; all sufficiently late supports lie in a common relatively compact open $V\subset U$. The mass bound makes their $T$-values Cauchy. The same estimate applied to the difference of any two approximating sequences proves independence. It also proves continuity and uniqueness of the extension. If the original support lies in $W$, choose the mollifier radii so the approximating supports also lie in $W$. Uniform approximation in the finite-dimensional comass norm gives upper bounds $1+\varepsilon _ j$ for the approximating comasses; divide by $1+\varepsilon _ j$ to obtain admissible smooth tests. Thus allowing continuous tests does not change the supremum. This is the extension preceding [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.8), with comass in place of the Euclidean norm. $\square$ Proposition 5.7.6 (Open-set mass from the positive variation functional) . F553EACEBF96 Apply Theorem 5.7.4 to the continuous extension of a locally finite-mass $m$-current, with $E=\Lambda ^ m(\mathbb R^ N)^*$ carrying comass. Its measure satisfies $\mu (W)=\mathbf M_ W(T)$ for every open $W\subset U$. The dual field has mass norm one almost everywhere and need not be simple. Proof For a continuous test supported in $W$ with comass at most one, the polar representation gives $|T(\omega )|\leq \mu (W)$. Conversely, if $0\leq g\leq 1$ has compact support in $W$, every test for $\lambda (g)$ is such a continuous mass test. Hence $\mathbf M_ W(T)\geq \lambda (g)=\int g\, d\mu $. Taking the supremum over these scalar cutoffs gives $\mu (W)$ by Radon regularity, including when it is infinite. The mass norm is precisely the dual of comass, so the unit-norm assertion follows from the vector representation theorem. Nothing in that theorem imposes decomposability of the polar multivector. $\square$

title: 16.14 A normal current without rectifiability
search_title: A normal current without rectifiability
section: 16.14 A normal current without rectifiability
text: Normality controls a current and its boundary by measures, but does not force its mass to lie on a set of its own dimension. The following elementary example also makes visible the distinction between Euclidean and mass norms in [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 6, Remark 2.7, printed p. 160. Example 16.14.1 (A nonsimple bivector and its two norms) . 5584C114BE31 In oriented $\mathbb R^4$, put $\zeta =e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$. Its Euclidean norm is $\sqrt2$, while its mass norm is $2$. It is not simple. Proof The two basis bivectors are orthonormal, giving the Euclidean norm. Their individual mass norms are one, so the triangle inequality gives $|\zeta |_{\mathrm{mass}}\leq 2$. For the reverse inequality, let $\omega _0=dx^1\wedge dx^2+dx^3\wedge dx^4$. Define the orthogonal complex structure $Je_1=e_2$, $Je_2=-e_1$, $Je_3=e_4$, $Je_4=-e_3$. Then $\omega _0(u,v)=\langle Ju,v\rangle $, whose absolute value is at most one on orthonormal pairs. Equality holds at $(e_1,e_2)$, so $\omega _0$ has comass one. As $\langle \omega _0,\zeta \rangle =2$, duality gives the opposite mass bound. Finally $\zeta \wedge \zeta =2e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4\ne 0$, whereas the square of a simple bivector is zero. $\square$ Example 16.14.2 (A diffuse finite-mass two-current) . 4B74DFD48D85 Let $Q=[0,1]^4$ and define a two-current on $\mathbb R^4$ by \[  T(\omega )=\int _ Q\bigl (\omega _{12}(x)+\omega _{34}(x)\bigr )\, dx.  \] Then $\| T\| =2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$, its polar bivector is $\zeta /2$, and $\mathbf M(T)=2$. Its support is $Q$, and its mass measure is non-atomic. Proof The bound $|\langle \omega ,\zeta \rangle |\leq 2\| \omega \| _*$ shows that the formula is a current and bounds its mass by $2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$. For any open $W$ and any smooth scalar cutoff $0\leq g\leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$, the form $g\omega _0$ has comass at most one and $T(g\omega _0)=2\int _ Qg\, dx$. Taking the supremum of these cutoffs yields the reverse open-set mass bound. This identifies the measure and the polar field. Every ball about a point of $Q$ meets $Q$ in positive four-dimensional measure, while tests outside $Q$ vanish; hence the support is $Q$. Singletons have zero Lebesgue measure. $\square$ Proposition 16.14.3 (The diffuse current has a finite-mass boundary) . 852428C98493 The current in Example 16.14.2 is normal and satisfies $\mathbf M(\partial T)\leq 8$. Proof For a smooth compactly supported one-form $\eta =\sum _ i\eta _ i\, dx^ i$, \[  \partial T(\eta )=\int _ Q(\partial _1\eta _2-\partial _2\eta _1 +\partial _3\eta _4-\partial _4\eta _3)\, dx.  \] Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus in the differentiated coordinate and Fubini's theorem to each of the four terms. The result is a sum of eight integrals over unit three-dimensional faces, each of a single component of $\eta $, with its appropriate sign. If the comass of $\eta $ is at most one, each component is bounded by one, so the absolute value is at most eight. Taking the supremum proves the boundary mass bound. Together with $\mathbf M(T)=2$, this proves normality. The face integrals define a one-current distributed over three-dimensional faces; they are not integration currents of those faces in dimension three. $\square$ Lemma 16.14.4 (Lower-dimensional Lipschitz images have zero ambient volume) . FF7C6E81ADF7 If $m<N$ and $f:A\subset \mathbb R^ m\to \mathbb R^ N$ is Lipschitz, then $\mathcal L^ N(f(A))=0$, where outer measure suffices if measurability has not been specified. Proof First suppose $A\subset [-R,R]^ m$ and let $L$ be a Lipschitz constant. Cover this cube by at most $C_ R\delta ^{-m}$ cubes of side $\delta $. For each cube meeting $A$, choose a point of $A$ in it. Its image and the image of the portion of $A$ in that cube lie in a ball of radius $L\sqrt m\delta $ (if $L=0$, the image is a singleton). The sum of the volumes of these covering balls is at most $C\delta ^{N-m}$, tending to zero. Thus the outer measure vanishes. Intersect an unbounded domain with countably many bounded cubes to obtain the general case. $\square$ Proposition 16.14.5 (Normality does not imply rectifiability) . D93B08103DE9 The current in Example 16.14.2 is not a rectifiable two-current, even with real multiplicities. Proof The mass of a rectifiable two-current is concentrated on a countably two-rectifiable set $M$. Such a set is covered, up to an $\mathcal H^2$-null set, by countably many Lipschitz images from subsets of $\mathbb R^2$. Lemma 16.14.4 makes all these images $\mathcal L^4$-null. The remaining $\mathcal H^2$-null set is also $\mathcal L^4$-null: covers with arbitrarily small diameters satisfy $\sum _ i(\operatorname {diam}U_ i)^4\leq \delta ^2\sum _ i(\operatorname {diam}U_ i)^2$. Hence $\mathcal L^4(M)=0$. But the explicitly computed mass measure $2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$ assigns zero mass to $M$ and total mass two to $Q$. It cannot be concentrated on $M$. Thus the current is not rectifiable, despite its finite mass and finite boundary mass. $\square$ Proposition 16.14.6 (Rectifiable normal currents can converge to a diffuse current) . 7038E9854215 For each positive integer $j$, let $P_ j$ be the $j^2$ centers of the equal grid squares in $[0,1]^2$. Let $S_ p^{12}$ be the integration current of $[0,1]^2\times \{ p\} $ with orientation $e_1\wedge e_2$, and let $S_ p^{34}$ be that of $\{ p\} \times [0,1]^2$ with orientation $e_3\wedge e_4$. Then \[  T_ j=j^{-2}\sum _{p\in P_ j}(S_ p^{12}+S_ p^{34})  \] are compactly supported rectifiable normal two-currents with real multiplicities, $\mathbf M(T_ j)=2$ and $\mathbf M(\partial T_ j)=8$. They converge weakly to the nonrectifiable current $T$ of Example 16.14.2 . Their multiplicities are not integer-valued for $j>1$. Proof Each current is a finite real linear combination of oriented squares. Within each family the squares are disjoint. A square in one family intersects a square in the other in at most one point, a set of zero two-dimensional measure. Their positive mass measures therefore add and give $2j^2j^{-2}=2$. Each square has boundary mass four. The grid centers are in the interior of the transverse square, so boundary edges from the two families do not meet; within one family they are also disjoint. Thus the boundary masses add to eight. For a smooth test form $\omega $, the first-family contribution is the midpoint Riemann sum for the continuous function \[  p\longmapsto \int _{[0,1]^2}\omega _{12}(x_1,x_2,p_1,p_2)\, dx_1dx_2.  \] It converges to $\int _ Q\omega _{12}\, dx$. The second family gives $\int _ Q\omega _{34}\, dx$. Their sum is $T(\omega )$, proving weak convergence. Almost every point on any one square lies on no other square, and there the multiplicity is $j^{-2}$. For $j>1$ it is not an integer. This example is consistent with integral-current compactness: omitting integer multiplicities changes the conclusion, even with fixed compact support and uniform mass and boundary-mass bounds. $\square$ Proposition 16.14.7 (The diffuse approximation also converges in the real flat norm) . 2AAA27455AE0 For the currents $T_ j$ of Proposition 16.14.6 , the real-current flat norm of Definition 5.3.14 satisfies \[  \mathcal F_{\mathbb R}(T_ j-T)\leq \frac{5\sqrt2}{j}.  \] Thus even flat convergence, fixed compact support, and uniform mass and boundary-mass bounds do not preserve real rectifiability without an additional hypothesis. Proof For $y\in [0,1]^2$, write $S_ y^{12}$ for the corresponding oriented square, and let $p_ j(y)$ be the center of its grid cell. Values on grid boundaries may be assigned arbitrarily. The displacement is at most $\delta _ j=\sqrt2/(2j)$. Translating $S_ y^{12}$ along the segment from $y$ to $p_ j(y)$ gives the homotopy decomposition of Proposition 5.3.13 : \[  S_{p_ j(y)}^{12}-S_ y^{12}=\partial R_ y+B_ y, \qquad \mathbf M(R_ y)\leq \delta _ j, \qquad \mathbf M(B_ y)\leq 4\delta _ j.  \] Here $R_ y$ is the image of the interval product with the square, and $B_ y$ is the image of the interval product with its boundary. The estimates are exactly Proposition 5.3.17 with Lipschitz constant one, square mass one and boundary mass four. Define averaged currents by integrating their test-form evaluations over $y$. These evaluations are measurable (smooth on each cell apart from its boundary), and all supports lie in the fixed cube $Q$. The uniform mass bounds imply that the integrals define finite-mass currents $R$ and $B$, with masses at most $\delta _ j$ and $4\delta _ j$. Their boundary identity follows by evaluating $R$ on the exterior derivative of a test form and interchanging the finite integrals. The average of $S_{p_ j(y)}^{12}$ is the first-family Riemann sum, while the average of $S_ y^{12}$ is the first summand of $T$. Thus this family's difference is $\partial R+B$ and has real flat norm at most $5\delta _ j$. Repeat for the second family and add the decompositions. The total bound is $10\delta _ j=5\sqrt2/j$. No integer-coefficient filling or integer flat-norm assertion is involved. $\square$

text: Example 16.14.1 (A nonsimple bivector and its two norms) . 5584C114BE31 In oriented $\mathbb R^4$, put $\zeta =e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$. Its Euclidean norm is $\sqrt2$, while its mass norm is $2$. It is not simple. Proof The two basis bivectors are orthonormal, giving the Euclidean norm. Their individual mass norms are one, so the triangle inequality gives $|\zeta |_{\mathrm{mass}}\leq 2$. For the reverse inequality, let $\omega _0=dx^1\wedge dx^2+dx^3\wedge dx^4$. Define the orthogonal complex structure $Je_1=e_2$, $Je_2=-e_1$, $Je_3=e_4$, $Je_4=-e_3$. Then $\omega _0(u,v)=\langle Ju,v\rangle $, whose absolute value is at most one on orthonormal pairs. Equality holds at $(e_1,e_2)$, so $\omega _0$ has comass one. As $\langle \omega _0,\zeta \rangle =2$, duality gives the opposite mass bound. Finally $\zeta \wedge \zeta =2e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3\wedge e_4\ne 0$, whereas the square of a simple bivector is zero. $\square$

text: Example 16.14.2 (A diffuse finite-mass two-current) . 4B74DFD48D85 Let $Q=[0,1]^4$ and define a two-current on $\mathbb R^4$ by \[  T(\omega )=\int _ Q\bigl (\omega _{12}(x)+\omega _{34}(x)\bigr )\, dx.  \] Then $\| T\| =2\mathcal L^4\llcorner Q$, its polar bivector is $\zeta /2$, and $\mathbf M(T)=2$. title: 4.6 Measure representation for BV functions
search_title: Measure representation for BV functions
section: 4.6 Measure representation for BV functions
text: This section proves the measure representation used in Definition 4.1.1 and uses the constancy statement already proved in Lemma 6.5.1 . The source definition and representation are [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, equations (2.1)–(2.4), pp. 52–53. We retain the convention $\int u\, \operatorname {div}X=-\int X\cdot dDu$; changing the sign of a polar vector does not change its variation measure. Proposition 4.6.1 (Distributional derivatives as vector measures) . B3DA56F70CE7 Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ n$ be open. For $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, local finiteness of the variation supremum in Definition 4.1.1 is equivalent to representation of its distributional gradient by a locally finite vector-valued Radon measure. There is a Radon measure $\mu $ and a Borel vector field $\sigma $ such that \[  Du=\sigma \mu ,\qquad |\sigma |=1\quad \mu \text{-almost everywhere},\qquad \mu (W)=\sup _{\substack {X\in C_ c^1(W;\mathbb R^ n)\\ |X|\leq 1}}\int _ Wu\, \operatorname {div}X  \] for every open $W\subset U$. Thus $\mu =|Du|$ is exactly the total variation measure, including on open sets of infinite variation. Proof Define $L(X)=-\int u\, \operatorname {div}X$ on smooth compactly supported vector fields. The symmetry of the admissible tests under $X\mapsto -X$ bounds $|L(X)|$ by the local variation times $\| X\| _\infty $. Uniform approximation by smooth fields, with supports in a common compact neighborhood, extends $L$ uniquely to $C_ c(U;\mathbb R^ n)$. Independence of the approximation follows from the same local bound. Apply Theorem 5.7.4 with the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^ n$. It gives $L(X)=\int X\cdot \sigma \, d\mu $, with $|\sigma |=1$ almost everywhere. To identify the open-set supremum, note first that each admissible smooth test has $|L(X)|\leq \mu (W)$. Conversely, for $0\leq g\leq 1$ compactly supported in $W$, the positive variation functional of Lemma 5.7.3 gives \[  \int g\, d\mu =\sup \{ L(F):F\in C_ c(U;\mathbb R^ n),\  |F|\leq g\} .  \] Every such $F$ has support in $W$ and norm at most one. Extend it by zero and mollify with sufficiently small scale. Its smooth approximants stay supported in $W$, have norm at most one, and converge uniformly. Hence the original smooth supremum is at least $\int g\, d\mu $. Inner regularity and cutoff functions, exhausted over compact subsets of $W$, give the reverse inequality $\mu (W)$. The coordinate distributional identities characterize $Du$ uniquely, since smooth tests determine Radon measures. Conversely, a locally finite vector measure representing $Du$ bounds the variation on $W\Subset U$ by its total variation there. The already established representation then identifies the minimal positive dominating measure with the stated supremum. This completes the equivalence without a separate vector-valued representation theorem left external. $\square$

title: 4.7 BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
search_title: BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
section: 4.7 BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
text: The measure definition of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2, becomes particularly explicit on a bounded interval $I=(a,b)$. The proofs below develop this one-dimensional specialization directly. All endpoint traces are one-sided limits of the specified representative; arbitrary values assigned at single points have no effect on $Du$. Lemma 4.7.1 (The cumulative function of a signed measure) . 155DCE2632C6 Let $\mu $ be a finite signed Radon measure on $(a,b)$. Define $F(x)=\mu ((a,x])$. Then $F$ is bounded and right-continuous, has left limit $F(x-)=\mu ((a,x))$, and satisfies $DF=\mu $ in distributions. Its endpoint limits are $F(a+)=0$ and $F(b-)=\mu ((a,b))$. Proof The bound $|F|\leq |\mu |(I)$ is immediate. Continuity from above and below for the finite positive measure $|\mu |$ gives the asserted one-sided limits for $\mu $. For $\phi \in C_ c^1(I)$, Fubini applies to the finite product of $|\mu |$ and Lebesgue measure and gives \[  -\int _ a^ bF(x)\phi '(x)\, dx =-\int _ I\left(\int _ t^ b\phi '(x)\, dx\right)d\mu (t) =\int _ I\phi (t)\, d\mu (t).  \] This proves the distributional identity with the prescribed sign. $\square$ Theorem 4.7.2 (The regulated representative of an interval BV function) . 6B835FA933C4 For $u\in BV(I)$, with $\mu =Du$, there is a constant $c$ such that the right-continuous representative \[  u^+(x)=c+\mu ((a,x])  \] equals $u$ almost everywhere. It has left limits $u^-(x)=c+\mu ((a,x))$, finite endpoint traces, and \[  u^+(x)-u^-(x)=\mu (\{ x\} ).  \] There are at most countably many nonzero jumps. Its pointwise variation, defined by the supremum of $\sum _{j=1}^ N|u^+(x_ j)-u^+(x_{j-1})|$ over finite partitions $a<x_0<\cdots <x_ N<b$, equals $|Du|(I)$. The proof below derives the interval statement directly from the distributional BV framework of [ Sim18 ] . Proof Subtract the cumulative function in Lemma 4.7.1 . The difference has zero distributional derivative, so Lemma 6.5.1 gives the constant $c$. The one-sided limits and jump identity follow from that lemma. For every $\varepsilon >0$, at most $|\mu |(I)/\varepsilon $ points can have $|\mu (\{ x\} )|\geq \varepsilon $; a countable union gives countability. Each increment is $\mu ((x_{j-1},x_ j])$, so the variation is at most $|\mu |(I)$. For the reverse inequality, take $\psi \in C_ c(I)$ with $|\psi |\leq 1$. Choose endpoints outside its support and subdivide their compact interval into intervals of length at most $h$. Step functions constant on these half-open intervals, zero outside, approximate $\psi $ uniformly as $h\to 0$. Their integrals against $\mu $ have absolute value at most the sum of the absolute interval masses, hence at most the pointwise variation. Passing to the limit gives $|\int \psi \, d\mu |$ bounded by that variation. The continuous-test characterization of total variation in Proposition 4.6.1 , or the scalar case of its proof, gives $|\mu |(I)$ as the supremum of these integrals. This proves equality. The right-continuous representative is unique: two such representatives equal almost everywhere agree at every interior point by taking a sequence of equality points approaching from the right. $\square$ Proposition 4.7.3 (Absolute continuity and Lipschitz bounds) . EFDCA0BE54A1 For $u\in BV(I)$, its regulated representative is absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$, using its endpoint traces, if and only if $Du=f\mathcal L^1$ for some $f\in L^1(I)$. It is Lipschitz with constant at most $L$ if and only if $|Du|\leq L\mathcal L^1$ as measures on $I$. Proof If $Du=f\mathcal L^1$, Theorem 4.7.2 gives $u^+(x)=c+\int _ a^ xf(t)\, dt$. The absolute continuity of the integral and the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus give the assertion. Conversely, that theorem for absolutely continuous functions identifies the distributional derivative with the integrable classical derivative. The measure bound gives, for $x<y$, $|u^+(y)-u^+(x)|=|Du((x,y])|\leq L(y-x)$, and endpoint limits give the same bound on the closure. Conversely, a Lipschitz function is absolutely continuous with classical derivative bounded by $L$ almost everywhere, by the line differentiation result used in the Lipschitz foundations. Its derivative measure therefore has the stated domination. An absolutely continuous derivative measure here means absolute continuity relative to Lebesgue measure; it is distinct from merely having no atoms. $\square$ Theorem 4.7.4 (Finite-perimeter sets in an interval) . D5E9F98A6434 A measurable $E\subset I$ has finite perimeter in $I$ if and only if it agrees almost everywhere with a finite union of intervals relative to $I$. Choose the intervals with disjoint interiors and with no artificial common endpoint separating two occupied intervals. Then \[  D\chi _ E=\sum _{\text{interior left endpoints }\ell }\delta _\ell -\sum _{\text{interior right endpoints }r}\delta _ r,  \] and $P(E;I)$ is the number of those interior endpoints. Endpoints at $a$ or $b$ make no contribution to relative perimeter. This is a direct one-dimensional consequence of the BV definition of perimeter in [ Sim18 ] ; the proof is included below. Proof Assume finite perimeter. The right-continuous representative of $\chi _ E$ takes only values zero and one: approach any point from the right through points where it agrees with the original characteristic function. The left limits also take only these values. Every nonzero jump consequently has size one in absolute value. There are finitely many such jumps, since their total absolute mass is at most $P(E;I)$. Away from those finitely many points the representative is continuous: the two one-sided limits agree with its value. On each intervening interval, a continuous function with values in $\{ 0,1\} $ is constant. Thus $E$ is almost everywhere a finite union of occupied intervals. Its derivative there is exactly the displayed sum, by integration of a test derivative on each interval. The positive and negative endpoint atoms have distinct supports after the stated merging, so total variation counts them. Conversely, that same computation for any finite union produces a finite derivative measure and hence finite perimeter. In particular the empty set and the whole interval both have relative perimeter zero. $\square$ Proposition 4.7.5 (Zero extension and endpoint traces) . 33F783392B7C Let $u\in BV(a,b)$ and extend it by zero to $\widetilde u\in L^1(\mathbb R)$. Then \[  D\widetilde u=(Du)\lfloor (a,b)+u(a+)\delta _ a-u(b-)\delta _ b,  \] where the first term means the derivative measure extended by zero. Consequently \[  |D\widetilde u|(\mathbb R)=|Du|((a,b))+|u(a+)|+|u(b-)|.  \] Proof Use the representation $u(x)=c+\mu ((a,x])$ almost everywhere. For $\phi \in C_ c^1(\mathbb R)$, Fubini as in Lemma 4.7.1 , now retaining the endpoint term, gives \[  -\int _ a^ bu\phi ' =\int _{(a,b)}\phi \, d\mu +c\phi (a)-(c+\mu ((a,b)))\phi (b).  \] The two coefficients are the endpoint traces. text: Lemma 4.7.1 (The cumulative function of a signed measure) . 155DCE2632C6 Let $\mu $ be a finite signed Radon measure on $(a,b)$. Define $F(x)=\mu ((a,x])$. Then $F$ is bounded and right-continuous, has left limit $F(x-)=\mu ((a,x))$, and satisfies $DF=\mu $ in distributions. Its endpoint limits are $F(a+)=0$ and $F(b-)=\mu ((a,b))$. Proof The bound $|F|\leq |\mu |(I)$ is immediate. Continuity from above and below for the finite positive measure $|\mu |$ gives the asserted one-sided limits for $\mu $. For $\phi \in C_ c^1(I)$, Fubini applies to the finite product of $|\mu |$ and Lebesgue measure and gives \[  -\int _ a^ bF(x)\phi '(x)\, dx =-\int _ I\left(\int _ t^ b\phi '(x)\, dx\right)d\mu (t) =\int _ I\phi (t)\, d\mu (t).  \] This proves the distributional identity with the prescribed sign. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.7.2 (The regulated representative of an interval BV function)

section: 4.7 BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
text: Theorem 4.7.2 (The regulated representative of an interval BV function) . 6B835FA933C4 For $u\in BV(I)$, with $\mu =Du$, there is a constant $c$ such that the right-continuous representative \[  u^+(x)=c+\mu ((a,x])  \] equals $u$ almost everywhere. It has left limits $u^-(x)=c+\mu ((a,x))$, finite endpoint traces, and \[  u^+(x)-u^-(x)=\mu (\{ x\} ).  \] There are at most countably many nonzero jumps. Its pointwise variation, defined by the supremum of $\sum _{j=1}^ N|u^+(x_ j)-u^+(x_{j-1})|$ over finite partitions $a<x_0<\cdots <x_ N<b$, equals $|Du|(I)$. The proof below derives the interval statement directly from the distributional BV framework of [ Sim18 ] . Proof Subtract the cumulative function in Lemma 4.7.1 . The difference has zero distributional derivative, so Lemma 6.5.1 gives the constant $c$. The one-sided limits and jump identity follow from that lemma. For every $\varepsilon >0$, at most $|\mu |(I)/\varepsilon $ points can have $|\mu (\{ x\} )|\geq \varepsilon $; a countable union gives countability. Each increment is $\mu ((x_{j-1},x_ j])$, so the variation is at most $|\mu |(I)$. For the reverse inequality, take $\psi \in C_ c(I)$ with $|\psi |\leq 1$. Choose endpoints outside its support and subdivide their compact interval into intervals of length at most $h$. Step functions constant on these half-open intervals, zero outside, approximate $\psi $ uniformly as $h\to 0$. Their integrals against $\mu $ have absolute value at most the sum of the absolute interval masses, hence at most the pointwise variation. Passing to the limit gives $|\int \psi \, d\mu |$ bounded by that variation. The continuous-test characterization of total variation in Proposition 4.6.1 , or the scalar case of its proof, gives $|\mu |(I)$ as the supremum of these integrals. This proves equality. The right-continuous representative is unique: two such representatives equal almost everywhere agree at every interior point by taking a sequence of equality points approaching from the right. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.7.3 (Absolute continuity and Lipschitz bounds)
search_title: Absolute continuity and Lipschitz bounds
section: 4.7 BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
text: Proposition 4.7.3 (Absolute continuity and Lipschitz bounds) . EFDCA0BE54A1 For $u\in BV(I)$, its regulated representative is absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$, using its endpoint traces, if and only if $Du=f\mathcal L^1$ for some $f\in L^1(I)$. It is Lipschitz with constant at most $L$ if and only if $|Du|\leq L\mathcal L^1$ as measures on $I$. Proof If $Du=f\mathcal L^1$, Theorem 4.7.2 gives $u^+(x)=c+\int _ a^ xf(t)\, dt$. The absolute continuity of the integral and the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus give the assertion. Conversely, that theorem for absolutely continuous functions identifies the distributional derivative with the integrable classical derivative. The measure bound gives, for $x<y$, $|u^+(y)-u^+(x)|=|Du((x,y])|\leq L(y-x)$, and endpoint limits give the same bound on the closure. Conversely, a Lipschitz function is absolutely continuous with classical derivative bounded by $L$ almost everywhere, by the line differentiation result used in the Lipschitz foundations. Its derivative measure therefore has the stated domination. An absolutely continuous derivative measure here means absolute continuity relative to Lebesgue measure; it is distinct from merely having no atoms. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.7.4 (Finite-perimeter sets in an interval)
search_title: Finite-perimeter sets in an interval
section: 4.7 BV representatives and perimeter on an interval
text: Theorem 4.7.4 (Finite-perimeter sets in an interval) . D5E9F98A6434 A measurable $E\subset I$ has finite perimeter in $I$ if and only if it agrees almost everywhere with a finite union of intervals relative to $I$. Choose the intervals with disjoint interiors and with no artificial common endpoint separating two occupied intervals. Then \[  D\chi _ E=\sum _{\text{interior left endpoints }\ell }\delta _\ell -\sum _{\text{interior right endpoints }r}\delta _ r,  \] and $P(E;I)$ is the number of those interior endpoints. Endpoints at $a$ or $b$ make no contribution to relative perimeter. This is a direct one-dimensional consequence of the BV definition of perimeter in [ Sim18 ] ; the proof is included below. Proof Assume finite perimeter. The right-continuous representative of $\chi _ E$ takes only values zero and one: approach any point from the right through points where it agrees with the original characteristic function. The left limits also take only these values. Every nonzero jump consequently has size one in absolute value. There are finitely many such jumps, since their total absolute mass is at most $P(E;I)$. Away from those finitely many points the representative is continuous: the two one-sided limits agree with its value. On each intervening interval, a continuous function with values in $\{ 0,1\} $ is constant. Thus $E$ is almost everywhere a finite union of occupied intervals. Its derivative there is exactly the displayed sum, by integration of a test derivative on each interval. The positive and negative endpoint atoms have distinct supports after the stated merging, so total variation counts them. Conversely, that same computation for any finite union produces a finite derivative measure and hence finite perimeter. In particular the empty set and the whole interval both have relative perimeter zero. $\square$

title: 4.8 Products and nonlinear jumps in one-dimensional BV
search_title: Products and nonlinear jumps in one-dimensional BV
section: 4.8 Products and nonlinear jumps in one-dimensional BV
text: Let $I=(a,b)$ be bounded. We use the right-continuous representatives and left limits from Theorem 4.7.2 . The measure framework is that of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Section 2; the partition arguments below give explicit one-dimensional proofs of the calculus formulas. At a jump, evaluating an ordinary derivative at only one side generally gives the wrong coefficient. Theorem 4.8.1 (The divided-difference chain rule on an interval) . 24962712EC88 Let $u\in BV(I)$ and $\Phi \in C^1(\mathbb R)$. Then $\Phi (u)\in BV(I)$ and \[  D(\Phi (u))=K_\Phi (u^-,u^+)\, Du, \qquad K_\Phi (s,t)=\int _0^1\Phi '((1-\theta )s+\theta t)\, d\theta .  \] Equivalently $K_\Phi (s,t)=(\Phi (t)-\Phi (s))/(t-s)$ for $s\ne t$, and $K_\Phi (s,s)=\Phi '(s)$. In particular, at a jump point $x$ the new atom has mass $\Phi (u^+(x))-\Phi (u^-(x))$. Away from the countable jump set the coefficient equals $\Phi '(u^+(x))$. We prove this one-dimensional formula directly from the measure formulation of BV in [ Sim18 ] , including its jump and singular-continuous parts. Proof The regulated representative of $u$ is bounded. On an interval containing its range, $\Phi '$ is bounded; extend the restriction of $\Phi $ to a globally Lipschitz function. Proposition 4.4.6 , together with boundedness of $I$ and the composition, gives $\Phi (u)\in BV(I)$. Its right-continuous representative is $\Phi (u^+)$. The integral defining $K_\Phi $ shows that it is continuous and bounded on the compact square containing all one-sided values. Fix $a<s<t<b$ and take partitions $s=x_0<\cdots <x_ N=t$ with mesh tending to zero. Write $u_ i=u^+(x_ i)$ and $\mu =Du$. Telescoping and the interval representation give \[  \Phi (u^+(t))-\Phi (u^+(s)) =\sum _ iK_\Phi (u_{i-1},u_ i)\mu ((x_{i-1},x_ i]).  \] Regard the coefficients as a bounded step function on $(s,t]$. For each fixed $r$ in that interval, the upper endpoint of its half-open cell tends to $r$ from the right or equals $r$, and the lower endpoint tends to $r$ strictly from the left. Therefore the corresponding values converge to $u^+(r)$ and $u^-(r)$. Continuity of $K_\Phi $ and dominated convergence with respect to the finite measure $|\mu |$ yield \[  \Phi (u^+(t))-\Phi (u^+(s)) =\int _{(s,t]}K_\Phi (u^-,u^+)\, d\mu .  \] The left side is $D(\Phi (u))((s,t])$ by Theorem 4.7.2 . Equality on these half-open intervals determines the finite signed measure on $I$, by exhaustion and the uniqueness of a measure on its interval generators. Multiplying the coefficient at an atom by $Du(\{ x\} )=u^+(x)-u^-(x)$ gives the asserted jump mass. $\square$ Proposition 4.8.2 (The midpoint product rule) . AAACCD4144D2 For $u,v\in BV(I)$ define $\overline u=(u^-+u^+)/2$ and $\overline v=(v^-+v^+)/2$. Then $uv\in BV(I)$ and \[  D(uv)=\overline u\, Dv+\overline v\, Du.  \] One also has the asymmetric formula $D(uv)=u^+Dv+v^-Du$; the symmetric formula makes the role of simultaneous jumps explicit. Proof Boundedness of the representatives implies \[  \operatorname {Var}(u^+v^+;I) \leq \| u^+\| _\infty \operatorname {Var}(v^+;I) +\| v^+\| _\infty \operatorname {Var}(u^+;I).  \] Alternatively, membership in $BV$ follows from $uv=((u+v)^2-(u-v)^2)/4$ and Theorem 4.8.1 . Apply that theorem to the squares: $D(w^2)=(w^-+w^+)Dw=2\overline w\, Dw$. Linearity of $D$ and of the midpoint representative gives the symmetric formula. To compare the asymmetric formula, their difference is \[  \tfrac 12(u^+-u^-)Dv-\tfrac 12(v^+-v^-)Du.  \] Both coefficient functions vanish off their countable jump sets. A nonatomic part of either finite measure gives zero mass to that countable union. At a point $x$, the atom of the first term is $\tfrac 12\Delta u(x)\Delta v(x)$, exactly the atom of the second. Thus the measures cancel. This verification includes common jump points and does not assume either function continuous. $\square$ Corollary 4.8.3 (Stieltjes integration by parts with traces) . 87F88951FED0 For $u,v\in BV(a,b)$, \[  \int _{(a,b)}\overline u\, dDv+\int _{(a,b)}\overline v\, dDu =u(b-)v(b-)-u(a+)v(a+).  \] In particular, for $\phi \in C^1([a,b])$, \[  \int _{(a,b)}\phi \, dDu+\int _ a^ bu\phi '\, dx =u(b-)\phi (b)-u(a+)\phi (a).  \] Proof The total mass of $Dw$ for an interval BV function is $w(b-)-w(a+)$ by its cumulative representation. Apply this to $w=uv$ in Proposition 4.8.2 . The bounded midpoint representatives are Borel, so both integrals against finite signed measures are well defined. For smooth $\phi $, its two one-sided representatives agree, $D\phi =\phi '\mathcal L^1$, and $\overline u=u$ almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure. This gives the second formula with the stated signs. $\square$ Example 4.8.4 (Squaring a singular-continuous function) . 691370FB4A4D Let $C$ be the Cantor function on $(0,1)$. Then \[  D(C^2)=2C\, \mu _ C,  \] a singular-continuous positive measure of total mass one. In particular $\int C\, d\mu _ C=1/2$. Proof The function $C$ is continuous, with $DC=\mu _ C$ by Example 16.1.11 . Theorem 4.8.1 therefore reduces to the coefficient $2C$ everywhere. The derivative is singular because it is supported on the Cantor set, and nonatomic because $\mu _ C$ is nonatomic. It is positive since $C\geq 0$. Its mass equals $C(1-)^2-C(0+)^2=1$ by the trace identity, yielding the integral. This also provides the variation of $C^2$ without replacing its derivative by the almost-everywhere classical derivative, which vanishes off the Cantor set. $\square$ Example 4.8.5 (Why a one-sided derivative is wrong at a jump) . 531B009B734F For $0<c<1$, set $u=\chi _{[c,1)}$ on $(0,1)$. Then $Du=\delta _ c$ and $D(u^ k)=\delta _ c$ for every integer $k\geq 1$. For $k=2$, the formula $2u^+Du$ would instead give $2\delta _ c$, and $2u^-Du$ would give zero. For $k=3$, evaluating the ordinary derivative at the midpoint would give $\tfrac 34\delta _ c$, also incorrect. Proof The function takes only the values zero and one, so $u^ k=u$. Its single jump is from zero to one. The chain coefficient for $\Phi (s)=s^ k$ is the divided difference $K_\Phi (0,1)=1$, as in Theorem 4.8.1 . For a square this happens to equal $2(0+1)/2$, explaining the midpoint product rule. For a cube the value of $\Phi '$ at $1/2$ is $3/4$, whereas its average along the whole jump is $\int _0^13\theta ^2\, d\theta =1$. Thus the general nonlinear rule needs that average, not a single chosen value of the classical derivative. $\square$

u /\lambda  igr )(V)=\Pi dX(V)-dX(AV)/\lambda =0.  \] Therefore $\Pi X-

u angle +1/\lambda .  \] The left side and last term are constant. Replacing a normal direction by its opposite gives $C=0$, and then $\lambda ^2=1/(2k)$. This is the claimed radius. text: Proposition 14.17.3 (Finite Gaussian area forces parallel curvature at the gap) . 66389D683640 Suppose $\Sigma $ is complete and boundaryless, $\int _\Sigma \rho \, d\mu <\infty $, and $|A|^2\leq 1/2$. Then $\nabla A=0$ and $(1-2|A|^2)|A|^2=0$ everywhere. On each connected component, $|A|^2$ is identically zero or identically $1/2$. Proof Fix a point in a component. title: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension

section: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension
text:
These examples use the vector convention $\vec H=\operatorname {tr}B=\Delta X=-X^\perp /2$ for a smooth Euclidean immersion $X:M^ n	o \mathbb R^ N$, where $n\geq 1$. Thus the squared curvature is $|B|^2=\sum _{i,j}|B(e_ i,e_ j)|^2$. The primary models are [ CL12 ] , Section 5, pp. 8–9, rescaled from that paper's convention $\vec H=-X^\perp $. The scalar hypersurface formulas of Section 14.17 cannot simply be used for a higher-rank normal bundle. Proposition 16.15.1 (Minimal submanifolds of a sphere give shrinkers) . F8D9EB520CEE Let $X:M^ n	o S^{N-1}(R)\subset \mathbb R^ N$, $n\geq 1$ and $R>0$, be a smooth immersion. It is a Euclidean self-shrinker if and only if $R=\sqrt{2n}$ and it is minimal in that sphere. For this radius, \[  |B^{\mathbb R^ N}|^2=|B^{S^{N-1}(R)}|^2+ rac12.  \] Proof The sphere's vector second fundamental form in Euclidean space is $-(1/R^2)gX$. Decomposing the ambient derivative first relative to $M$ in the sphere and then relative to the sphere in Euclidean space gives \[  B^{\mathbb R^ N}_{ij}=B^{S^{N-1}(R)}_{ij}- rac{\delta _{ij}}{R^2}X, \qquad \vec H^{\mathbb R^ N}=\vec H^{S^{N-1}(R)}- rac n{R^2}X.  \] The two normal summands are perpendicular. Also $X^\perp =X$, since $|X|$ is constant. The equation $\vec H^{\mathbb R^ N}=-X/2$ therefore says separately that the spherical mean curvature vanishes and $n/R^2=1/2$. Squaring the orthogonal decomposition of $B$ gives the norm identity, since the radial summand has squared norm $n/R^2=1/2$. $\square$ Example 16.15.2 (Products of round factors and a Euclidean factor) . 1069828FDBF6 Let $p\geq 1$, $d_1,\ldots ,d_ p\geq 1$ and $q\geq 0$ be integers, and put $m=\sum _ i d_ i$, $n=m+q$. The embedded product \[  M=\prod _{i=1}^ p S^{d_ i}(\sqrt{2d_ i})	imes \mathbb R^ q\subset \mathbb R^{n+p}  \] is a complete proper self-shrinker. Its curvature satisfies $|B|^2=p/2$ and $|\vec H|^2=m/2$. It has polynomial area growth, is compact exactly when $q=0$, and in that case is minimal in $S^{n+p-1}(\sqrt{2n})$. Proof For arbitrary radii $r_ i$, the mean-curvature vector has $i$th spherical block $-d_ iX_ i/r_ i^2$ and zero Euclidean block. The normal projection of $X=(X_1,\ldots ,X_ p,y)$ is $(X_1,\ldots ,X_ p,0)$. Thus the shrinker equation holds exactly when $r_ i^2=2d_ i$ for every $i$. The different radial normals are orthogonal, so \[  |B|^2=\sum _ i rac{d_ i}{r_ i^2}=p/2, \qquad |\vec H|^2=\sum _ i rac{d_ i^2}{r_ i^2}=m/2.  \] A product of complete round metrics and a Euclidean metric is complete. Compactness of the spherical factors and boundedness of the Euclidean coordinate on ambient compact sets prove properness. The portion in an ambient ball is bounded by the product of the total spherical volumes and a radius-$R$ Euclidean ball volume, hence has growth at most $C(1+R)^ q$. When $q=0$, the squared ambient radius is $\sum _ i2d_ i=2n$ and Proposition 16.15.1 proves spherical minimality. Compare [ CL12 ] , Examples 5.1–5.2. $\square$ Proposition 16.15.3 (Gaussian area of the product models) . A67A81338F21 Write $\sigma _ d=\mathcal H^ d(S^ d(1))$. The normalized Gaussian area of Example 16.15.2 is \[  F_{0,1}(M)=\prod _{i=1}^ p\left[(4\pi )^{-d_ i/2}e^{-d_ i/2}\sigma _{d_ i}(2d_ i)^{d_ i/2}ight].  \] It is independent of the dimension $q$ of the Euclidean factor. Proof The product area element factors, and $|X|^2=2\sum _ i d_ i+|y|^2$. Tonelli's theorem separates the positive Gaussian integral into the spherical factors and \[  (4\pi )^{-q/2}\int _{\mathbb R^ q}e^{-|y|^2/4}\, dy=1.  \] The radius-$\sqrt{2d_ i}$ sphere has area $\sigma _{d_ i}(2d_ i)^{d_ i/2}$, on which the Gaussian exponential is the constant $e^{-d_ i/2}$. Multiplying gives the formula. The statement computes Gaussian area at center zero and scale one; it does not invoke a separate theorem identifying an entropy supremum over all centers and scales. $\square$ Example 16.15.4 (The Clifford torus shrinker in four dimensions) . 2E92C8C6AAA0 The map \[  X(	heta ,\varphi )=(\sqrt2\cos 	heta ,\sqrt2\sin 	heta , \sqrt2\cos \varphi ,\sqrt2\sin \varphi )  \] on $(\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2$ is a flat embedded torus in $\mathbb R^4$ with $|B|^2=1$, $|\vec H|^2=1$, area $8\pi ^2$ and $F_{0,1}=2\pi /e$. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$, where its squared second fundamental form is $1/2$. Proof The metric is $2(d	heta ^2+d\varphi ^2)$, so it is flat with area $8\pi ^2$. Apply Example 16.15.2 with two circle factors. Since $|X|^2=4$, direct substitution gives $F_{0,1}=(4\pi )^{-1}e^{-1}8\pi ^2=2\pi /e$. Proposition 16.15.1 subtracts $1/2$ from the Euclidean curvature norm to give the spherical value. This is a codimension-two shrinker and its Euclidean curvature exceeds the hypersurface gap threshold. $\square$ Proposition 16.15.5 (The compact mean-curvature threshold) . 5BF54675E5EE On every connected closed Euclidean self-shrinker $M^ n$, in any codimension, \[   rac1{\operatorname {Vol}(M)}\int _ M|\vec H|^2\, d\mu = rac n2.  \] If $|\vec H|^2$ is everywhere at most $n/2$, everywhere at least $n/2$, or constant, then the image lies in $S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ and is minimal there. See [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.2, for the source normalization. Proof The immersion identities give \[  \Delta |X|^2=2n+2\langle X,\vec Hangle =2n-4|\vec H|^2.  \] Integrating on a closed manifold gives the average identity. Each stated pointwise condition forces $|\vec H|^2=n/2$ everywhere, so $|X|^2$ is harmonic and hence constant on the connected compact manifold. It follows that $X^ T=
abla |X|^2/2=0$. The shrinker equation now gives $|X|^2=4|\vec H|^2=2n$, and Proposition 16.15.1 gives spherical minimality. This conclusion does not say that an arbitrary-codimension example is a round hypersphere. $\square$ Proposition 16.15.6 (There is no closed Euclidean self-expander) . 3A94265F2B89 For $n\geq 1$, no nonempty closed immersed $n$-manifold in Euclidean space satisfies $\vec H=X^\perp /2$, in any codimension. Proof For an expander the same immersion calculation gives $\Delta |X|^2=2n+|X^\perp |^2>0$. Its integral on a closed manifold would be positive, whereas the divergence theorem makes that integral zero. This proves the contradiction and the observation in [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.3, directly with the present normalization. $\square$ Lemma 16.15.7 (The Gaussian radial identity in any codimension) . 36F00EED1081 Let $X:M^ n	o \mathbb R^ N$ be a connected complete smooth boundaryless self-shrinker with polynomial area growth, counting area on the parameter manifold. With $ho =(4\pi )^{-n/2}e^{-|X|^2/4}$, \[  \int _ M |X|^2ho \, d\mu =2n\int _ Mho \, d\mu .  \] Neither a global unit normal nor hypersurface codimension is required. Proof The identities $\Delta X=\vec H=-X^\perp /2$ and $|DX|^2=n$ give $\Delta |X|^2=2n-|X^\perp |^2$. Since $
abla |X|^2=2X^ T$, subtraction of the Gaussian drift gives \[  \mathcal D|X|^2=2n-|X|^2,\qquad \mathcal D=\Delta -	frac 12
abla _{X^ T} =ho ^{-1}\operatorname {div}(ho 
abla \, \cdot \, ).  \] Polynomial area growth implies integrability of $(1+|X|^2)ho $ by exactly the annular estimate in Lemma 14.7.4 ; that estimate uses only area, not codimension. Take intrinsic compact cutoffs $\eta _ R$ equal to one on a radius-$R$ ball, zero outside radius $2R$, with $|
abla \eta _ R|\leq 2/R$. Completeness supplies compact support. Weighted integration by parts gives \[  \int \eta _ R(2n-|X|^2)ho =-\int \langle 
abla \eta _ R,2X^ Tangle ho .  \] The right side has absolute value at most $(4/R)\int |X|ho $, tending to zero. Dominated convergence gives the conclusion on the left. This explicitly extends the hypersurface computation instead of invoking a hypersurface statement for a higher-codimension immersion. $\square$ Proposition 16.15.8 (A complete mean-curvature bound forces spherical containment) . 97FDF140143F Under the hypotheses of Lemma 16.15.7 , assume $|\vec H|^2\geq n/2$ everywhere. Then $|\vec H|^2=n/2$, $X^ T=0$, and the immersed image is a minimal submanifold of $S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$. This is the rescaled assertion of [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.1. It does not classify all minimal submanifolds of that sphere. Proof The shrinker equation gives the pointwise identity \[  |X|^2=|X^ T|^2+4|\vec H|^2\geq 2n.  \] The preceding lemma says that its Gaussian average is exactly $2n$. The nonnegative continuous function $|X|^2-2n$ therefore has zero weighted integral and vanishes everywhere. Both nonnegative terms in $|X^ T|^2+4(|\vec H|^2-n/2)=0$ vanish. The fixed-radius criterion in Proposition 16.15.1 now gives spherical minimality. The Euclidean-factor models of Example 16.15.2 , with $q>0$, have $|\vec H|^2=(n-q)/2<n/2$ and unbounded image, showing why that lower threshold cannot simply be omitted. $\square$

The normalized Gaussian area of Example 16.15.2 is \[  F_{0,1}(M)=\prod _{i=1}^ p\left[(4\pi )^{-d_ i/2}e^{-d_ i/2}\sigma _{d_ i}(2d_ i)^{d_ i/2}\right].  \] It is independent of the dimension $q$ of the Euclidean factor. Tonelli's theorem separates the positive Gaussian integral into the spherical factors and \[  (4\pi )^{-q/2}\int _{\mathbb R^ q}e^{-|y|^2/4}\, dy=1.  \] The radius-$\sqrt{2d_ i}$ sphere has area $\sigma _{d_ i}(2d_ i)^{d_ i/2}$, on which the Gaussian exponential is the constant $e^{-d_ i/2}$. Multiplying gives the formula. The statement computes Gaussian area at center zero and scale one; it does not invoke a separate theorem identifying an entropy supremum over all centers and scales. $\square$

title: Example 16.15.4 (The Clifford torus shrinker in four dimensions)
search_title: The Clifford torus shrinker in four dimensions
section: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension
text: Example 16.15.4 (The Clifford torus shrinker in four dimensions) . 2E92C8C6AAA0 The map \[  X(\theta ,\varphi )=(\sqrt2\cos \theta ,\sqrt2\sin \theta , \sqrt2\cos \varphi ,\sqrt2\sin \varphi )  \] on $(\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2$ is a flat embedded torus in $\mathbb R^4$ with $|B|^2=1$, $|\vec H|^2=1$, area $8\pi ^2$ and $F_{0,1}=2\pi /e$. It is minimal in $S^3(2)$, where its squared second fundamental form is $1/2$. Proof The metric is $2(d\theta ^2+d\varphi ^2)$, so it is flat with area $8\pi ^2$. Apply Example 16.15.2 with two circle factors. Since $|X|^2=4$, direct substitution gives $F_{0,1}=(4\pi )^{-1}e^{-1}8\pi ^2=2\pi /e$. Proposition 16.15.1 subtracts $1/2$ from the Euclidean curvature norm to give the spherical value. This is a codimension-two shrinker and its Euclidean curvature exceeds the hypersurface gap threshold. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.15.5 (The compact mean-curvature threshold)
search_title: The compact mean-curvature threshold
section: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension
text: Proposition 16.15.5 (The compact mean-curvature threshold) . 5BF54675E5EE On every connected closed Euclidean self-shrinker $M^ n$, in any codimension, \[  \frac1{\operatorname {Vol}(M)}\int _ M|\vec H|^2\, d\mu =\frac n2.  \] If $|\vec H|^2$ is everywhere at most $n/2$, everywhere at least $n/2$, or constant, then the image lies in $S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$ and is minimal there. See [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.2, for the source normalization. Proof The immersion identities give \[  \Delta |X|^2=2n+2\langle X,\vec H\rangle =2n-4|\vec H|^2.  \] Integrating on a closed manifold gives the average identity. Each stated pointwise condition forces $|\vec H|^2=n/2$ everywhere, so $|X|^2$ is harmonic and hence constant on the connected compact manifold. It follows that $X^ T=\nabla |X|^2/2=0$. The shrinker equation now gives $|X|^2=4|\vec H|^2=2n$, and Proposition 16.15.1 gives spherical minimality. This conclusion does not say that an arbitrary-codimension example is a round hypersphere. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.15.6 (There is no closed Euclidean self-expander)
search_title: There is no closed Euclidean self-expander
section: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension
text: Proposition 16.15.6 (There is no closed Euclidean self-expander) . 3A94265F2B89 For $n\geq 1$, no nonempty closed immersed $n$-manifold in Euclidean space satisfies $\vec H=X^\perp /2$, in any codimension. Proof For an expander the same immersion calculation gives $\Delta |X|^2=2n+|X^\perp |^2>0$. Its integral on a closed manifold would be positive, whereas the divergence theorem makes that integral zero. This proves the contradiction and the observation in [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.3, directly with the present normalization. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.15.8 (A complete mean-curvature bound forces spherical containment)
search_title: A complete mean-curvature bound forces spherical containment
section: 16.15 Self-shrinkers in higher codimension
text: Proposition 16.15.8 (A complete mean-curvature bound forces spherical containment) . 97FDF140143F Under the hypotheses of Lemma 16.15.7 , assume $|\vec H|^2\geq n/2$ everywhere. Then $|\vec H|^2=n/2$, $X^ T=0$, and the immersed image is a minimal submanifold of $S^{N-1}(\sqrt{2n})$. This is the rescaled assertion of [ CL12 ] , Proposition 5.1. It does not classify all minimal submanifolds of that sphere. Proof The shrinker equation gives the pointwise identity \[  |X|^2=|X^ T|^2+4|\vec H|^2\geq 2n.  \] The preceding lemma says that its Gaussian average is exactly $2n$. The nonnegative continuous function $|X|^2-2n$ therefore has zero weighted integral and vanishes everywhere. Both nonnegative terms in $|X^ T|^2+4(|\vec H|^2-n/2)=0$ vanish. The fixed-radius criterion in Proposition 16.15.1 now gives spherical minimality. The Euclidean-factor models of Example 16.15.2 , with $q>0$, have $|\vec H|^2=(n-q)/2<n/2$ and unbounded image, showing why that lower threshold cannot simply be omitted. $\square$

title: 16.16 Jumps, representatives, and boundary traces
search_title: Jumps, representatives, and boundary traces
section: 16.16 Jumps, representatives, and boundary traces
text: These examples supplement the singular-continuous model in Example 16.1.11 . They use the exact interval representation of Section 4.7 to distinguish a function's almost-everywhere class, its canonical representative, and its endpoint traces. Example 16.16.1 (A BV function with dense jumps) . CBACB926FFB5 Enumerate the rationals in $(0,1)$ without repetition as $q_1,q_2,\ldots $ and set \[  u(x)=\sum _{j=1}^\infty 2^{-j}\chi _{[q_ j,1)}(x),\qquad 0<x<1.  \] Then $u$ is right-continuous, strictly increasing and in $BV(0,1)$, with \[  Du=\sum _{j=1}^\infty 2^{-j}\delta _{q_ j},\qquad |Du|((0,1))=1.  \] It jumps by $2^{-j}$ at $q_ j$ and is continuous at every irrational point. Its endpoint traces are zero and one. Proof The series converges uniformly by the summable bounds. The measure $\mu =\sum _ j2^{-j}\delta _{q_ j}$ is a Radon probability measure by the summable-tail argument of Example 16.1.1 , now enumerating only interior rationals. The displayed function is its cumulative function; Lemma 4.7.1 gives its derivative, one-sided continuity and traces. Every nonempty interval contains a rational carrying positive mass, so every increment between distinct points is strictly positive. The atom formula in Theorem 4.7.2 gives the jumps. At an irrational point the measure has no atom, so the left and right limits agree. Thus dense discontinuities are compatible with finite total variation; their amplitudes must be summable. $\square$ Example 16.16.2 (Pointwise variation depends on the representative) . 78C1D3DF08E9 The function $u=\chi _{\mathbb Q\cap (0,1)}$ is zero almost everywhere, belongs to $BV(0,1)$ and has distributional variation zero. As a specified pointwise function it has infinite classical variation. Its canonical right-continuous BV representative is identically zero. Proof Countability makes the rationals Lebesgue null, so all distributional pairings agree with those of zero. To obtain arbitrarily large pointwise variation, choose an arbitrarily long increasing sequence alternating between rational and irrational points, possible by density of both sets. Every successive function increment has absolute value one. The regulated representative theorem applies to the almost-everywhere class and gives the zero representative; it does not assign finite classical variation to every null modification of that class. $\square$ Example 16.16.3 (A boundary layer can retain a trace while disappearing in the interior) . 3A54E25A86CC Let $u_ j=\chi _{(0,1/j)}$ on $I=(0,1)$, $j\geq 2$. Then $u_ j\to 0$ in $L^1(I)$, $|Du_ j|(I)=1$, and $Du_ j\rightharpoonup 0$ against compactly supported continuous tests in $I$. Yet $u_ j(0+)=1$ for every $j$. The zero extensions to $\mathbb R$ have derivative $\delta _0-\delta _{1/j}$ and total variation two. Proof The $L^1$ norm is $1/j$. Within the open interval there is only the right endpoint, so $Du_ j=-\delta _{1/j}$ by Theorem 4.7.4 . Every compact support stays away from zero and eventually misses that atom. The interior right trace at zero is one. Proposition 4.7.5 adds the missing boundary atom $\delta _0$, whose support is distinct from $1/j$. The example shows that an $L^1$ limit with uniformly bounded variation does not alone preserve boundary traces. $\square$ Example 16.16.4 (Three derivative types in one BV function) . 49385BB539FF Let $C$ be the Cantor distribution function on $[0,1]$, and let $0<c<1$. The function $u(x)=x+C(x)+\chi _{[c,1)}(x)$ on $(0,1)$ is in $BV(0,1)$ and \[  Du=\mathcal L^1\lfloor (0,1)+\mu _ C\lfloor (0,1)+\delta _ c, \qquad |Du|((0,1))=3.  \] Its absolutely continuous, singular-continuous and atomic summands are mutually singular, even when $c$ belongs to the Cantor set. Proof Differentiate each summand in distributions, using Example 16.1.11 and the interval endpoint formula. The Cantor measure is singular to Lebesgue measure and has no atoms, including at the endpoints and at $c$. All three measures are positive of mass one, so their sum has total variation three. Nonatomicity lets one remove $c$ from a full-measure support of the Cantor part to obtain disjoint carriers for the three types. This also shows why absence of jumps does not by itself imply absolute continuity. $\square$

title: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
search_title: A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
section: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
text: We solve the normalized obstacle problem in a ball, with obstacle zero and constant boundary height. The normalization is [ Fig18 ] , equation (5.2), p. 9, and Definition 13.3.4 ; the explicit radial computations below illustrate that equation and the regular and singular models of Sections 7.1–7.2 of the source. Proposition 16.17.1 (A radial profile with a prescribed contact ball) . 3A54999BC942 Let $n\geq 2$ and $a>0$. Put $U_ a(r)=0$ for $0\leq r\leq a$ and, for $r>a$, set \[  U_ a(r)=\int _ a^ r\frac{s^ n-a^ n}{ns^{n-1}}\, ds.  \] Then $u_ a(x)=U_ a(|x|)$ is a globally $C^{1,1}$ normalized obstacle solution on $\mathbb R^ n$, with contact set $\overline B_ a$ and positivity outside that ball. Explicitly, \[  U_ a(r)=\begin{cases}  \dfrac {r^2-a^2}{4}-\dfrac {a^2}{2}\log (r/a),& n=2,\\[4pt] \dfrac {r^2-a^2}{2n}+\dfrac {a^ n}{n(n-2)}(r^{2-n}-a^{2-n}),& n>2 \end{cases}\qquad (r>a).  \] Proof The radial equation is $(r^{n-1}U')'=r^{n-1}$. Integrating with $U'(a)=0$ gives $U'(r)=(r^ n-a^ n)/(nr^{n-1})$, and a second integration with $U(a)=0$ gives the stated formulas. For $r>a$ the derivative is positive, so the contact set is exactly the closed ball. The tangential and radial eigenvalues of its Hessian there are \[  \frac{U_ a'}r=\frac1n\left(1-(a/r)^ n\right),\qquad U_ a''=\frac1n+\frac{n-1}{n}(a/r)^ n.  \] They lie in $[0,1]$ and have sum, with tangential multiplicity $n-1$, equal to one. On the contact ball the gradient and Hessian vanish. Since $U_ a(a)=U_ a'(a)=0$, the gradient is continuous across the sphere and no surface measure appears in its distributional derivative. Its bounded weak Hessian makes the gradient globally Lipschitz, with bound one. The function is therefore $C^{1,1}$ and has Laplacian equal to one outside contact and zero inside, as required. It is not $C^2$ across the sphere: the radial second derivative jumps from zero to one. $\square$ Theorem 16.17.2 (All constant-height Dirichlet cases in a ball) . C9817DF3B271 Fix $n\geq 2$, $R>0$ and $h\geq 0$. The unique minimizer of \[  J(v)=\int _{B_ R}\left(\tfrac 12|Dv|^2+v\right),\qquad v\geq 0,\quad v-h\in H^1_0(B_ R),  \] is as follows, with $h_*=R^2/(2n)$: \[  u_ h(x)=\begin{cases}  0,& h=0,\\  U_ a(|x|),\quad U_ a(R)=h,\  0<a<R,& 0<h<h_*,\\  |x|^2/(2n),& h=h_*,\\  h-h_*+|x|^2/(2n),& h>h_*. \end{cases}  \] In the middle range the contact radius $a$ is uniquely determined and decreases strictly as $h$ increases. These explicit solutions illustrate the normalized obstacle equation in [ Fig18 ] ; the proof below verifies minimality against all admissible competitors. Proof Existence and uniqueness follow from Theorem 13.2.1 with forcing $f=-1$. For $0<a<R$ set $g(a)=U_ a(R)$. Differentiating its integral expression, whose integrand vanishes at the moving lower endpoint, gives \[  g'(a)=-a^{n-1}\int _ a^ R s^{1-n}\, ds<0.  \] The explicit formulas show $g(a)\to h_*$ as $a\downarrow 0$ and $g(a)\to 0$ as $a\uparrow R$. Continuity and strict monotonicity supply exactly one radius for each intermediate $h$. Every displayed function is nonnegative, has boundary value $h$, and is $C^{1,1}$ with $\Delta u_ h=\chi _{\{ u_ h>0\} }$ almost everywhere. For a competitor $v$, integration by parts yields \[  \int _{B_ R}Du_ h\cdot D(v-u_ h)+\int _{B_ R}(v-u_ h) =\int _{\{ u_ h=0\} \cap B_ R}v\geq 0.  \] Thus each candidate satisfies the variational inequality and is the unique minimizer. This verifies the global boundary-value problem directly; rotational symmetry alone is not used to assume away possible nonradial competitors. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.3 (Contact is not the same as positive reaction mass) . 20576B580998 For $0<h<h_*$ the reaction measure of $u_ h$ is $\lambda _ h=\chi _{B_ a}\mathcal L^ n$ and its mass is $\omega _ n a^ n$. At $h=h_*$ the contact set is the singleton $\{ 0\} $ but the reaction is zero. At $h>h_*$ contact is empty and the reaction remains zero; at $h=0$ the whole ball is in contact and $\lambda _0=\mathcal L^ n\lfloor B_ R$. Proof With forcing $f=-1$, Proposition 13.2.5 gives $\lambda _ h=1-\Delta u_ h$. Substitute the Laplacians computed in Theorem 16.17.2 . The sphere $\partial B_ a$ has zero Lebesgue measure and carries no singular reaction, since the gradient is continuous across it. At the threshold the Laplacian of $|x|^2/(2n)$ is one even at zero, while its value vanishes there. Thus a nonempty contact set need not carry nonzero reaction measure. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.4 (The regular sphere and the singular point have different blow-ups) . DE855AC5E65E For $0<h<h_*$ and $p=ae\in \partial B_ a$, $|e|=1$, the full family of quadratic rescalings satisfies \[  \frac{u_ h(p+ry)}{r^2}\longrightarrow \frac12((y\cdot e)^+)^2 \quad \text{in }C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)\quad (r\downarrow 0).  \] At $h=h_*$ the blow-up at the sole contact point is exactly $|y|^2/(2n)$ at every scale. Hence the contact sphere consists of regular points, whereas the threshold point is singular with a positive-definite blow-up matrix. Proof Near $a$, Taylor's theorem on the exterior side gives $U_ a(a+t)=\frac12(t^+)^2+O(|t|^3)$ and $U_ a'(a+t)=t^++O(t^2)$, with zero values for $t\leq 0$. On bounded $y$ sets, \[  |p+ry|-a=r(y\cdot e)+O(r^2),\qquad \frac{p+ry}{|p+ry|}=e+O(r).  \] Substitution into the function and radial gradient formulas gives uniform convergence of both the rescaled function and gradient. The estimates remain valid across the changing positivity interface because $t\mapsto t^+$ is Lipschitz. At the threshold, exact quadratic homogeneity gives the second assertion. Apply Definitions 13.3.12 and 13.3.13 ; the singular matrix is $I/n$ and has zero-dimensional kernel. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.5 (How the contact radius approaches its endpoints) . EED8D8469AD3 As $h\downarrow 0$, the contact radius satisfies $R-a\sim \sqrt{2h}$. As $h\uparrow h_*$, it tends to zero. In dimension two the exact deficit is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2}\log (R/a)+\frac{a^2}{4}.  \] In dimensions $n>2$ it is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2(n-2)}-\frac{a^ nR^{2-n}}{n(n-2)}, \qquad a\sim \sqrt{2(n-2)(h_*-h)}.  \] Here $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to 1$ in the indicated limit. Proof Subtract the explicit value $U_ a(R)$ from $h_*$ to obtain the deficit identities. For $n>2$ the second term is lower order than $a^2$ as $a\downarrow 0$, giving the stated asymptotic. In dimension two the logarithm grows without bound and cannot be dropped. At the other endpoint, differentiate the formula for $g'(a)$ in Theorem 16.17.2 ; it gives $g(R)=g'(R)=0$ and $g''(R)=1$ by continuous extension from the left. Taylor's theorem yields $h=g(a)=(R-a)^2/2+o((R-a)^2)$, proving the first assertion. These calculations exhibit a change in contact geometry even though the minimizer remains controlled in $C^{1,1}$. $\square$ Proposition 16.17.6 (The derivative of the minimized energy) . AEA8FAF2A27B Let $E(h)=J(u_ h)$ for $h\geq 0$. It is continuously differentiable from the right at zero and differentiable elsewhere, with \[  E'(h)=\begin{cases}  \omega _ n(R^ n-a(h)^ n),& 0<h<h_*,\\  \omega _ nR^ n,& h\geq h_*, \end{cases} \qquad E'(0+)=0.  \] It is strictly convex on $(0,h_*)$ and affine on $[h_*,\infty )$. Proof In the intermediate range, $g'(a)<0$ makes $a(h)$ smooth. Differentiate the energy as a radial integral over $a<|x|<R$. There is no moving-interface contribution because both $U_ a$ and its gradient vanish at $r=a$. Integration by parts in the resulting first variation leaves only the outer boundary term: the interior term has coefficient $1-\Delta u_ h=0$ on positivity, and the parameter derivative is zero in contact. The boundary derivative with respect to $h$ is one. Consequently \[  E'(h)=\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial B_ R)U_ a'(R) =n\omega _ nR^{n-1}\frac{R^ n-a^ n}{nR^{n-1}} =\omega _ n(R^ n-a^ n).  \] This derivative is strictly increasing because $a'(h)<0$. Above threshold the solution is the threshold solution plus the constant $h-h_*$, so its gradient energy is unchanged and its linear energy increases by $(h-h_*)|B_ R|$. The explicit profiles and their gradients converge uniformly on the closed ball at both limiting heights, so $E$ is continuous there. The interior derivative has limits zero at $h=0$ and $\omega _ nR^ n$ at $h=h_*$. The mean value theorem, applied on one-sided intervals and then taking their endpoints to the threshold, gives the claimed matching derivatives. This proves the endpoint assertions without differentiating an undefined inverse radius at zero. $\square$

text: Theorem 16.17.2 (All constant-height Dirichlet cases in a ball) . C9817DF3B271 Fix $n\geq 2$, $R>0$ and $h\geq 0$. The unique minimizer of \[  J(v)=\int _{B_ R}\left(\tfrac 12|Dv|^2+v\right),\qquad v\geq 0,\quad v-h\in H^1_0(B_ R),  \] is as follows, with $h_*=R^2/(2n)$: \[  u_ h(x)=\begin{cases}  0,& h=0,\\  U_ a(|x|),\quad U_ a(R)=h,\  0<a<R,& 0<h<h_*,\\  |x|^2/(2n),& h=h_*,\\  h-h_*+|x|^2/(2n),& h>h_*. \end{cases}  \] In the middle range the contact radius $a$ is uniquely determined and decreases strictly as $h$ increases. These explicit solutions illustrate the normalized obstacle equation in [ Fig18 ] ; the proof below verifies minimality against all admissible competitors. Proof Existence and uniqueness follow from Theorem 13.2.1 with forcing $f=-1$. For $0<a<R$ set $g(a)=U_ a(R)$. Differentiating its integral expression, whose integrand vanishes at the moving lower endpoint, gives \[  g'(a)=-a^{n-1}\int _ a^ R s^{1-n}\, ds<0.  \] The explicit formulas show $g(a)\to h_*$ as $a\downarrow 0$ and $g(a)\to 0$ as $a\uparrow R$. Continuity and strict monotonicity supply exactly one radius for each intermediate $h$. Every displayed function is nonnegative, has boundary value $h$, and is $C^{1,1}$ with $\Delta u_ h=\chi _{\{ u_ h>0\} }$ almost everywhere. For a competitor $v$, integration by parts yields \[  \int _{B_ R}Du_ h\cdot D(v-u_ h)+\int _{B_ R}(v-u_ h) =\int _{\{ u_ h=0\} \cap B_ R}v\geq 0.  \] Thus each candidate satisfies the variational inequality and is the unique minimizer. This verifies the global boundary-value problem directly; rotational symmetry alone is not used to assume away possible nonradial competitors. $\square$
