text: Proposition 16.17.3 (Contact is not the same as positive reaction mass) . 20576B580998 For $0<h<h_*$ the reaction measure of $u_ h$ is $\lambda _ h=\chi _{B_ a}\mathcal L^ n$ and its mass is $\omega _ n a^ n$. At $h=h_*$ the contact set is the singleton $\{ 0\} $ but the reaction is zero. At $h>h_*$ contact is empty and the reaction remains zero; at $h=0$ the whole ball is in contact and $\lambda _0=\mathcal L^ n\lfloor B_ R$. Proof With forcing $f=-1$, Proposition 13.2.5 gives $\lambda _ h=1-\Delta u_ h$. Substitute the Laplacians computed in Theorem 16.17.2 . The sphere $\partial B_ a$ has zero Lebesgue measure and carries no singular reaction, since the gradient is continuous across it. At the threshold the Laplacian of $|x|^2/(2n)$ is one even at zero, while its value vanishes there. Thus a nonempty contact set need not carry nonzero reaction measure. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.17.4 (The regular sphere and the singular point have different blow-ups)
search_title: The regular sphere and the singular point have different blow-ups
section: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
text: Proposition 16.17.4 (The regular sphere and the singular point have different blow-ups) . DE855AC5E65E For $0<h<h_*$ and $p=ae\in \partial B_ a$, $|e|=1$, the full family of quadratic rescalings satisfies \[  \frac{u_ h(p+ry)}{r^2}\longrightarrow \frac12((y\cdot e)^+)^2 \quad \text{in }C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^ n)\quad (r\downarrow 0).  \] At $h=h_*$ the blow-up at the sole contact point is exactly $|y|^2/(2n)$ at every scale. Hence the contact sphere consists of regular points, whereas the threshold point is singular with a positive-definite blow-up matrix. Proof Near $a$, Taylor's theorem on the exterior side gives $U_ a(a+t)=\frac12(t^+)^2+O(|t|^3)$ and $U_ a'(a+t)=t^++O(t^2)$, with zero values for $t\leq 0$. On bounded $y$ sets, \[  |p+ry|-a=r(y\cdot e)+O(r^2),\qquad \frac{p+ry}{|p+ry|}=e+O(r).  \] Substitution into the function and radial gradient formulas gives uniform convergence of both the rescaled function and gradient. The estimates remain valid across the changing positivity interface because $t\mapsto t^+$ is Lipschitz. At the threshold, exact quadratic homogeneity gives the second assertion. Apply Definitions 13.3.12 and 13.3.13 ; the singular matrix is $I/n$ and has zero-dimensional kernel. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.17.5 (How the contact radius approaches its endpoints)
search_title: How the contact radius approaches its endpoints
section: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
text: Proposition 16.17.5 (How the contact radius approaches its endpoints) . EED8D8469AD3 As $h\downarrow 0$, the contact radius satisfies $R-a\sim \sqrt{2h}$. As $h\uparrow h_*$, it tends to zero. In dimension two the exact deficit is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2}\log (R/a)+\frac{a^2}{4}.  \] In dimensions $n>2$ it is \[  h_*-h=\frac{a^2}{2(n-2)}-\frac{a^ nR^{2-n}}{n(n-2)}, \qquad a\sim \sqrt{2(n-2)(h_*-h)}.  \] Here $f\sim g$ means $f/g\to 1$ in the indicated limit. Proof Subtract the explicit value $U_ a(R)$ from $h_*$ to obtain the deficit identities. For $n>2$ the second term is lower order than $a^2$ as $a\downarrow 0$, giving the stated asymptotic. In dimension two the logarithm grows without bound and cannot be dropped. At the other endpoint, differentiate the formula for $g'(a)$ in Theorem 16.17.2 ; it gives $g(R)=g'(R)=0$ and $g''(R)=1$ by continuous extension from the left. Taylor's theorem yields $h=g(a)=(R-a)^2/2+o((R-a)^2)$, proving the first assertion. These calculations exhibit a change in contact geometry even though the minimizer remains controlled in $C^{1,1}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.17.6 (The derivative of the minimized energy)
search_title: The derivative of the minimized energy
section: 16.17 A radial obstacle problem and its contact transition
text: Proposition 16.17.6 (The derivative of the minimized energy) . AEA8FAF2A27B Let $E(h)=J(u_ h)$ for $h\geq 0$. It is continuously differentiable from the right at zero and differentiable elsewhere, with \[  E'(h)=\begin{cases}  \omega _ n(R^ n-a(h)^ n),& 0<h<h_*,\\  \omega _ nR^ n,& h\geq h_*, \end{cases} \qquad E'(0+)=0.  \] It is strictly convex on $(0,h_*)$ and affine on $[h_*,\infty )$. Proof In the intermediate range, $g'(a)<0$ makes $a(h)$ smooth. Differentiate the energy as a radial integral over $a<|x|<R$. There is no moving-interface contribution because both $U_ a$ and its gradient vanish at $r=a$. Integration by parts in the resulting first variation leaves only the outer boundary term: the interior term has coefficient $1-\Delta u_ h=0$ on positivity, and the parameter derivative is zero in contact. The boundary derivative with respect to $h$ is one. Consequently \[  E'(h)=\mathcal H^{n-1}(\partial B_ R)U_ a'(R) =n\omega _ nR^{n-1}\frac{R^ n-a^ n}{nR^{n-1}} =\omega _ n(R^ n-a^ n).  \] This derivative is strictly increasing because $a'(h)<0$. Above threshold the solution is the threshold solution plus the constant $h-h_*$, so its gradient energy is unchanged and its linear energy increases by $(h-h_*)|B_ R|$. The explicit profiles and their gradients converge uniformly on the closed ball at both limiting heights, so $E$ is continuous there. The interior derivative has limits zero at $h=0$ and $\omega _ nR^ n$ at $h=h_*$. The mean value theorem, applied on one-sided intervals and then taking their endpoints to the threshold, gives the claimed matching derivatives. This proves the endpoint assertions without differentiating an undefined inverse radius at zero. $\square$

For the second assertion, every sufficiently small smooth variation of the projected compact surface pulls back to a spherical variation avoiding the pole. section: 10.4 Willmore energy, multiplicity and inversion

The multiplicity inequality is due to Li–Yau [ LY82 ] , Theorem 6, p. 286. otin F(\partial M)$. Its preimage is a finite set of interior points, of cardinality $m$. For small $\varepsilon >0$, remove from each such sheet the region $|F-y|<\varepsilon $. abla ^\perp _{e_1}B)(e_2,e_2)=(
abla ^\perp _{e_2}B)(e_1,e_2)$ gives $

text: Throughout this section $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ is a smooth compact immersion of a nonempty surface without boundary. Set $X=F-y$, $r=|X|$, $M_ s=\{ r<s\} $, $A(s)=\mu (M_ s)$ and $\mathcal W(E)=\frac14\int _ E|\vec H|^2d\mu $. The cutoff calculation follows [ SimW93 ] , pp. 284–286. Proposition 10.5.1 (The two-radius square identity) . 1EB2A47C45B3 For positive regular values $0<\sigma <\rho $ of $r$, let $M_{\sigma ,\rho }=\{ \sigma <r<\rho \} $. Its nonsmooth radii can be approximated by smooth radial cutoffs; the coefficients and tangential derivatives are uniformly bounded for fixed $\sigma >0$, and the two regular level sets have zero surface measure. Consequently \[  \left(\sqrt a-\frac{\sqrt w}{2}\right)^2\leq \frac W4, \qquad \sqrt a\leq \frac{\sqrt w+\sqrt W}{2}\leq \sqrt W.  \] This proves $a\leq W$. section: 6.12 Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
text: The first-variation convention is Definition 6.1.3 , based on [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, equations (2.3)–(2.10), pp. 239–240. A singular boundary part must not be discarded when discussing continuity of curvature energy. We formulate an extended energy through smooth ambient tests and prove its lower semicontinuity using the representation results already established in the measure chapter. Definition 6.12.1 (An extended quadratic first-variation energy) . A25C61F4660D For an $m$-varifold $V$ in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, with weight $\mu =\| V\| $, define \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\sup _{X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)} \left\{ \delta V(X)-\int _ U|X|^2d\mu \right\} \in [0,+\infty ].  \] The zero test makes the supremum nonnegative. This definition uses the entire first variation. In dimension two it agrees with one quarter of the squared generalized mean curvature when that curvature represents the first variation without a singular part and is globally square integrable, as proved next. Theorem 6.12.2 (Finite quadratic energy is equivalent to square-integrable mean curvature) . 03E7797CCA57 The quantity $\mathcal E_ U(V)$ is finite if and only if there is $H\in L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$ such that \[  \delta V(X)=-\int _ UH\cdot X\, d\mu \quad \text{for every }X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N).  \] In that case $H$ is unique up to $\mu $-null sets and \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\frac14\int _ U|H|^2d\mu .  \] The first variation therefore has no singular boundary part in $U$. This is a dual formulation of the mean-curvature representation in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 239–240; the $L^2$ equivalence is proved here. Proof Suppose $E=\mathcal E_ U(V)<\infty $. For a fixed test $X$, applying the definition to $tX$ for every real $t$ gives \[  t\delta V(X)-t^2\| X\| _{L^2(\mu )}^2\leq E.  \] If $\| X\| _2=0$, this forces $\delta V(X)=0$. Otherwise optimize the quadratic polynomial in $t$ to obtain $|\delta V(X)|\leq 2\sqrt E\| X\| _2$. Thus the first variation is well defined and bounded on the $L^2$ equivalence classes of smooth compactly supported fields. These fields are dense in $L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$. Indeed Theorem 2.3.8 approximates each component by a continuous compactly supported function. Extending such a function by zero and mollifying gives uniform smooth approximation with support in a fixed compact neighborhood inside $U$; local finiteness of $\mu $ converts uniform convergence to $L^2$ convergence. The bounded functional extends to the Hilbert space. Lemma 5.7.1 gives a unique vector field $-H$ representing it, with $\| H\| _2\leq 2\sqrt E$. Conversely, if such $H$ exists, completion of the square gives \[  \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\mu =\frac14\int |H|^2d\mu -\int |X+H/2|^2d\mu .  \] The right side is bounded above by the claimed energy. Smooth compactly supported approximations to $-H/2$ in $L^2$ make the last term tend to zero, proving equality. The same density proves uniqueness. The representing vector measure $-H\mu $ is locally finite by Cauchy–Schwarz and local finiteness of $\mu $, and is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $, so there is no additional singular first-variation measure. $\square$ Theorem 6.12.3 (Lower semicontinuity of quadratic varifold energy) . 365150F73639 If $V_ j\rightharpoonup V$ as varifolds in $U$, then \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)\leq \liminf _{j\to \infty }\mathcal E_ U(V_ j).  \] In particular, if the liminf is finite, the limit has a generalized mean curvature in $L^2(\| V\| )$ representing its entire first variation, with the corresponding squared-norm bound. This argument uses the first-variation formula of [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.3), and does not assume integrality. Proof For a fixed $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)$, both $(x,S)\mapsto \operatorname {div}_ SX(x)$ and $(x,S)\mapsto |X(x)|^2$ are continuous with compact support on the Grassmann bundle. Thus \[  \delta V_ j(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V_ j\|  \longrightarrow \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V\| .  \] Each term before the limit is bounded above by $\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)$. For every fixed test the limiting expression is therefore at most the liminf of the energies. Taking the supremum over tests proves the inequality, including an infinite liminf. If it is finite, apply Theorem 6.12.2 to identify the limit curvature and its norm. The proof does not interchange a supremum with a limit as an equality. $\square$ Proposition 6.12.4 (Comparison with the energy of a smooth immersion) . DF57C01B9F0F Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth closed immersion, and let $V_ F$ be its induced varifold with parameter multiplicity. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathbb R^ N}(V_ F)\leq \mathcal W(F).  \] For an embedding there is equality. For every compact set $K\subset U$ and any varifold of finite quadratic energy, \[  \| \delta V\| (K)\leq 2\sqrt{\mathcal E_ U(V)}\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}.  \] Proof The smooth first variation gives $\delta V_ F(X)=-\int _ M\vec H_ F\cdot X(F)d\mu _ M$, and the weight identity gives $\int |X|^2d\| V_ F\| =\int _ M|X(F)|^2d\mu _ M$. Completing the square on the parameter surface bounds their difference by $\frac14\int _ M|\vec H_ F|^2$. Take the supremum. For an embedding, the geometric mean curvature defines a vector field on the image representing the entire first variation, so Theorem 6.12.2 gives equality. The weaker assertion for an arbitrary immersion suffices here and avoids requiring a separate identification of curvatures on coincident sheets. For the last estimate, finite energy represents the first variation by $-H\| V\| $. Its total variation on $K$ is $\int _ K|H|d\| V\| $. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds this by $\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}\| H\| _{L^2(U)}$, and the norm identity gives the claimed constant. The same argument applies to relatively compact Borel sets. $\square$ Corollary 6.12.5 (An integral compactness consequence, with its external input) . 71DC1770F6D7 Let $V_ j$ be integral two-varifolds in $U$ with locally uniformly bounded weights and $\sup _ j\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges to an integral two-varifold $V$, and $\mathcal E_ U(V)\leq \liminf _ j\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)$ after taking a subsequence attaining the energy liminf. The integrality conclusion uses the externally proved Allard compactness theorem 6.2.1 ; it is not a consequence of the Hilbert-space duality alone. Proof First pass to a subsequence whose energies tend to the liminf. Proposition 6.12.4 bounds the total variation of $\delta V_ j$ uniformly on each relatively compact set from the assumed weight and energy bounds. Apply Theorem 6.2.1 , whose hypotheses are now verified, to obtain an integral varifold subsequential limit. Theorem 6.12.3 supplies the energy inequality. This proves the deduction conditional on the explicitly named external compactness theorem; it does not replace its geometric proof. $\square$ Corollary 6.12.6 (A bounded-energy sequence of closed surfaces has local compactness) . 12AB1072F745 Let $F_ j:M_ j^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be smooth closed embedded surfaces with $\mathcal W(F_ j)\leq \Lambda $. Their induced varifolds have a subsequence converging locally to an integral two-varifold $V$ with $\mathcal E_{\mathbb R^ N}(V)\leq \Lambda $. Its weight satisfies \[  \| V\| (B_ r(y))\leq \Lambda r^2  \] for every ball, and has no atoms. The limit is allowed to be zero. Integrality again uses Theorem 6.2.1 externally. Proof Theorem 10.5.4 gives uniform mass bounds on every ball and hence on every compact set. Proposition 6.12.4 identifies the energy of each embedding with its classical Willmore energy. Corollary 6.12.5 gives the claimed limit and energy bound. Weak varifold convergence implies weak convergence of the weights, since the Grassmannian is compact. The open-set lower semicontinuity of Radon measures then yields $\| V\| (B_ r(y))\leq \liminf _ j\| V_ j\| (B_ r(y))\leq \Lambda r^2$. Let $r\downarrow 0$ to get $\| V\| (\{ y\} )=0$. title: Definition 6.12.1 (An extended quadratic first-variation energy)

text: Definition 6.12.1 (An extended quadratic first-variation energy) . A25C61F4660D For an $m$-varifold $V$ in an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ N$, with weight $\mu =\| V\| $, define \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\sup _{X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)} \left\{ \delta V(X)-\int _ U|X|^2d\mu \right\} \in [0,+\infty ].  \] The zero test makes the supremum nonnegative. This definition uses the entire first variation. In dimension two it agrees with one quarter of the squared generalized mean curvature when that curvature represents the first variation without a singular part and is globally square integrable, as proved next.

title: Theorem 6.12.2 (Finite quadratic energy is equivalent to square-integrable mean curvature)
search_title: Finite quadratic energy is equivalent to square-integrable mean curvature
section: 6.12 Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
text: Theorem 6.12.2 (Finite quadratic energy is equivalent to square-integrable mean curvature) . 03E7797CCA57 The quantity $\mathcal E_ U(V)$ is finite if and only if there is $H\in L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$ such that \[  \delta V(X)=-\int _ UH\cdot X\, d\mu \quad \text{for every }X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N).  \] In that case $H$ is unique up to $\mu $-null sets and \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)=\frac14\int _ U|H|^2d\mu .  \] The first variation therefore has no singular boundary part in $U$. This is a dual formulation of the mean-curvature representation in [ Sim18 ] , pp. 239–240; the $L^2$ equivalence is proved here. Proof Suppose $E=\mathcal E_ U(V)<\infty $. For a fixed test $X$, applying the definition to $tX$ for every real $t$ gives \[  t\delta V(X)-t^2\| X\| _{L^2(\mu )}^2\leq E.  \] If $\| X\| _2=0$, this forces $\delta V(X)=0$. Otherwise optimize the quadratic polynomial in $t$ to obtain $|\delta V(X)|\leq 2\sqrt E\| X\| _2$. Thus the first variation is well defined and bounded on the $L^2$ equivalence classes of smooth compactly supported fields. These fields are dense in $L^2(\mu ;\mathbb R^ N)$. Indeed Theorem 2.3.8 approximates each component by a continuous compactly supported function. Extending such a function by zero and mollifying gives uniform smooth approximation with support in a fixed compact neighborhood inside $U$; local finiteness of $\mu $ converts uniform convergence to $L^2$ convergence. The bounded functional extends to the Hilbert space. Lemma 5.7.1 gives a unique vector field $-H$ representing it, with $\| H\| _2\leq 2\sqrt E$. Conversely, if such $H$ exists, completion of the square gives \[  \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\mu =\frac14\int |H|^2d\mu -\int |X+H/2|^2d\mu .  \] The right side is bounded above by the claimed energy. Smooth compactly supported approximations to $-H/2$ in $L^2$ make the last term tend to zero, proving equality. The same density proves uniqueness. The representing vector measure $-H\mu $ is locally finite by Cauchy–Schwarz and local finiteness of $\mu $, and is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu $, so there is no additional singular first-variation measure. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.12.3 (Lower semicontinuity of quadratic varifold energy)
search_title: Lower semicontinuity of quadratic varifold energy
section: 6.12 Quadratic curvature energy under varifold convergence
text: Theorem 6.12.3 (Lower semicontinuity of quadratic varifold energy) . 365150F73639 If $V_ j\rightharpoonup V$ as varifolds in $U$, then \[  \mathcal E_ U(V)\leq \liminf _{j\to \infty }\mathcal E_ U(V_ j).  \] In particular, if the liminf is finite, the limit has a generalized mean curvature in $L^2(\| V\| )$ representing its entire first variation, with the corresponding squared-norm bound. This argument uses the first-variation formula of [ Sim18 ] , equation (2.3), and does not assume integrality. Proof For a fixed $X\in C_ c^1(U;\mathbb R^ N)$, both $(x,S)\mapsto \operatorname {div}_ SX(x)$ and $(x,S)\mapsto |X(x)|^2$ are continuous with compact support on the Grassmann bundle. Thus \[  \delta V_ j(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V_ j\|  \longrightarrow \delta V(X)-\int |X|^2d\| V\| .  \] Each term before the limit is bounded above by $\mathcal E_ U(V_ j)$. For every fixed test the limiting expression is therefore at most the liminf of the energies. Taking the supremum over tests proves the inequality, including an infinite liminf. If it is finite, apply Theorem 6.12.2 to identify the limit curvature and its norm. The proof does not interchange a supremum with a limit as an equality. $\square$

text: Proposition 6.12.4 (Comparison with the energy of a smooth immersion) . DF57C01B9F0F Let $F:M^2\to \mathbb R^ N$ be a smooth closed immersion, and let $V_ F$ be its induced varifold with parameter multiplicity. Then \[  \mathcal E_{\mathbb R^ N}(V_ F)\leq \mathcal W(F).  \] For an embedding there is equality. For every compact set $K\subset U$ and any varifold of finite quadratic energy, \[  \| \delta V\| (K)\leq 2\sqrt{\mathcal E_ U(V)}\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}.  \] Proof The smooth first variation gives $\delta V_ F(X)=-\int _ M\vec H_ F\cdot X(F)d\mu _ M$, and the weight identity gives $\int |X|^2d\| V_ F\| =\int _ M|X(F)|^2d\mu _ M$. Completing the square on the parameter surface bounds their difference by $\frac14\int _ M|\vec H_ F|^2$. Take the supremum. For an embedding, the geometric mean curvature defines a vector field on the image representing the entire first variation, so Theorem 6.12.2 gives equality. The weaker assertion for an arbitrary immersion suffices here and avoids requiring a separate identification of curvatures on coincident sheets. For the last estimate, finite energy represents the first variation by $-H\| V\| $. Its total variation on $K$ is $\int _ K|H|d\| V\| $. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds this by $\sqrt{\| V\| (K)}\| H\| _{L^2(U)}$, and the norm identity gives the claimed constant. The same argument applies to relatively compact Borel sets. $\square$

text:
These calculations use the averaged energy $\mathcal W= rac14\int H^2$ in Euclidean space and $\mathcal W_1=\int (1+H^2/4)$ in the unit three-sphere, where $H$ is the trace. The circular torus and its relation to the Clifford torus appear in [ MNWill ] , p. 684; the calculations here supply their metrics, curvature and exact energies. The global positive-genus theorem remains the separate Theorem 10.1.2 . Proposition 16.18.1 (Geometry of a circular ring torus) . 737F11A69F2E For $R>r>0$, the map \[  T(	heta ,\varphi )= igl ((R+r\cos 	heta )\cos \varphi , (R+r\cos 	heta )\sin \varphi ,r\sin 	heta  igr ), \qquad (	heta ,\varphi )\in (\mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z)^2,  \] is an embedded torus with metric $r^2d	heta ^2+(R+r\cos 	heta )^2d\varphi ^2$ and area $4\pi ^2Rr$. With the outward normal $
u =(\cos 	heta \cos \varphi ,\cos 	heta \sin \varphi ,\sin 	heta )$, its principal curvatures are $1/r$ and $\cos 	heta /(R+r\cos 	heta )$. Proof Differentiate the parametrization. The two coordinate derivatives are orthogonal and have respective lengths $r$ and $R+r\cos 	heta >0$, so it is an immersion with the stated metric. The positive distance to the rotation axis determines $\varphi $, while that distance minus $R$ together with height determines $(r\cos 	heta ,r\sin 	heta )$ and hence $	heta $. This proves injectivity and thus embeddedness by compactness. The area density is $r(R+r\cos 	heta )$, whose double integral is $4\pi ^2Rr$. Differentiating the stated normal gives $
u _	heta =T_	heta /r$ and $
u _\varphi =\cos 	heta \, T_\varphi /(R+r\cos 	heta )$, proving the principal curvatures with $A=D
u $. $\square$ Theorem 16.18.2 (The energy minimum within the circular ring family) . CC8C3F901960 The preceding torus has \[  \mathcal W(T)= rac{\pi ^2R^2}{r\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}\geq 2\pi ^2,  \] with equality exactly when $R/r=\sqrt2$. Its energy tends to infinity as $R/r\downarrow 1$ or $R/r	o \infty $. This is the circular-family calculation motivating the conjecture recalled in [ LY82 ] , p. 270, and [ MNWill ] , p. 684; it does not prove the inequality for arbitrary immersed tori. Proof Proposition 16.18.1 gives \[  \mathcal W(T)= rac{\pi }{2r}\int _0^{2\pi }  rac{(R+2r\cos 	heta )^2}{R+r\cos 	heta }\, d	heta .  \] Polynomial division makes the integrand $4r\cos 	heta +R^2/(R+r\cos 	heta )$. The cosine integrates to zero. The substitution $t=	an (	heta /2)$ on $(-\pi ,\pi )$ gives \[  \int _0^{2\pi } rac{d	heta }{R+r\cos 	heta } =2\int _{-\infty }^{\infty } rac{dt}{(R+r)+(R-r)t^2} = rac{2\pi }{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}.  \] This proves the formula. Put $a=R/r>1$. The derivative of $a^2/\sqrt{a^2-1}$ is $a(a^2-2)/(a^2-1)^{3/2}$, negative below $\sqrt2$ and positive above it. Its value there is two, and the endpoint limits are infinite. Only the scale-free ratio matters, as conformal dilation invariance predicts. $\square$ Example 16.18.3 (Total Gauss curvature does not determine the torus energy) . 70E5321ABD3C Every circular ring torus above satisfies \[  \int _ TK\, d\mu =0,\qquad \int _ T|K|\, d\mu =8\pi , \qquad \int _{\{ K>0\} }K\, d\mu =4\pi ,  \] although its Willmore energy varies from $2\pi ^2$ to arbitrarily large values. Proof The principal curvatures give $K=\cos 	heta /[r(R+r\cos 	heta )]$. Multiplying by area leaves $\cos 	heta \, d	heta d\varphi $. The integrals of $\cos 	heta $, $|\cos 	heta |$ and its positive part over a period are zero, four and two. Multiply each by $2\pi $. The energy variation follows from Theorem 16.18.2 . Thus even fixing these total intrinsic-curvature quantities does not fix the bending energy. $\square$ Proposition 16.18.4 (Product tori in the unit three-sphere) . F65993A50A9F For $a,b>0$ with $a^2+b^2=1$, the product torus \[  F(	heta ,\varphi )=(a\cos 	heta ,a\sin 	heta ,b\cos \varphi ,b\sin \varphi )  \] has area $4\pi ^2ab$, intrinsic Gauss curvature zero, and spherical principal curvatures $b/a$ and $-a/b$. Its spherical Willmore energy is $\pi ^2/(ab)\geq 2\pi ^2$, with equality exactly at $a=b=1/\sqrt2$. Within this family, only that Clifford torus is a Willmore critical surface. Proof The product metric is $a^2d	heta ^2+b^2d\varphi ^2$, flat with the claimed area. The field $
u =(b\cos 	heta ,b\sin 	heta ,-a\cos \varphi ,-a\sin \varphi )$ is a unit vector tangent to $S^3$ and normal to the torus. Its derivatives in the two product directions give $b/a$ and $-a/b$. Thus $H=(b^2-a^2)/(ab)$ is constant, and \[  1+ rac{H^2}{4}= rac{4a^2b^2+(b^2-a^2)^2}{4a^2b^2} = rac1{4a^2b^2}.  \] Multiplication by area gives the energy. The inequality $ab\leq (a^2+b^2)/2=1/2$ proves its minimum. The trace-free curvature is nonzero everywhere, because the two principal curvatures have opposite signs. Hence the equation of Theorem 10.3.6 reduces to $H=0$, or $a=b$. The sphere here has radius one; it is different from the radius-two sphere containing the Clifford self-shrinker of Example 16.15.4 . $\square$ Example 16.18.5 (Stereographic projection gives the circular minimizer) . 12ADEC1AC317 The stereographic projection from $(0,0,0,1)$ of the unit Clifford torus is the ring torus with major radius $\sqrt2$ and minor radius one. Both descriptions therefore have Willmore energy $2\pi ^2$. Proof Write a Clifford point as $(\cos \varphi ,\sin \varphi ,\cos 	heta ,\sin 	heta )/\sqrt2$. Its projected cylindrical coordinates are \[  ho = rac1{\sqrt2-\sin 	heta },\qquad z= rac{\cos 	heta }{\sqrt2-\sin 	heta }.  \] The denominator is positive. Direct algebra gives $ho ^2+z^2+1=2\sqrt2ho $, or $(ho -\sqrt2)^2+z^2=1$. Thus the image lies in the stated ring torus. Stereographic projection is a diffeomorphism off its pole, and the Clifford torus avoids the pole, so its restriction is an embedding. Its image in the ring torus is open by the inverse function theorem and closed by compactness; connectedness gives the entire ring torus. Proposition 16.18.4 , Theorem 16.18.2 and the stereographic energy identity all give the same value. $\square$ Example 16.18.6 (All round latitudes have the same Willmore energy) . 46E3ED8F4006 For $0<\alpha <\pi $, the round latitude $F(\omega )=(\sin \alpha \, \omega ,\cos \alpha )$ in $S^3$, $\omega \in S^2$, has area $4\pi \sin ^2\alpha $, trace mean curvature $2\cot \alpha $ for a suitable normal, and $\mathcal W_1=4\pi $. Every latitude is Willmore critical, although only the equator is minimal. Proof The induced metric is $\sin ^2\alpha $ times the unit-sphere metric. The unit normal $
u =(\cos \alpha \, \omega ,-\sin \alpha )$ differentiates to $A=\cot \alpha I$, proving the curvature and minimality assertion. The energy is $4\pi \sin ^2\alpha (1+\cot ^2\alpha )=4\pi $. Since $A^0=0$ and $H$ is constant, the Willmore equation vanishes. The ambient-curvature term one is necessary: the integral of $H^2/4$ alone is $4\pi \cos ^2\alpha $ and is not constant in this spherical family. $\square$ Example 16.18.7 (An affine plane becomes a punctured round sphere) . E2F8CCE1C5C6 In a three-dimensional affine subspace identified with $\mathbb R^3$, invert at zero the plane $\{ x\cdot n=d\} $, where $|n|=1$ and $d
e 0$. Its image is the sphere of center $n/(2d)$ and radius $1/(2|d|)$ with the origin removed. The plane has zero Willmore energy, while the punctured sphere has energy $4\pi $. Proof Writing $z=x/|x|^2$, the plane equation becomes $z\cdot n=d|z|^2$, equivalently $|z-n/(2d)|^2=1/(4d^2)$. Every nonzero point of this sphere inverts to a point of the plane, proving the image assertion. A plane is minimal; the round sphere's energy is $4\pi $, and removing one point does not change its integral. The original plane is noncompact, so invariance for a closed surface with a pole off its image does not apply in that direction. Inverting the completed sphere at its origin instead fits Proposition 10.4.5 : it loses exactly $4\pi $ and becomes the plane. $\square$ Proposition 16.18.8 (The full Willmore equation on a ring torus) . 3F8B80E15359 For the circular ring torus of Proposition 16.18.1 , write $s=R+r\cos 	heta $. Then \[  \Delta H+H|A^0|^2= rac{R(R^2-2r^2)}{2r^3s^3}.  \] Consequently the ratio $R/r=\sqrt2$ gives a critical point under all smooth variations, not merely under variations within the ring family. Proof The trace is $H=1/r+\cos 	heta /s$, and its derivative is $H_	heta =-R\sin 	heta /s^2$. For a function of $	heta $ alone, the product metric gives \[  \Delta H= rac1{r^2}H_{	heta 	heta }+ rac{s_	heta }{r^2s}H_	heta =- rac{R\cos 	heta }{r^2s^2}- rac{R\sin ^2	heta }{rs^3}.  \] Also $|A^0|^2=(1/r-\cos 	heta /s)^2/2=R^2/(2r^2s^2)$. Bringing the sum to the common denominator $2r^3s^3$ leaves \[  R igl [-2r\cos 	heta \, s-2r^2\sin ^2	heta +R(s+r\cos 	heta ) igr ] =R(R^2-2r^2).  \] The denominator is everywhere positive. The first-variation theorem therefore gives the assertion, including the converse within this circular family. A minimum found in a restricted family would not by itself justify the full criticality conclusion; the displayed equation does. $\square$ Proposition 16.18.9 (Second variation at a round Euclidean sphere) . 24AEED595178 For the round sphere $S_ R^2\subset \mathbb R^3$, a smooth variation with initial normal speed $f$ has \[  \left. rac{d^2}{dt^2}ight|_0\mathcal W(F_ t) = rac12\int _{S_ R^2}(\Delta f)^2d\mu - rac1{R^2}\int _{S_ R^2}|
abla f|^2d\mu =\int _{S_ R^2}\left|
abla ^2f- rac{\Delta f}{2}gight|^2d\mu .  \] In particular every such second variation is nonnegative, independently of the second-order choice of the variation. Proof On the sphere, $H=2/R$ is constant and $A^0=0$. Differentiate the integrand of Theorem 10.3.6 . Since the original Euler–Lagrange expression is zero, derivatives of speed and area do not contribute. The derivative of $H|A^0|^2$ is zero. The derivative of the Laplacian acting on the original constant $H$ is also zero, because every Laplacian annihilates a constant. Thus only $\Delta \dot H$ remains. The Euclidean linearization gives $\dot H=-\Delta f-2f/R^2$. This yields \[  \ddot{\mathcal W}= rac12\int f\Delta (\Delta +2/R^2)f,  \] which is the first formula after integration by parts. For completeness, commuting one covariant derivative of $
abla f$ gives $\operatorname {div}(
abla ^2f)=
abla \Delta f+\operatorname {Ric}(
abla f,\cdot )$. On this two-sphere $\operatorname {Ric}=R^{-2}g$. Integrating the divergence identity against $
abla f$ gives \[  \int |
abla ^2f|^2=\int (\Delta f)^2- rac1{R^2}\int |
abla f|^2.  \] Subtracting half the squared trace produces exactly the preceding Hessian formula. Nonnegativity is now the integral of a squared norm; no spectral decomposition is needed. $\square$ Proposition 16.18.10 (Only dilations and translations lie in the spherical kernel) . FF20FCA045C5 The second variation in Proposition 16.18.9 vanishes exactly for functions $f=c+a\cdot X$, with $c\in \mathbb R$ and $a\in \mathbb R^3$. The constant mode is the normal speed of a change of radius; the linear modes are normal translation speeds up to a fixed factor. The normal kernel is therefore four-dimensional. Proof Vanishing of the square gives $
abla ^2f=(\Delta f/2)g$. Take its divergence and use the commutation identity from the preceding proof. It follows that $
abla (\Delta f+2f/R^2)=0$. Averaging this constant expression over the sphere shows that $u=f-\overline f$ satisfies $\Delta u=-2u/R^2$ and hence $
abla ^2u=-ug/R^2$. Regard $
abla u$ as an ambient tangent vector. The Euclidean derivative of $Z=
abla u+(u/R^2)X$ in a tangent direction $V$ is zero: its tangential terms are $-uV/R^2+uV/R^2$, and its normal terms are $-(V u)X/R^2+(V u)X/R^2$, because the sphere's vector-valued second fundamental form is $B(V,W)=-g(V,W)X/R^2$. Connectedness makes $Z=a$ one constant ambient vector. Dotting with $X$ gives $u=a\cdot X$. Conversely every such linear function has Hessian $-ug/R^2$, and constants have zero Hessian, so they lie in the kernel. A translation by a vector $b$ has normal speed $b\cdot X/R$, which spans the same three-dimensional space. These are infinitesimal kernel statements and do not assert convergence of a geometric flow. $\square$

search_title: Product tori in the unit three-sphere
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text: Proposition 16.18.4 (Product tori in the unit three-sphere) . F65993A50A9F For $a,b>0$ with $a^2+b^2=1$, the product torus \[  F(\theta ,\varphi )=(a\cos \theta ,a\sin \theta ,b\cos \varphi ,b\sin \varphi )  \] has area $4\pi ^2ab$, intrinsic Gauss curvature zero, and spherical principal curvatures $b/a$ and $-a/b$. Its spherical Willmore energy is $\pi ^2/(ab)\geq 2\pi ^2$, with equality exactly at $a=b=1/\sqrt2$. Within this family, only that Clifford torus is a Willmore critical surface. Proof The product metric is $a^2d\theta ^2+b^2d\varphi ^2$, flat with the claimed area. The field $\nu =(b\cos \theta ,b\sin \theta ,-a\cos \varphi ,-a\sin \varphi )$ is a unit vector tangent to $S^3$ and normal to the torus. Its derivatives in the two product directions give $b/a$ and $-a/b$. Thus $H=(b^2-a^2)/(ab)$ is constant, and \[  1+\frac{H^2}{4}=\frac{4a^2b^2+(b^2-a^2)^2}{4a^2b^2} =\frac1{4a^2b^2}.  \] Multiplication by area gives the energy. The inequality $ab\leq (a^2+b^2)/2=1/2$ proves its minimum. The trace-free curvature is nonzero everywhere, because the two principal curvatures have opposite signs. Hence the equation of Theorem 10.3.6 reduces to $H=0$, or $a=b$. The sphere here has radius one; it is different from the radius-two sphere containing the Clifford self-shrinker of Example 16.15.4 . $\square$

title: Example 16.18.5 (Stereographic projection gives the circular minimizer)
search_title: Stereographic projection gives the circular minimizer
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text: Example 16.18.5 (Stereographic projection gives the circular minimizer) . 12ADEC1AC317 The stereographic projection from $(0,0,0,1)$ of the unit Clifford torus is the ring torus with major radius $\sqrt2$ and minor radius one. Both descriptions therefore have Willmore energy $2\pi ^2$. Proof Write a Clifford point as $(\cos \varphi ,\sin \varphi ,\cos \theta ,\sin \theta )/\sqrt2$. Its projected cylindrical coordinates are \[  \rho =\frac1{\sqrt2-\sin \theta },\qquad z=\frac{\cos \theta }{\sqrt2-\sin \theta }.  \] The denominator is positive. Direct algebra gives $\rho ^2+z^2+1=2\sqrt2\rho $, or $(\rho -\sqrt2)^2+z^2=1$. Thus the image lies in the stated ring torus. Stereographic projection is a diffeomorphism off its pole, and the Clifford torus avoids the pole, so its restriction is an embedding. Its image in the ring torus is open by the inverse function theorem and closed by compactness; connectedness gives the entire ring torus. Proposition 16.18.4 , Theorem 16.18.2 and the stereographic energy identity all give the same value. $\square$

title: Example 16.18.6 (All round latitudes have the same Willmore energy)
search_title: All round latitudes have the same Willmore energy
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text: Example 16.18.6 (All round latitudes have the same Willmore energy) . 46E3ED8F4006 For $0<\alpha <\pi $, the round latitude $F(\omega )=(\sin \alpha \, \omega ,\cos \alpha )$ in $S^3$, $\omega \in S^2$, has area $4\pi \sin ^2\alpha $, trace mean curvature $2\cot \alpha $ for a suitable normal, and $\mathcal W_1=4\pi $. Every latitude is Willmore critical, although only the equator is minimal. Proof The induced metric is $\sin ^2\alpha $ times the unit-sphere metric. The unit normal $\nu =(\cos \alpha \, \omega ,-\sin \alpha )$ differentiates to $A=\cot \alpha I$, proving the curvature and minimality assertion. The energy is $4\pi \sin ^2\alpha (1+\cot ^2\alpha )=4\pi $. Since $A^0=0$ and $H$ is constant, the Willmore equation vanishes. The ambient-curvature term one is necessary: the integral of $H^2/4$ alone is $4\pi \cos ^2\alpha $ and is not constant in this spherical family. $\square$

title: Example 16.18.7 (An affine plane becomes a punctured round sphere)
search_title: An affine plane becomes a punctured round sphere
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text: Example 16.18.7 (An affine plane becomes a punctured round sphere) . E2F8CCE1C5C6 In a three-dimensional affine subspace identified with $\mathbb R^3$, invert at zero the plane $\{ x\cdot n=d\} $, where $|n|=1$ and $d\ne 0$. Its image is the sphere of center $n/(2d)$ and radius $1/(2|d|)$ with the origin removed. The plane has zero Willmore energy, while the punctured sphere has energy $4\pi $. Proof Writing $z=x/|x|^2$, the plane equation becomes $z\cdot n=d|z|^2$, equivalently $|z-n/(2d)|^2=1/(4d^2)$. Every nonzero point of this sphere inverts to a point of the plane, proving the image assertion. A plane is minimal; the round sphere's energy is $4\pi $, and removing one point does not change its integral. The original plane is noncompact, so invariance for a closed surface with a pole off its image does not apply in that direction. Inverting the completed sphere at its origin instead fits Proposition 10.4.5 : it loses exactly $4\pi $ and becomes the plane. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.18.8 (The full Willmore equation on a ring torus)
search_title: The full Willmore equation on a ring torus
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text: Proposition 16.18.8 (The full Willmore equation on a ring torus) . 3F8B80E15359 For the circular ring torus of Proposition 16.18.1 , write $s=R+r\cos \theta $. Then \[  \Delta H+H|A^0|^2=\frac{R(R^2-2r^2)}{2r^3s^3}.  \] Consequently the ratio $R/r=\sqrt2$ gives a critical point under all smooth variations, not merely under variations within the ring family. Proof The trace is $H=1/r+\cos \theta /s$, and its derivative is $H_\theta =-R\sin \theta /s^2$. For a function of $\theta $ alone, the product metric gives \[  \Delta H=\frac1{r^2}H_{\theta \theta }+\frac{s_\theta }{r^2s}H_\theta =-\frac{R\cos \theta }{r^2s^2}-\frac{R\sin ^2\theta }{rs^3}.  \] Also $|A^0|^2=(1/r-\cos \theta /s)^2/2=R^2/(2r^2s^2)$. Bringing the sum to the common denominator $2r^3s^3$ leaves \[  R\bigl [-2r\cos \theta \, s-2r^2\sin ^2\theta +R(s+r\cos \theta )\bigr ] =R(R^2-2r^2).  \] The denominator is everywhere positive. The first-variation theorem therefore gives the assertion, including the converse within this circular family. A minimum found in a restricted family would not by itself justify the full criticality conclusion; the displayed equation does. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.18.9 (Second variation at a round Euclidean sphere)
search_title: Second variation at a round Euclidean sphere
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori

Proposition 16.18.9 (Second variation at a round Euclidean sphere) . 24AEED595178 For the round sphere $S_ R^2\subset \mathbb R^3$, a smooth variation with initial normal speed $f$ has \[  \left. rac{d^2}{dt^2}ight|_0\mathcal W(F_ t) = rac12\int _{S_ R^2}(\Delta f)^2d\mu - rac1{R^2}\int _{S_ R^2}|
abla f|^2d\mu =\int _{S_ R^2}\left|
abla ^2f- rac{\Delta f}{2}gight|^2d\mu .  \] In particular every such second variation is nonnegative, independently of the second-order choice of the variation. Proof On the sphere, $H=2/R$ is constant and $A^0=0$. Differentiate the integrand of Theorem 10.3.6 . Since the original Euler–Lagrange expression is zero, derivatives of speed and area do not contribute. The derivative of $H|A^0|^2$ is zero. The derivative of the Laplacian acting on the original constant $H$ is also zero, because every Laplacian annihilates a constant. Thus only $\Delta \dot H$ remains. The Euclidean linearization gives $\dot H=-\Delta f-2f/R^2$. This yields \[  \ddot{\mathcal W}= rac12\int f\Delta (\Delta +2/R^2)f,  \] which is the first formula after integration by parts. For completeness, commuting one covariant derivative of $
abla f$ gives $\operatorname {div}(
abla ^2f)=
abla \Delta f+\operatorname {Ric}(
abla f,\cdot )$. On this two-sphere $\operatorname {Ric}=R^{-2}g$. Integrating the divergence identity against $
abla f$ gives \[  \int |
abla ^2f|^2=\int (\Delta f)^2- rac1{R^2}\int |
abla f|^2.  \] Subtracting half the squared trace produces exactly the preceding Hessian formula. Nonnegativity is now the integral of a squared norm; no spectral decomposition is needed. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.18.10 (Only dilations and translations lie in the spherical kernel)
search_title: Only dilations and translations lie in the spherical kernel
section: 16.18 Round surfaces and circular Willmore tori
text:
Proposition 16.18.10 (Only dilations and translations lie in the spherical kernel) . FF20FCA045C5 The second variation in Proposition 16.18.9 vanishes exactly for functions $f=c+a\cdot X$, with $c\in \mathbb R$ and $a\in \mathbb R^3$. The constant mode is the normal speed of a change of radius; the linear modes are normal translation speeds up to a fixed factor. The normal kernel is therefore four-dimensional. Proof Vanishing of the square gives $
abla ^2f=(\Delta f/2)g$. Take its divergence and use the commutation identity from the preceding proof. It follows that $
abla (\Delta f+2f/R^2)=0$. Averaging this constant expression over the sphere shows that $u=f-\overline f$ satisfies $\Delta u=-2u/R^2$ and hence $
abla ^2u=-ug/R^2$. Regard $
abla u$ as an ambient tangent vector. The Euclidean derivative of $Z=
abla u+(u/R^2)X$ in a tangent direction $V$ is zero: its tangential terms are $-uV/R^2+uV/R^2$, and its normal terms are $-(V u)X/R^2+(V u)X/R^2$, because the sphere's vector-valued second fundamental form is $B(V,W)=-g(V,W)X/R^2$. Connectedness makes $Z=a$ one constant ambient vector. Dotting with $X$ gives $u=a\cdot X$. Conversely every such linear function has Hessian $-ug/R^2$, and constants have zero Hessian, so they lie in the kernel. A translation by a vector $b$ has normal speed $b\cdot X/R$, which spans the same three-dimensional space. These are infinitesimal kernel statements and do not assert convergence of a geometric flow. $\square$

title: 16.19 A finite-energy inversion with a nonsmooth closing point
search_title: A finite-energy inversion with a nonsmooth closing point
section: 16.19 A finite-energy inversion with a nonsmooth closing point
text: The catenoid of Example 16.2.2 and the inversion identity of Section 10.4 give an explicit warning about compactification. The calculations use the first-variation boundary flux in [ SimW93 ] , equation (1.5), but do not assert a removable-singularity theorem. Proposition 16.19.1 (The inverted catenoid has energy eight pi) . A26F36C721D5 For $a>0$, let \[  C_ a(\theta ,v)=(a\cosh v\cos \theta ,a\cosh v\sin \theta ,av), \qquad \theta \in \mathbb R/2\pi \mathbb Z,\  v\in \mathbb R.  \] It avoids zero, and $I_0\circ C_ a$ is a smooth embedded noncompact surface of finite Willmore energy $8\pi $. For its portion with $|v|<T$, $T>0$, the energy is \[  8\pi \frac{\cosh T\sinh T+T}{\cosh ^2T+T^2}.  \] Both ends converge to the origin in the target. Proof The original catenoid is embedded and minimal, and $|C_ a|^2=a^2(\cosh ^2v+v^2)\geq a^2$, so inversion is a diffeomorphism on its image. Lemma 10.4.1 expresses the inverted energy on $|v|<T$ as $4\int |C_ a^\perp |^2/|C_ a|^4$. Apply Theorem 10.4.3 to the compact truncated catenoid with pole zero. It has no pole preimages and zero original mean curvature, so this energy is twice its boundary flux. At $v=T$, the outward conormal is $C_{a,v}/(a\cosh T)$ and the boundary arclength is $a\cosh T\, d\theta $. Therefore that circle contributes \[  \int _0^{2\pi }\frac{C_ a\cdot C_{a,v}}{|C_ a|^2}d\theta =2\pi \frac{\cosh T\sinh T+T}{\cosh ^2T+T^2}.  \] The lower boundary gives the same value, because both $v$ and the outward derivative reverse sign. Multiplying the sum by two proves the displayed energy. Increasing $T$ exhausts the parameter surface, so monotone convergence of the nonnegative energy density and the ratio limit one give $8\pi $. Finally $|I_0(C_ a)|=1/|C_ a|\to 0$ as $v\to \pm \infty $. $\square$ Proposition 16.19.2 (The closing sheets have no twice-differentiable extension) . D49D00FDACD8 Each end of the inverted catenoid can be filled at zero as a rotational graph that is continuously differentiable with horizontal tangent plane, but it has no $C^2$ graph extension there. In particular its finite energy does not make the closure a smooth closed immersed surface to which the smooth Li–Yau theorem can simply be applied. Proof For the upper end, the radial and height coordinates are \[  \rho (v)=\frac{\cosh v}{a(\cosh ^2v+v^2)},\qquad z(v)=\frac{v}{a(\cosh ^2v+v^2)}.  \] As $v\to +\infty $, they satisfy \[  \rho (v)=\frac2a e^{-v}(1+o(1)),\qquad z(v)=\frac4a v e^{-2v}(1+o(1)), \qquad \frac{z(v)}{\rho (v)^2}=av\left(1+\frac{v^2}{\cosh ^2v}\right)\longrightarrow \infty .  \] Differentiating the exact rational expressions shows $\rho '(v)=-(2/a)e^{-v}(1+o(1))<0$ eventually and $z'(v)/\rho '(v)=O(ve^{-v})\to 0$. Thus the end is a graph $z=f(\rho )$ for small positive $\rho $, with $f(0)=0$ and radial gradient tending to zero. This gives a $C^1$ extension on the planar disk. If it had a $C^2$ extension, its zero value and gradient at the origin and Taylor's theorem would imply $f(\rho )=O(\rho ^2)$, contradicting the displayed divergent quotient. The lower end is its reflection and has the same conclusion. The two closing sheets therefore cannot be treated as smooth parameter sheets at their common limiting point. $\square$

title: 16.20 Curvature concentration and boundary energy
search_title: Curvature concentration and boundary energy
section: 16.20 Curvature concentration and boundary energy
text: These examples test the hypotheses in Section 6.12 . They distinguish the area measure, the squared-curvature measure and the singular part of first variation. The weak framework is that of [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 8, Section 2. Example 16.20.1 (A collapsing sphere loses mass and concentrates curvature energy) . BA6CFF390155 Let $S_ j=\partial B_{r_ j}(0)\subset \mathbb R^3$ with $r_ j\downarrow 0$ and multiplicity one. Then $V_{S_ j}\rightharpoonup 0$ as varifolds and $\mathcal W(S_ j)=4\pi $, but their curvature-energy measures satisfy \[  \frac14|\vec H_ j|^2\mathcal H^2\llcorner S_ j\rightharpoonup 4\pi \delta _0.  \] Thus the weak limit's zero curvature energy does not account for all the energy in the approximating sequence. Proof The sphere has area $4\pi r_ j^2$ and $|\vec H_ j|=2/r_ j$. Its varifold mass therefore tends to zero, bounding every compactly supported test integral by its supremum times that mass. The energy is $4\pi $. For a continuous compactly supported scalar test $\phi $, changing variables $x=r_ j\omega $ gives \[  \frac14\int _{S_ j}\phi (x)|\vec H_ j|^2d\mu _ j =\int _{S^2}\phi (r_ j\omega )d\mu _{S^2}\longrightarrow 4\pi \phi (0).  \] Uniform continuity or dominated convergence proves the limit. The zero varifold has zero first variation and zero extended energy. This is strict lower semicontinuity and concentration, not an equality of limit energies. $\square$ Example 16.20.2 (Energy can escape to infinity) . 01D295A558FF The unit spheres centered at $je_1$ converge locally as varifolds to zero while each has area and Willmore energy $4\pi $. Their curvature-energy measures converge vaguely to zero, rather than to a nonzero point mass. Proof Every fixed compact subset of Euclidean space misses those spheres for all sufficiently large $j$. Hence every compactly supported varifold or scalar measure test is eventually zero. Translation does not change either area or mean curvature, giving the constant totals. The loss occurs at infinity and shows why local convergence alone cannot preserve global mass or energy. $\square$ Example 16.20.3 (A disk has zero classical bending energy but infinite full first-variation energy) . 1A05A5759283 Let $V$ be the multiplicity-one varifold of a closed planar disk $D_ R\subset \mathbb R^3$, considered in all of $\mathbb R^3$. Its smooth interior mean curvature is zero, but $\mathcal E_{\mathbb R^3}(V)=+\infty $. The singular boundary first variation is essential. Proof The divergence theorem gives $\delta V(X)=\int _{\partial D_ R}X\cdot \eta \, ds$. Choose smooth compactly supported ambient fields $X_\varepsilon $ that equal the outward radial unit vector on the boundary circle and are supported, on the disk, in an annulus of width at most $\varepsilon $, with uniformly bounded magnitude. Such fields come from smooth radial cutoffs near $r=R$ and a cutoff in the normal coordinate. Then \[  \delta V(X_\varepsilon )=2\pi R,\qquad b_\varepsilon =\int |X_\varepsilon |^2d\| V\| =O(\varepsilon ).  \] The energy definition tested with $tX_\varepsilon $ gives a supremum over $t$ equal to $(2\pi R)^2/(4b_\varepsilon )$, which tends to infinity. If instead one works in an ambient open set not meeting the boundary circle, its first variation is zero there. The ambient domain is therefore part of the assertion. $\square$ Example 16.20.4 (Real multiplicity scales the energy) . 7B753EE4AB09 For the round sphere varifold $V=q|S_ R^2|$ with a constant real multiplicity $q>0$, \[  \mathcal E_{\mathbb R^3}(V)=4\pi q.  \] If $0<q<1$, this is below the smooth closed-surface bound $4\pi $. For every noninteger $q$ the varifold is rectifiable but not integral, and cannot come from a closed immersion counted with ordinary parameter multiplicity. For positive integer $q$ it is integral. Proof Multiplying both first variation and weight by $q$ does not change the representing geometric mean curvature. Its norm is $2/R$ and its weighted area is $4\pi qR^2$. Theorem 6.12.2 therefore gives $4\pi q$. Its density is the real number $q$, so it is nonintegral for $q\notin \mathbb N$. The case $0<q<1$ demonstrates why no unqualified extension of Theorem 10.4.4 to all nonzero varifolds is being asserted. $\square$

title: 15.3 From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
search_title: From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
section: 15.3 From a circular torus to a min-max theorem
text: The sources here are the authors' papers: [ LY82 ] , the opening pages of [ SimW93 ] , and the introduction of [ MNWill ] . The entries distinguish the historical questions of identifying a candidate, proving existence of an optimizer, and determining the sharp value. They do not replace the mathematical statements and proof dependencies linked below. Remark 15.3.1 (A family calculation suggested a global conjecture) . E15742E4F29E Marques–Neves date Willmore's torus conjecture to 1965 in [ MNWill ] , Section 1.1, p. 684. The circular torus with ratio $R/r=\sqrt2$ attains energy $2\pi ^2$, but a calculation over circular tori leaves all other immersions untreated. The same candidate is a stereographic image of the Clifford torus in $S^3$. Theorems 16.18.2 and 10.3.6 , and Example 16.18.5 , explain why this candidate is natural without assuming the eventual global theorem. Remark 15.3.2 (Conformal area separated the multiple-point obstruction) . 07DE29ED0FC2 In their 1982 paper [ LY82 ] , Li–Yau introduced conformal volume and proved a multiplicity bound for the bending energy of an immersed surface; see the introduction and Theorem 6, p. 286. A double point forces energy at least $8\pi $, already above the conjectured torus minimum $2\pi ^2$. Thus the unresolved low-energy problem concerned embeddings. Theorem 10.4.4 gives a direct radial proof of that obstruction, while Corollary 10.4.9 shows precisely how it combines with the later embedded theorem. The two numerical thresholds serve different purposes. Remark 15.3.3 (Existence and the exact minimum were separate achievements) . F2980A8D4351 Simon's 1993 paper [ SimW93 ] , pp. 281–283, established a smooth embedded torus minimizing Willmore energy among embedded tori in each Euclidean ambient dimension at least three. This supplied an optimizer without identifying its sharp energy in three-space. The 2014 paper of Marques–Neves [ MNWill ] , Theorem A, p. 685, determined the positive-genus bound in $S^3$ and its equality case through min-max theory. Their Corollary D, p. 687, realizes the Clifford torus through a five-parameter min-max family. The local square identities developed here illuminate Simon's estimates; neither his full existence proof nor the five-parameter min-max proof has been replaced by those local calculations.

text:
This section develops the explicit Euclidean calculation in [ KMN ] , Section 2.1, Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.2, pp. 4–6 of the supplied manuscript. It explains the scale in Remark 10.1.3 . It does not construct the manifold sweepout of that paper's Theorem 2.4, and it makes no conclusion about multiplicity in an unspecified min-max class. Proposition 10.6.1 (Two rotational catenoids with the same circular boundary) . 81AF723B08AA Fix $R>0$ and $h>0$. A rotational catenoid of waist radius $a>0$, centered at height zero, meets the planes $z=\pm h$ in circles of radius $R$ exactly when \[  R=a\cosh (h/a).  \] There is a unique $t_*>0$ satisfying $t_*	anh t_*=1$. Set $q_*=t_*/\cosh t_*$. If $0<h/R<q_*$, there are exactly two such waist radii. At equality there is exactly one, and above it there is none. The smaller waist corresponds to the larger solution $t=h/a>t_*$. The same threshold parameter occurs in the free-boundary catenoid of Example 16.7.5 ; the present assertion counts rotational solutions for prescribed boundary circles. Proof The catenoid parametrization in Example 16.2.2 has radius $a\cosh v$ at height $av$, giving the equation. On putting $t=h/a$, it becomes $h/R=t/\cosh t$. The derivative of the right side is $(1-t	anh t)/\cosh t$. The function $t	anh t$ is strictly increasing from zero to infinity, since its derivative is $	anh t+t/\cosh ^2t>0$. Thus the ratio increases strictly to a unique maximum and then decreases strictly to zero; its limit at zero is also zero. The number of roots follows by the intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity. Since $a=h/t$, the larger root has the smaller waist. This argument counts rotational solutions and does not assert uniqueness among all surfaces spanning the two circles, or prove their stability indices. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.2 (Exact excess over two disks) . 6672A8E926D4 For a truncated catenoid with waist $a$ and parameter range $|v|\leq T$, put $h=aT$ and $R=a\cosh T$. Its area $A$ and excess over the two radius-$R$ disks are \[  A=2\pi a^2(T+\sinh T\cosh T),\qquad A-2\pi R^2=2\pi a^2\left(T- rac12- rac12e^{-2T}ight).  \] In particular the excess is positive for all sufficiently large $T$, although its ratio to $h^2$ tends to zero as $T	o \infty $. Proof The induced metric is $a^2\cosh ^2v(dv^2+d	heta ^2)$. Integrating the area density over a full angular period and $[-T,T]$ gives the first formula. For the second, subtract $2\pi a^2\cosh ^2T$ and use \[  \sinh T\cosh T-\cosh ^2T=-\cosh T e^{-T} =- rac12(1+e^{-2T}).  \] Finally divide the excess by $h^2=a^2T^2$. The resulting expression is $2\pi (T-1/2-e^{-2T}/2)/T^2$, positive eventually and tending to zero. No limiting interchange with an area-minimizing problem is involved. $\square$ Theorem 10.6.3 (The sharp leading logarithmic neck cost) . AB484D5A03C6 Fix $R>0$ and let $h\downarrow 0$. Choose the smaller waist solution $a(h)$ of Proposition 10.6.1 . If $L=\log (R/h)$ and $T=h/a(h)$, then \[   rac{T}{L}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad T=L+\log L+\log 2+o(1),\qquad  rac{ igl (A(h)-2\pi R^2 igr )L}{h^2}\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] Consequently, for every $\varepsilon >0$ and all sufficiently small $h>0$, \[  A(h)\leq 2\pi R^2+ rac{2\pi (1+\varepsilon )h^2}{\log (R/h)}.  \] This is the dimensionless version of the leading estimate in [ KMN ] , Proposition 2.1 and Remark 2.2; it concerns the explicit rotational neck. Proof The larger root $T$ tends to infinity: on the strictly decreasing branch of $t/\cosh t$, its value $h/R$ tends to zero, and no bounded sequence on that branch can have this limit. The boundary equation yields \[  L=\log \cosh T-\log T =T-\log 2+\log (1+e^{-2T})-\log T.  \] Divide by $T$ to obtain $L/T	o 1$. Rearrangement and $\log T-\log L	o 0$ then give the second expansion. By Proposition 10.6.2 , \[   rac{(A-2\pi R^2)L}{h^2} =2\pi  rac{L}{T}\left(1- rac{1+e^{-2T}}{2T}ight)\longrightarrow 2\pi .  \] The asserted bound is the definition of this limit, with $L>0$ once $h<R$. The logarithm uses a ratio of lengths, so it is invariant under a common change of length units. $\square$ Example 10.6.4 (A cylindrical connector has a larger leading cost) . 2AE5C3C55721 For $0<h<R$, remove a disk of radius $ho \in [0,R]$ from each of the planar radius-$R$ disks at heights $\pm h$, and join the inner boundary circles by a cylinder of radius $ho $. The resulting piecewise smooth comparison set has area \[  2\pi R^2+4\pi hho -2\pi ho ^2.  \] The maximum along this explicit radius family is $2\pi R^2+2\pi h^2$, attained at $ho =h$. For fixed $R$ and $h\downarrow 0$, this excess is larger by an asymptotic factor $\log (R/h)$ than the thin catenoid's excess. Proof The two annuli contribute $2\pi (R^2-ho ^2)$ and the cylinder, of height $2h$, contributes $4\pi hho $. The excess is $2\pi h^2-2\pi (ho -h)^2$, which has the stated maximum because $h$ lies in the allowed interval. The ratio assertion follows from Theorem 10.6.3 . At the joins this comparison set has corners; the displayed calculation alone neither supplies a smooth sweepout with controlled smoothing errors nor identifies a variational width. Those additional requirements belong to the deformation theorem, not this elementary area comparison. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.5 (The exact planar annulus capacity) . C9FC5ED9776D Let $0<a<R$ and $\mathcal A=\{ x\in \mathbb R^2:a<|x|<R\} $. Among smooth functions on the closed annulus with boundary values zero on the inner circle and one on the outer circle, the unique minimizer of $\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2$ is \[  u_0(x)= rac{\log (|x|/a)}{\log (R/a)},\qquad \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u_0|^2= rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}.  \] For every such function $u$, the exact excess identity is \[  \int _{\mathcal A}|
abla u|^2 = rac{2\pi }{\log (R/a)}+\int _{\mathcal A}|
abla (u-u_0)|^2.  \] Proof The radial Laplacian of $\log |x|$ is zero away from zero, so $u_0$ is harmonic. Its radial derivative is $1/(|x|\log (R/a))$; polar integration gives the stated energy. Write $u=u_0+v$, where $v$ vanishes on both boundary circles. Integration by parts gives $\int 
abla u_0\cdot 
abla v=0$. Expanding the square gives the identity. Equality forces $
abla v=0$, and the boundary value then forces $v=0$. This is an exact minimization on a fixed planar annulus. Lemma 7.11.2 already uses the logarithmic profile to remove punctures; the present identity specifies the optimal constant and its equality case. $\square$ Proposition 10.6.6 (Quadratic sheet gain dominates a logarithmic error) . 4A98911260BF Let $\Sigma $ be a smooth closed embedded two-sided minimal surface in a smooth three-manifold, with chosen unit normal $
u $. Suppose $\phi >0$ is smooth and its area second variation satisfies $Q(\phi ,\phi )=-q<0$. For small $t$, set \[  \Sigma _ t=\{ \exp _ p(t\phi (p)
u (p)):p\in \Sigma \} .  \] Then \[  |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}|=2|\Sigma |-qt^2+O(t^4).  \] If a collection of comparison surfaces $S_{t,s}$ additionally satisfies, uniformly in its parameter $s$, \[  |S_{t,s}|\leq |\Sigma _ t|+|\Sigma _{-t}| + rac{Ct^2}{\log (1/|t|)}  \] for some fixed $C$ and all sufficiently small $0<|t|<1$, then every surface in that collection has area at most $2|\Sigma |-(q/2)t^2$ once $t$ is small enough. The existence, topology and continuity of such a collection are additional hypotheses here, not conclusions of this estimate. Proof For small $t$, the normal exponential map is a tubular coordinate map on the compact embedded surface. The positivity of $\phi $ makes the two graphs disjoint when $t
e 0$. Their area function $A(t)$ is smooth, with $A'(0)=0$ by minimality and $A''(0)=-q$ by Theorem 7.1.3 . Taylor expansion through the cubic term gives $A(t)+A(-t)=2A(0)-qt^2+O(t^4)$, because the odd terms cancel. Choose $t$ small enough that the absolute remainder is at most $(q/4)t^2$ and $C/\log (1/|t|)\leq q/4$. Substituting into the assumed uniform comparison gives the result. This algebra explains the competition described in [ KMN ] , p. 2; proving a uniformly controlled manifold deformation requires the separate geometric construction of its Section 2.2. $\square$

text: We use $q(t)=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$, $\psi =q'>0$, $V(t)=W''(q(t))=2-3\operatorname {sech}^2(t/\sqrt2)$ and \[  \mathscr L=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+V(t),\qquad Q(f)=\int _{\mathbb R}(|f'|^2+Vf^2),\qquad \| \psi \| _2^2=c_ W=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}.  \] The positive-gap and kernel questions are posed in [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2, pp. 28–29. We compute the sharp constant for this particular quartic potential. The ground-state identity of Proposition 12.6.2 is already available; the new point is coercivity after removing translation. Lemma 12.8.1 (Two first-order factorizations) . AFBF4999E313 Set \[  \mathcal A=\frac d{dt}+\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2),\qquad \mathcal B=\frac d{dt}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\tanh (t/\sqrt2).  \] Their formal $L^2$ adjoints reverse the derivative sign, and on smooth functions \[  \mathscr L=\mathcal A^*\mathcal A,\qquad \mathcal A\mathcal A^*=\mathcal B^*\mathcal B+\frac32, \qquad \mathcal B\mathcal B^*=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+\frac12.  \] For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$, $Q(f)=\| \mathcal A f\| _2^2$. Its zero space is exactly $\operatorname {span}\{ \psi \} $. Proof For $D=d/dt$ and a real function $b$, $(D+b)^*(D+b)=-D^2+b^2-b'$ and $(D+b)(D+b)^*=-D^2+b^2+b'$. Insert $b=\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ and then $b=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)/\sqrt2$, using $\tanh ^2+\operatorname {sech}^2=1$. Integration by parts proves the quadratic identity for compactly supported smooth functions. Boundedness of the coefficients and density extend it to $H^1$. Since $\psi '/\psi =-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$, $\mathcal A\psi =0$. If $Q(f)=0$, the weak first-order equation gives $(f/\psi )'=0$ on every bounded interval, where $\psi $ is smooth and bounded away from zero. The constants agree on overlaps, so $f=c\psi $ globally. Conversely these functions lie in $H^1$ and have zero quadratic form. $\square$ Proposition 12.8.2 (The bounded kernel on the line) . CF5564CA311E Every bounded $C^2$ solution of $\mathscr Lf=0$ on $\mathbb R$ is a constant multiple of $\psi $. More generally, all solutions have the form \[  f(t)=\psi (t)\left(c_1+c_2\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2}ds\right).  \] The second independent solution grows exponentially as $t\to +\infty $ and is unbounded. Proof Write $f=\psi v$ and use $\mathscr L\psi =0$. The equation becomes $(\psi ^2v')'=0$, yielding the formula. Since $\psi (t)=2\sqrt2 e^{-\sqrt2t}(1+o(1))$ as $t\to +\infty $, its second solution is asymptotic to a nonzero constant times $e^{\sqrt2t}$. A bounded solution therefore has $c_2=0$. Conversely $\psi $ is bounded. This proves the one-dimensional assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(b), without assuming that a bounded solution is square integrable in advance. $\square$ Lemma 12.8.3 (An adjoint primitive for compact orthogonal data) . DF91D11FE50F If $f\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\int f\psi =0$, then \[  g(t)=-\frac1{\psi (t)}\int _{-\infty }^ t f(s)\psi (s)ds  \] is smooth and compactly supported, $\mathcal A^*g=f$, and \[  Q(f)-\frac32\| f\| _2^2 =\| \mathcal B^*\mathcal B g\| _2^2+\frac32\| \mathcal B g\| _2^2.  \] Moreover $\| g\| _2^2\leq (2/3)\| f\| _2^2$. Proof The integral vanishes to the left of the support, and orthogonality makes it vanish to the right as well. Differentiate $\psi g$ to obtain $\mathcal A^*g=f$. Put $T=\mathcal A\mathcal A^*=\mathcal B^*\mathcal B+3/2$. Then $Q(f)=\| Tg\| _2^2$ and $\| f\| _2^2=\langle Tg,g\rangle $. Expand $T$ in these two expressions and integrate by parts; subtracting $3\langle Tg,g\rangle /2$ gives exactly the asserted sum. The lower bound $\langle Tg,g\rangle \geq (3/2)\| g\| _2^2$ gives the final estimate. All integrations here have compact support, so no endpoint behavior is assumed. $\square$ Theorem 12.8.4 (The exact gap away from translation) . 864856B2C443 If $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\int f\psi =0$, then \[  Q(f)\geq \frac32\| f\| _2^2.  \] Equality holds precisely for multiples of $\zeta (t)=\operatorname {sech}(t/\sqrt2)\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$. Thus $3/2$ is the optimal gap. For arbitrary $f\in H^1$, \[  Q(f)\geq \frac32\left(\| f\| _2^2- \frac{|\int f\psi |^2}{c_ W}\right).  \] The existence of a positive gap is the assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(c); the factorization determines its exact value here. Proof First apply Lemma 12.8.3 to compact orthogonal tests. For an arbitrary orthogonal $f$, approximate in $H^1$ by compact smooth functions and subtract a coefficient tending to zero times a fixed compact smooth function having nonzero pairing with $\psi $. This produces orthogonal $f_ j\to f$ in $H^1$, proving the inequality by continuity. Let $g_ j$ be their adjoint primitives. Applied to differences, the last estimate of the lemma makes $g_ j$ Cauchy in $L^2$. Since $g_ j'=\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)g_ j-f_ j$, the derivatives are also Cauchy in $L^2$. Thus $g_ j\to g$ in $H^1$ and $\mathcal A^*g=f$. If equality holds for $f$, the sum identity implies $\mathcal B g_ j\to 0$ in $L^2$, hence $\mathcal B g=0$. Solving this first-order equation gives $g=c\chi $, where $\chi =\operatorname {sech}(t/\sqrt2)$. Direct differentiation gives $\mathcal A^*\chi =(3/\sqrt2)\zeta $, so equality forces the stated form. Conversely $\mathcal B\chi =0$ and the factorization give $\mathscr L\zeta =(3/2)\zeta $. This function is in $H^1$ and is orthogonal to the even function $\psi $, so it realizes equality. For general $f$, subtract its $L^2$ projection onto $\psi $. The quadratic form is unchanged because $\mathcal A\psi =0$, while the squared norm loses exactly the displayed projection term. This proves the last formula. $\square$ Proposition 12.8.5 (All square-integrable eigenfunctions of the normal operator) . 0D25EFCEBA69 If a nonzero real $f\in H^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\mathscr Lf=\lambda f$, then either $\lambda =0$ and $f$ is a multiple of $\psi $, or $\lambda =3/2$ and $f$ is a multiple of $\zeta $. AFBF4999E313 Set \[  \mathcal A=\frac d{dt}+\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2),\qquad \mathcal B=\frac d{dt}+\frac1{\sqrt2}\tanh (t/\sqrt2).  \] Their formal $L^2$ adjoints reverse the derivative sign, and on smooth functions \[  \mathscr L=\mathcal A^*\mathcal A,\qquad \mathcal A\mathcal A^*=\mathcal B^*\mathcal B+\frac32, \qquad \mathcal B\mathcal B^*=-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+\frac12.  \] For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$, $Q(f)=\| \mathcal A f\| _2^2$. Its zero space is exactly $\operatorname {span}\{ \psi \} $. Proof For $D=d/dt$ and a real function $b$, $(D+b)^*(D+b)=-D^2+b^2-b'$ and $(D+b)(D+b)^*=-D^2+b^2+b'$. Insert $b=\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ and then $b=\tanh (t/\sqrt2)/\sqrt2$, using $\tanh ^2+\operatorname {sech}^2=1$. Integration by parts proves the quadratic identity for compactly supported smooth functions. Boundedness of the coefficients and density extend it to $H^1$. Since $\psi '/\psi =-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$, $\mathcal A\psi =0$. If $Q(f)=0$, the weak first-order equation gives $(f/\psi )'=0$ on every bounded interval, where $\psi $ is smooth and bounded away from zero. The constants agree on overlaps, so $f=c\psi $ globally. text: Proposition 12.8.2 (The bounded kernel on the line) . CF5564CA311E Every bounded $C^2$ solution of $\mathscr Lf=0$ on $\mathbb R$ is a constant multiple of $\psi $. More generally, all solutions have the form \[  f(t)=\psi (t)\left(c_1+c_2\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2}ds\right).  \] The second independent solution grows exponentially as $t\to +\infty $ and is unbounded. Proof Write $f=\psi v$ and use $\mathscr L\psi =0$. The equation becomes $(\psi ^2v')'=0$, yielding the formula. Conversely $\psi $ is bounded. This proves the one-dimensional assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(b), without assuming that a bounded solution is square integrable in advance. $\square$

DF91D11FE50F If $f\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\int f\psi =0$, then \[  g(t)=-\frac1{\psi (t)}\int _{-\infty }^ t f(s)\psi (s)ds  \] is smooth and compactly supported, $\mathcal A^*g=f$, and \[  Q(f)-\frac32\| f\| _2^2 =\| \mathcal B^*\mathcal B g\| _2^2+\frac32\| \mathcal B g\| _2^2.  \] Moreover $\| g\| _2^2\leq (2/3)\| f\| _2^2$. Proof The integral vanishes to the left of the support, and orthogonality makes it vanish to the right as well. Differentiate $\psi g$ to obtain $\mathcal A^*g=f$. Expand $T$ in these two expressions and integrate by parts; subtracting $3\langle Tg,g\rangle /2$ gives exactly the asserted sum. The lower bound $\langle Tg,g\rangle \geq (3/2)\| g\| _2^2$ gives the final estimate. All integrations here have compact support, so no endpoint behavior is assumed. $\square$

Thus $3/2$ is the optimal gap. For arbitrary $f\in H^1$, \[  Q(f)\geq \frac32\left(\| f\| _2^2- \frac{|\int f\psi |^2}{c_ W}\right).  \] The existence of a positive gap is the assertion in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(c); the factorization determines its exact value here. text: Write $x=(y,t)\in \mathbb R^ d\times \mathbb R$, $d\geq 1$, and retain $\psi =q'$, $V=W''(q)$ from Section 12.8 . We develop the bounded-kernel argument of [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2(d)–(g), pp. 28–29. Interior elliptic derivative estimates are explicitly retained as an analytic input in the decay step. Lemma 12.9.1 (A bounded positive subsolution cannot persist on all of Euclidean space) . 0A781005EAC2 If $G\in C^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ is bounded above and $\Delta G\geq cG$ for a constant $c>0$, then $G\leq 0$ everywhere. In particular a nonnegative bounded such function is zero. Proof If $G(y_0)>0$, choose $\eta >0$ with $2d\eta <cG(y_0)$. The function $G(y)-\eta |y-y_0|^2$ tends to minus infinity at infinity and attains its maximum at some $y_\eta $. At that point $G(y_\eta )\geq G(y_0)$ and $\Delta G(y_\eta )\leq 2d\eta $. These inequalities contradict $\Delta G\geq cG$. This proof uses only a penalized maximum on the full Euclidean domain; the conclusion need not hold on a bounded domain with positive boundary data. $\square$ Lemma 12.9.2 (Uniform decay in the normal direction) . 53B06602A64D Let $w\in C^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})\cap L^\infty $ solve \[  \Delta _ yw+w_{tt}-V(t)w=0.  \] For every $0<\sigma <\sqrt2$ there is $C_\sigma $ such that \[  |w(y,t)|+|Dw(y,t)|+|D^2w(y,t)| \leq C_\sigma e^{-\sigma |t|}  \] for every $(y,t)$. The constants are uniform in the tangential variable $y$. Proof Choose $0<\delta <1$ and then $\Lambda $ so large that $V(t)>\max \{ \sigma ^2,2\delta ^2\} $ for $|t|\geq \Lambda $. On the upper half-space $t\geq \Lambda $, put \[  B_\eta (y,t)=e^{\sigma (\Lambda -t)}+ \eta \cosh (\delta t)\sum _{i=1}^ d\cosh (\delta y_ i),\qquad \eta >0.  \] The operator $P=\Delta _ y+\partial _ t^2-V(t)$ is strictly negative on each positive summand. In particular the product summands have Laplacian $2\delta ^2$ times themselves; the coefficient is not multiplied by the number of tangential dimensions. The barrier is at least one on $t=\Lambda $ and tends to infinity along every sequence escaping to infinity in the half-space. Let $M=\| w\| _\infty $. If $M=0$ there is nothing to prove. Each of $\pm w-MB_\eta $ is nonpositive on the finite boundary, negative outside a sufficiently large compact set, and has $P(\pm w-MB_\eta )>0$. A positive interior maximum would have $P(\pm w-MB_\eta )<0$ because $V>0$, a contradiction. Therefore $|w|\leq MB_\eta $. Send $\eta \downarrow 0$ at a fixed point to obtain $|w(y,t)|\leq Me^{\sigma (\Lambda -t)}$. The lower half-space is identical, and the remaining strip is handled by increasing the constant. The coefficient $V$ and all its derivatives are uniformly bounded. Interior elliptic estimates on unit balls, followed by bootstrapping, bound first and second derivatives by a constant times the supremum of $|w|$ on a slightly larger ball. These estimates are the external local elliptic input used here. The proved exponential bound on that larger ball differs by at most a fixed factor, so it gives the displayed derivative bounds uniformly in $y$. This justifies the decay step requested in [ ChAC ] , Problem 2(e). $\square$ Proposition 12.9.3 (The translation coefficient is constant) . 8FC283F8B3D2 For a bounded solution as in Lemma 12.9.2 , define \[  a(y)=\frac1{c_ W}\int _{\mathbb R}w(y,t)\psi (t)dt.  \] Then $a$ is bounded and harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$, and hence constant. The remainder $v=w-a\psi $ solves the same linearized equation and satisfies $\int v(y,t)\psi (t)dt=0$ for every $y$. Proof The decay estimates and the exponential decay of $\psi $ justify two tangential derivatives under the integral and integrations by parts in $t$, with vanishing endpoint terms. Thus \[  c_ W\Delta _ y a=\int (Vw-w_{tt})\psi =\int w(V\psi -\psi '')=0.  \] Boundedness follows either from the decay or directly from bounded $w$ and integrable $\psi $. To recall the needed Liouville argument, the mean-value formula for a bounded harmonic function and differentiation of the moving ball give $|D a(y)|\leq C_ d\| a\| _\infty /R$ for every $R>0$. This can also be seen by writing the derivative of its ball average as a boundary integral. Let $R\to \infty $ to conclude $Da=0$. Subtracting the constant multiple of the kernel function gives both remaining assertions. The projection is defined before any conclusion about the entire kernel; no separation-of-variables assumption is used. $\square$ Theorem 12.9.4 (Bounded solutions of the flat linearized equation) . 4372C7E46BA5 Every bounded $C^2$ solution of \[  \Delta w-W''(q(x_{d+1}))w=0 \quad \text{on }\mathbb R^{d+1}  \] is $w(y,t)=a\psi (t)$ for one constant $a$. Together with Proposition 12.8.2 , this holds in every ambient dimension at least one. This is the kernel assertion in [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2, with its normal decay and orthogonality steps made explicit. Proof Take the orthogonal remainder $v$ from Proposition 12.9.3 and define $G(y)=\int _{\mathbb R}v(y,t)^2dt$. It is nonnegative, bounded and twice continuously differentiable by Lemma 12.9.2 . Differentiation, the equation and integration by parts give the exact identity \[  \Delta _ yG=2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+ 2\int \bigl (|v_ t|^2+V(t)v^2\bigr )dt.  \] Each normal slice lies in $H^1$ and is orthogonal to $\psi $. Theorem 12.8.4 therefore implies \[  \Delta _ yG\geq 2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+3G\geq 3G.  \] Lemma 12.9.1 forces $G=0$. Continuity then gives $v=0$, proving the claim. The displayed gradient term is tangential; the inequality is derived from the exact slice energy rather than by discarding the potentially negative normal potential. $\square$ Proposition 12.9.5 (Splitting the full quadratic form into translation and normal parts) . 4A01EE1BF148 For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d\times \mathbb R)$ set \[  a(y)=c_ W^{-1}\int f(y,t)\psi (t)dt,\qquad v(y,t)=f(y,t)-a(y)\psi (t).  \] Then $a\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, $v\in H^1$, and \[  \int \bigl (|Df|^2+Vf^2\bigr ) =c_ W\int |D_ ya|^2+ \int _{\mathbb R^ d}\left(\int _{\mathbb R}|D_ yv|^2dt+Q(v(y,\cdot ))\right)dy.  \] In particular the rightmost term is at least $\int |D_ yv|^2+(3/2)\int v^2$. Proof Cauchy–Schwarz in the normal variable bounds $a$ and each weak tangential derivative in $L^2$. Since $\psi ,\psi '\in L^2$, the product $a\psi $ lies in $H^1$, hence so does $v$. The normal pairing with $\psi $ is zero, including after a tangential weak derivative. Therefore tangential cross terms vanish on integrating in $t$. The normal cross term is $Q(\psi ,v)=0$ by the factorization, and $Q(\psi )=0$. Expanding the quadratic form proves the identity, first for smooth approximations and then by $H^1$ continuity. Apply the sharp normal gap on almost every slice and integrate by Fubini to obtain the estimate. $\square$ Example 12.9.6 (A normal gap does not give a full-space spectral gap) . 09EF9F42AC39 For $d\geq 1$, the full quadratic form of Proposition 12.9.5 is strictly positive on every nonzero $H^1(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ function, but its Rayleigh infimum is zero. Consequently it has no nonzero $H^1$ null vector despite the bounded translation solution $\psi (t)$. Proof If the form is zero, the splitting forces $v=0$ and $D_ ya=0$. A constant in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ is zero, proving strict positivity. For a nonzero $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, take $f_ R(y,t)=\eta (y/R)\psi (t)$. Its Rayleigh quotient is \[  R^{-2}\frac{\int |D\eta |^2}{\int \eta ^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] These are $H^1$ functions; cutting off the exponentially decaying normal factor approximates them by compactly supported tests with the same limiting quotients. The bounded function $\psi (t)$ is not in $L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ because the tangential factor has infinite volume. This separates bounded-kernel rigidity, normal coercivity and a positive spectral gap on the whole space. $\square$

Proof The decay estimates and the exponential decay of $\psi $ justify two tangential derivatives under the integral and integrations by parts in $t$, with vanishing endpoint terms. Thus \[  c_ W\Delta _ y a=\int (Vw-w_{tt})\psi =\int w(V\psi -\psi '')=0.  \] Boundedness follows either from the decay or directly from bounded $w$ and integrable $\psi $. To recall the needed Liouville argument, the mean-value formula for a bounded harmonic function and differentiation of the moving ball give $|D a(y)|\leq C_ d\| a\| _\infty /R$ for every $R>0$. This can also be seen by writing the derivative of its ball average as a boundary integral. Let $R\to \infty $ to conclude $Da=0$. Subtracting the constant multiple of the kernel function gives both remaining assertions. The projection is defined before any conclusion about the entire kernel; no separation-of-variables assumption is used. $\square$

text: Theorem 12.9.4 (Bounded solutions of the flat linearized equation) . 4372C7E46BA5 Every bounded $C^2$ solution of \[  \Delta w-W''(q(x_{d+1}))w=0 \quad \text{on }\mathbb R^{d+1}  \] is $w(y,t)=a\psi (t)$ for one constant $a$. Together with Proposition 12.8.2 , this holds in every ambient dimension at least one. This is the kernel assertion in [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 2, with its normal decay and orthogonality steps made explicit. Proof Take the orthogonal remainder $v$ from Proposition 12.9.3 and define $G(y)=\int _{\mathbb R}v(y,t)^2dt$. It is nonnegative, bounded and twice continuously differentiable by Lemma 12.9.2 . Differentiation, the equation and integration by parts give the exact identity \[  \Delta _ yG=2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+ 2\int \bigl (|v_ t|^2+V(t)v^2\bigr )dt.  \] Each normal slice lies in $H^1$ and is orthogonal to $\psi $. Theorem 12.8.4 therefore implies \[  \Delta _ yG\geq 2\int |D_ yv|^2dt+3G\geq 3G.  \] Lemma 12.9.1 forces $G=0$. Continuity then gives $v=0$, proving the claim. The displayed gradient term is tangential; the inequality is derived from the exact slice energy rather than by discarding the potentially negative normal potential. $\square$
