text: Proposition 12.9.5 (Splitting the full quadratic form into translation and normal parts) . 4A01EE1BF148 For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d\times \mathbb R)$ set \[  a(y)=c_ W^{-1}\int f(y,t)\psi (t)dt,\qquad v(y,t)=f(y,t)-a(y)\psi (t).  \] Then $a\in H^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, $v\in H^1$, and \[  \int \bigl (|Df|^2+Vf^2\bigr ) =c_ W\int |D_ ya|^2+ \int _{\mathbb R^ d}\left(\int _{\mathbb R}|D_ yv|^2dt+Q(v(y,\cdot ))\right)dy.  \] In particular the rightmost term is at least $\int |D_ yv|^2+(3/2)\int v^2$. Proof Cauchy–Schwarz in the normal variable bounds $a$ and each weak tangential derivative in $L^2$. Since $\psi ,\psi '\in L^2$, the product $a\psi $ lies in $H^1$, hence so does $v$. The normal pairing with $\psi $ is zero, including after a tangential weak derivative. Therefore tangential cross terms vanish on integrating in $t$. The normal cross term is $Q(\psi ,v)=0$ by the factorization, and $Q(\psi )=0$. Expanding the quadratic form proves the identity, first for smooth approximations and then by $H^1$ continuity. Apply the sharp normal gap on almost every slice and integrate by Fubini to obtain the estimate. $\square$

title: Example 12.9.6 (A normal gap does not give a full-space spectral gap)

text: Example 12.9.6 (A normal gap does not give a full-space spectral gap) . 09EF9F42AC39 For $d\geq 1$, the full quadratic form of Proposition 12.9.5 is strictly positive on every nonzero $H^1(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ function, but its Rayleigh infimum is zero. Consequently it has no nonzero $H^1$ null vector despite the bounded translation solution $\psi (t)$. Proof If the form is zero, the splitting forces $v=0$ and $D_ ya=0$. A constant in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ is zero, proving strict positivity. For a nonzero $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, take $f_ R(y,t)=\eta (y/R)\psi (t)$. Its Rayleigh quotient is \[  R^{-2}\frac{\int |D\eta |^2}{\int \eta ^2}\longrightarrow 0.  \] These are $H^1$ functions; cutting off the exponentially decaying normal factor approximates them by compactly supported tests with the same limiting quotients. The bounded function $\psi (t)$ is not in $L^2(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ because the tangential factor has infinite volume. This separates bounded-kernel rigidity, normal coercivity and a positive spectral gap on the whole space. $\square$

We follow the local calculations of [ ChAC ] , Appendix B, Problem 3, pp. 29–31, with explicit signs, boundedness conditions and error norms. Let $\Sigma ^2\subset \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth two-sided embedded surface, $
u $ a chosen unit normal, and $A=D
u $. Work on a relatively compact coordinate patch $K$ inside a larger patch $U$ on which \[  F(y,z)=y+z
u (y),\qquad |z|<ho ,  \] is an injective tubular parametrization, with $I+zA$ uniformly positive definite on a neighborhood of $K	imes [-ho ,ho ]$. All estimates below are uniform on this fixed tube over $K$, with constants depending on its geometry and the stated smooth functions. We write $H=\operatorname {tr}A$, $K_\Sigma =\det A$, and retain the quartic potential, profile $q$, and $\psi =q'$ from Section 12.8 . No closed nonflat minimal surface in Euclidean space is assumed. Lemma 12.10.1 (The exact metric, Jacobian and parallel curvature) . 5C6FEA2AE720 In these coordinates the Euclidean metric, volume density relative to $d\mu _\Sigma \, dz$, and parallel shape operator are \[  g_{\mathbb R^3}=dz^2+g_ z,\qquad g_ z(v,w)=g((I+zA)v,(I+zA)w),\qquad D(y,z)=\det (I+zA)=1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2,  \] \[  A_ z=A(I+zA)^{-1},\qquad H_ z=\partial _ z\log D=\sum _{i=1}^2 rac{\kappa _ i}{1+z\kappa _ i}, \qquad \partial _ zH_ z=-|A_ z|^2.  \] Here $\kappa _1,\kappa _2$ are the principal curvatures at $y$, and $A_ z$ is identified through the parallel tangent planes. Proof Differentiate $F$ tangentially to get $dF(v)=(I+zA)v$, while $\partial _ zF=
u $ is orthogonal to every tangential derivative and has length one. This proves the metric formula. Diagonalizing $A$ gives the positive volume ratio $(1+z\kappa _1)(1+z\kappa _2)$ and its stated polynomial. The normal of each parallel surface is still $
u (y)$, so differentiation along its tangent vector $(I+zA)v$ gives $Av$. Thus its shape operator is $A(I+zA)^{-1}$. Taking its trace and differentiating each eigenvalue proves both remaining formulas. Positivity and injectivity of the chosen tube are used to avoid a focal point or a self-intersection, not inferred merely from the formulas. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.2 (The Laplacian and the special cancellation for minimal surfaces) . 022784D6AABA For every smooth function $f$ in the tube, \[  \Delta f=f_{zz}+H_ zf_ z+\Delta _{g_ z}f.  \] If $\Sigma $ is minimal and $a(y)=|A(y)|^2$, then \[  D=1- rac{a z^2}{2},\qquad H_ z=- rac{az}{1-az^2/2}=-az+O(z^3).  \] For a smooth function $h(y)$ independent of $z$, $\Delta _{g_ z}h=\Delta _\Sigma h+O(|z|)$ uniformly on the fixed patch, with the last constant controlled by its first two derivatives and the local geometry. Proof In block diagonal coordinates the divergence formula for the Laplacian separates into $D^{-1}\partial _ z(Df_ z)$ and the tangential Laplace–Beltrami operator. Lemma 12.10.1 gives the coefficient of $f_ z$. For a minimal surface the principal curvatures are $\kappa ,-\kappa $, hence $a=2\kappa ^2$ and $D=1-az^2/2$. Differentiating its logarithm gives the exact rational expression. Its difference from $-az$ is $-a^2z^3/[2(1-az^2/2)]$, uniformly of order $z^3$ on the chosen tube. Finally the coefficients of $\Delta _{g_ z}$ and their first tangential derivatives vary smoothly with $z$. Subtract their values at zero in the coordinate formula; every difference is bounded by $C|z|$. This gives the last estimate without asserting an equality between the metrics at nonzero $z$. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.3 (When the distance profile is an exact solution) . 8A22C57A90B9 Put $u_\varepsilon (F(y,z))=q(z/\varepsilon )$ and $R_\varepsilon =\varepsilon ^2\Delta u_\varepsilon -W'(u_\varepsilon )$. Then $R_\varepsilon =\varepsilon H_ z\psi (z/\varepsilon )$, which is uniformly $O(\varepsilon )$, and is uniformly $O(\varepsilon ^2)$ when $\Sigma $ is minimal. If this profile is an exact solution throughout a tube for even one $\varepsilon >0$, then $A=0$ on its base; every connected base patch is contained in a plane. If $H(y_0)
e 0$, the general $O(\varepsilon )$ estimate is sharp at $(y_0,0)$. Proof The equation $q''=W'(q)$ cancels the normal second derivative, leaving precisely the residual already identified in Proposition 12.4.4 . The boundedness of $H_ z$ gives the general estimate. In the minimal case $|H_ z|\leq C|z|$, and $|t|\psi (t)$ is bounded, giving $C\varepsilon ^2$. If the residual vanishes identically, positivity of $\psi $ forces $H_ z=0$ for every $z$ in the tube. Differentiate at zero using Lemma 12.10.1 : $0=-|A|^2$. The normal is therefore constant on each connected patch, and $y\cdot 
u $ is constant along it, proving planarity. Finally $R_\varepsilon (y_0,0)=\varepsilon H(y_0)\psi (0)$ proves sharpness when the mean curvature does not vanish. $\square$ Lemma 12.10.4 (The bounded odd normal corrector) . C4389C0124F3 There is exactly one bounded solution $j$ of \[  j''-Vj=t\psi ,\qquad j(0)=0.  \] It is odd, belongs to $H^2(\mathbb R)$, and is given by \[  j(t)=\psi (t)\int _0^ t\psi (s)^{-2} \left(\int _{-\infty }^ s	au \psi (	au )^2\, d	au ight)ds.  \] It is negative for $t>0$, orthogonal to $\psi $, and satisfies $|j|+|j'|+|j''|\leq C(1+t^2)e^{-\sqrt2|t|}$. Its primitive $I(s)$ from minus infinity is even and strictly negative at every finite $s$: for $s\leq 0$ this is immediate, and for $s>0$ use $I(s)=-\int _ s^\infty 	au \psi (	au )^2d	au $. D44443082E59 Assume $\Sigma $ is minimal and set $a=|A|^2$, $t=z/\varepsilon $ and \[  u_\varepsilon =q(t)+\varepsilon ^2a(y)j(t).  \] Then $\| \varepsilon ^2\Delta u_\varepsilon -W'(u_\varepsilon )\| _{C^0(K	imes (-ho ,ho ))} \leq C\varepsilon ^4$ for $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. Proof Since $W'(u)=u^3-u$, direct substitution and Lemma 12.10.4 give the exact residual \[  \varepsilon (H_ z+az)\psi (t)+ \varepsilon ^3H_ z a j'(t)+\varepsilon ^4j(t)\Delta _{g_ z}a -3\varepsilon ^4q(t)a^2j(t)^2-\varepsilon ^6a^3j(t)^3.  \] The first term is bounded by $C\varepsilon |z|^3\psi (t)\leq C\varepsilon ^4$, because $|t|^3\psi (t)$ is bounded. The improved order uses the odd expansion of $H_ z$ for a two-dimensional minimal surface in Euclidean three-space; it is not an asserted dimension-independent cancellation. $\square$ Lemma 12.10.6 (Shifted layers and the cubic error) . B460B0616D6E On a minimal patch let $h$ be smooth and put \[  u_\varepsilon (y,z)=q(t-\varepsilon h(y))+\varepsilon ^2a(y)j(t).  \] With $a=|A|^2$ and $t=z/\varepsilon $, its residual is \[  R_\varepsilon (y,\varepsilon t)=\varepsilon ^3 \left[-\psi (t)\Delta _\Sigma h+ ah\{ t\psi '(t)+W'''(q(t))\psi (t)j(t)\} ight]+O(\varepsilon ^4)  \] uniformly for $y\in K$, $|t|<ho /\varepsilon $. The displacement of the profile's center is $\varepsilon ^2h$, not $\varepsilon h$. Proof Write $s=t-\varepsilon h$. Tangential differentiation gives $\Delta _{g_ z}q(s)=-\varepsilon \psi (s)\Delta _{g_ z}h+\varepsilon ^2q''(s)|D_{g_ z}h|^2$. Normal differentiation and expansion of the cubic potential give \[  R_\varepsilon =\varepsilon H_ z\psi (s) -\varepsilon ^3\psi (s)\Delta _{g_ z}h +\varepsilon ^4q''(s)|D_{g_ z}h|^2 +\varepsilon ^2a\{ j''-W''(q(s))j\}  +\varepsilon ^3H_ zaj'+\varepsilon ^4j\Delta _{g_ z}a -3\varepsilon ^4q(s)a^2j^2-\varepsilon ^6a^3j^3.  \] Use $H_ z=-a\varepsilon t+O(\varepsilon ^3|t|^3)$, $\psi (s)=\psi (t)-\varepsilon h\psi '(t)+O(\varepsilon ^2)$, and $W''(q(s))=V(t)-\varepsilon hW'''(q(t))\psi (t)+O(\varepsilon ^2)$. Taylor remainders for a shift of size at most $\varepsilon \| h\| _\infty $ have the same decay with a fixed larger constant; factors $|t|^ m$ are therefore harmless. These are $C^0$ estimates in the physical tube. Unscaled normal derivatives introduce powers of $\varepsilon ^{-1}$, so no assertion about errors of the same order in every unscaled derivative is made. Finally the center equation $s=0$ gives $z=\varepsilon ^2h$. $\square$ Proposition 12.10.7 (Projection onto translation produces the surface Jacobi operator) . 3B888F82739D Under Lemma 12.10.6 , \[  \int _{-ho /\varepsilon }^{ho /\varepsilon } R_\varepsilon (y,\varepsilon t)\psi (t)\, dt =-\varepsilon ^3c_ W(\Delta _\Sigma h+|A|^2h)+O(\varepsilon ^4)  \] uniformly for $y\in K$. Thus cancellation of the leading projected residual is the Jacobi equation on the interface. This is the solvability calculation in [ ChAC ] , Problem 3(o)–(p); it does not supply a global inverse or a nonlinear gluing theorem. Proof All endpoint terms below vanish by the corrector and profile bounds. First, \[  I_1=\int t\psi '\psi =- rac12\int \psi ^2=- rac{c_ W}{2}.  \] Differentiating $\psi ''-V\psi =0$ gives $\psi '''-V\psi '=V'\psi =W'''(q)\psi ^2$. The self-adjoint one-dimensional integration by parts then yields \[  I_2=\int W'''(q)\psi ^2j =\int (\psi '''-V\psi ')j =\int \psi '(j''-Vj)=\int t\psi '\psi =- rac{c_ W}{2}.  \] Pair the cubic residual with $\psi $: its coefficient is $-c_ W\Delta _\Sigma h+ah(I_1+I_2)=-c_ W(\Delta _\Sigma h+ah)$. Replacing the finite interval by the line in this coefficient incurs only an exponentially small error. The uniform remainder, paired with the integrable $\psi $, is still $O(\varepsilon ^4)$, without a factor equal to the length of the interval. This proves the formula and identifies exactly which geometric operator arises. $\square$

Uniformity on the expanding interval in $t$ follows from exponential decay of every positive-order derivative of $q$ and the polynomial-times-exponential bounds on $j$. Taylor remainders for a shift of size at most $\varepsilon \| h\| _\infty $ have the same decay with a fixed larger constant; factors $|t|^ m$ are therefore harmless. These are $C^0$ estimates in the physical tube. Unscaled normal derivatives introduce powers of $\varepsilon ^{-1}$, so no assertion about errors of the same order in every unscaled derivative is made. Finally the center equation $s=0$ gives $z=\varepsilon ^2h$. $\square$

text: Proposition 12.10.7 (Projection onto translation produces the surface Jacobi operator) . 3B888F82739D Under Lemma 12.10.6 , \[  \int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon } R_\varepsilon (y,\varepsilon t)\psi (t)\, dt =-\varepsilon ^3c_ W(\Delta _\Sigma h+|A|^2h)+O(\varepsilon ^4)  \] uniformly for $y\in K$. Thus cancellation of the leading projected residual is the Jacobi equation on the interface. This is the solvability calculation in [ ChAC ] , Problem 3(o)–(p); it does not supply a global inverse or a nonlinear gluing theorem. Proof All endpoint terms below vanish by the corrector and profile bounds. First, \[  I_1=\int t\psi '\psi =-\frac12\int \psi ^2=-\frac{c_ W}{2}.  \] Differentiating $\psi ''-V\psi =0$ gives $\psi '''-V\psi '=V'\psi =W'''(q)\psi ^2$. The self-adjoint one-dimensional integration by parts then yields \[  I_2=\int W'''(q)\psi ^2j =\int (\psi '''-V\psi ')j =\int \psi '(j''-Vj)=\int t\psi '\psi =-\frac{c_ W}{2}.  \] Pair the cubic residual with $\psi $: its coefficient is $-c_ W\Delta _\Sigma h+ah(I_1+I_2)=-c_ W(\Delta _\Sigma h+ah)$. Replacing the finite interval by the line in this coefficient incurs only an exponentially small error. The uniform remainder, paired with the integrable $\psi $, is still $O(\varepsilon ^4)$, without a factor equal to the length of the interval. This proves the formula and identifies exactly which geometric operator arises. $\square$

Here $(M^ n,g)$ is a smooth nonempty closed Riemannian manifold, $n\geq 1$, and $\varepsilon >0$ is fixed. We develop the compactness calculation suggested in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4, p. 14. The residual retains the correct $\varepsilon ^2$ factor. The needed Sobolev compactness is proved in Section 7.18 ; elliptic regularity remains an analytic input identified in the proofs. The resulting compactness statement alone is not a mountain-pass existence theorem. Proposition 12.11.1 (An energy identity for every closed critical point) . 1605E7AF7DC3 A smooth solution of $\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u=u^3-u$ satisfies \[  \varepsilon ^2\int _ M|
abla u|^2=\int _ M(u^2-u^4),\qquad E_\varepsilon (u;M)= rac{\operatorname {Vol}(M)-\int _ Mu^4}{4\varepsilon }.  \] In particular $0\leq E_\varepsilon (u;M)\leq \operatorname {Vol}(M)/(4\varepsilon )$ and $\int _ M|
abla u|^2\leq \operatorname {Vol}(M)/(4\varepsilon ^2)$. Equality in the energy upper bound occurs precisely for $u=0$. Proof Multiply the equation by $u$ and integrate by parts on the closed manifold. This gives the first identity. Substitute its gradient term into $E_\varepsilon =\varepsilon \int |
abla u|^2/2+(4\varepsilon )^{-1}\int (1-2u^2+u^4)$; the $u^2$ terms cancel and give the second. Nonnegativity follows from the original energy definition. Proposition 12.2.3 gives $|u|\leq 1$, and $u^2-u^4\leq 1/4$, proving the gradient bound. The energy upper bound follows from $u^4\geq 0$, and equality forces $u=0$ by continuity. The identities concern critical points, not arbitrary functions with the same pointwise bound. $\square$ Theorem 12.11.2 (Strong compactness for a bounded residual sequence) . A1F06EA746A2 Let $u_ j\in H^1(M)$ satisfy $|u_ j|\leq 1$ almost everywhere and $E_\varepsilon (u_ j;M)\leq C$. Suppose that \[  r_ j=-\varepsilon ^2\Delta _ g u_ j+W'(u_ j)\longrightarrow 0 \quad 	ext{in }H^{-1}(M),  \] where $H^{-1}$ is the dual of $H^1(M)$ with its full norm. Then a subsequence converges strongly in $H^1$ and in every finite $L^ p$ to a smooth critical point $u$, with $|u|\leq 1$ and $E_\varepsilon (u_ j;M)	o E_\varepsilon (u;M)$. This develops the bounded-range compactness mechanism in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4, with the residual normalized to the displayed $\varepsilon $-equation. For this same residual, convergence in $L^2$ implies the $H^{-1}$ convergence assumed here. Proof The pointwise bound controls the $L^2$ norms, and the energy controls the gradients because $\varepsilon $ is fixed. Weak $H^1$ compactness and Theorem 7.18.2 supply a subsequence with $u_ jightharpoonup u$ in $H^1$ and $u_ j	o u$ strongly in $L^2$ and almost everywhere. The limit lies in $[-1,1]$. Since $W'$ is Lipschitz on this interval, $W'(u_ j)	o W'(u)$ in $L^2$. Passing to the equation against smooth tests shows that $u$ is a weak solution, and density gives the equation against every $H^1$ test. Subtract the limit equation and test with $u_ j-u$: \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |
abla (u_ j-u)|^2 =\langle r_ j,u_ j-uangle -\int (W'(u_ j)-W'(u))(u_ j-u).  \] The dual pairing tends to zero because the tests stay bounded in $H^1$, and the second term tends to zero by strong $L^2$ convergence. Thus convergence is strong in $H^1$. Boundedness by one upgrades it to every finite $L^ p$: for $p\geq 2$ use $|u_ j-u|^ p\leq 2^{p-2}|u_ j-u|^2$, and for smaller $p$ use finite volume. The potential $W$ is Lipschitz on $[-1,1]$, so its integrals converge; strong gradient convergence then gives energy convergence. Finally a bounded weak solution of this smooth semilinear equation is smooth by interior elliptic $W^{2,p}$ estimates followed by Sobolev embedding and bootstrapping in finitely many coordinate charts. These elliptic regularity inputs are external here. There is no restriction $n\leq 4$: the assumed uniform range bound supplies the integrability of the nonlinearity even when $H^1$ alone would not embed into $L^4$. $\square$ Corollary 12.11.3 (The entire critical set is compact for fixed epsilon) . AC5DCB969E47 For a fixed $\varepsilon >0$ and fixed smooth closed $(M,g)$, every sequence of smooth Allen–Cahn critical points has a subsequence converging in $C^ k(M)$ for every finite $k$ to a smooth critical point. The constants in these compactness estimates may depend on $\varepsilon $. Proof The maximum bound and Proposition 12.11.1 supply all assumptions of Theorem 12.11.2 , with residual zero. For the stronger convergence, the equation has uniformly bounded right-hand side after division by the fixed $\varepsilon ^2$. Global estimates obtained from the finitely many local elliptic charts give uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for every finite $p$. Choose $p>n$ to control $C^{1,\alpha }$, and bootstrap the smooth polynomial nonlinearity to uniform bounds of all derivative orders. These are the same external elliptic estimates used in the theorem. Arzela–Ascoli and a diagonal subsequence give every $C^ k$ convergence. The limit equation follows either from this convergence or from the preceding weak argument. These estimates do not assert compactness as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. $\square$ Proposition 12.11.4 (Index cannot increase in a bounded-range strong limit) . 30298CFE6EFF Fix $\varepsilon >0$. If $|u_ j|,|u|\leq 1$ almost everywhere and $u_ j	o u$ in $L^2(M)$, define the index of each quadratic form \[  Q_{\varepsilon ,u}(\phi )=\int _ M  igl (\varepsilon |
abla \phi |^2+\varepsilon ^{-1}(3u^2-1)\phi ^2 igr )  \] as the supremum of dimensions of negative definite subspaces of smooth tests. Then $\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u}) \leq \liminf _ j\operatorname {index}(Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j})$. In particular a fixed upper bound for the indices of the critical points passes to the limit in Theorem 12.11.2 . Proof Take any finite-dimensional negative subspace for the limit form and a smooth basis $\phi _1,\ldots ,\phi _ m$. Since $|u_ j^2-u^2|\leq 2|u_ j-u|$, the potential terms in every matrix entry $Q_{\varepsilon ,u_ j}(\phi _ r,\phi _ s)$ converge to those of the limit form by $L^2$ convergence and boundedness of the fixed tests. The negative definite limit matrix is bounded above by $-\delta $ times the Euclidean norm squared on its coefficient vectors for some $\delta >0$, using compactness of the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^ m$. Entrywise convergence preserves negative definiteness for all large $j$. Therefore the approximating indices are eventually at least $m$. Taking all possible finite $m$ proves the claim, including the case of an infinite limit index. No convergence of eigenfunction bases is assumed. $\square$ Proposition 12.11.5 (A sharp necessary parameter range for nonconstant solutions) . 8EFAD482DAF6 Assume $M$ is connected, and let \[  \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {v\in H^1(M),\  \int _ Mv=0\ v
e 0}}  rac{\int _ M|
abla v|^2}{\int _ Mv^2}>0.  \] If $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$, every smooth Allen–Cahn critical point is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $. On a circle this threshold is sharp, as the periodic examples exist for every $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1<1$. Proof Corollary 7.18.3 gives positivity of $\lambda _1$ and the Poincare inequality. Let $ ar u$ be the average of a critical point and set $v=u- ar u$. Testing its equation with $v$ gives \[  \varepsilon ^2\int |
abla u|^2-\int v^2 +\int (u^3- ar u^3)(u- ar u)=0.  \] The first two terms together are nonnegative by $\varepsilon ^2\lambda _1\geq 1$ and Poincare. The final integrand is nonnegative because the cubic is strictly increasing, and vanishes only when $u= ar u$. It follows that $u$ is constant, including in the equality case of the threshold. The equation then forces one of the three stated values. On the circle of length $\ell $, $\lambda _1=(2\pi /\ell )^2$, from the Fourier modes. Example 16.21.6 supplies a one-oscillation solution exactly for $\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$, proving sharpness on this model. No sufficiency claim for a general manifold is made. $\square$

text: The Hamiltonian in Lemma 12.2.5 describes many solutions outside the finite-energy class. We develop the infinite-energy examples suggested in [ ChAC ] , Section 2.2 and Exercise 2.2, and unpack the periodic orbit appearing in Lemma 12.6.9 . Throughout this section $\varepsilon =1$ unless explicitly rescaled. Proposition 16.21.1 (Every bounded entire profile stays between the wells) . 828FD329FEDF If $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ is bounded and solves $f''=f^3-f$, then $|f|\leq 1$. If it takes the value $+1$ or $-1$, it is that constant. For its Hamiltonian $C=(f')^2/2-W(f)$ one has $-1/4\leq C\leq 0$. Proof Suppose $f(t_0)=b>1$. Reverse time if necessary so that $f'(t_0)\geq 0$. As long as $f\geq b$, its second derivative is at least $b^3-b>0$. Integration shows that it remains above $b$ with increasing derivative for every later time, contradicting boundedness. Apply the same argument to $-f$ to exclude values below $-1$. At a well, a nonzero derivative would cross outside the allowed range; with zero derivative, ODE uniqueness gives the constant solution. Since $W(f)\leq 1/4$, the Hamiltonian is at least $-1/4$. If it were positive, the identity $(f')^2=2(W(f)+C)\geq 2C$ would make $f'$ nonvanishing with constant sign and magnitude bounded below on the line. That again contradicts boundedness. This proves both endpoints of the permitted range without assuming that a global maximum is attained. $\square$ Theorem 16.21.2 (Classification of bounded entire profiles) . C7DBCCB764C2 Every bounded entire solution is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $, a translated and possibly reversed heteroclinic, or a periodic profile with amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ oscillating between $-a$ and $a$. For each amplitude there is, up to translation and reversal, exactly one such periodic solution. It satisfies \[  (f')^2=\frac12(a^2-f^2)(2-a^2-f^2),\qquad C=-W(a).  \] The periodic profiles and the zero constant have infinite total energy on the line. This extends the finite-energy classification of Theorem 12.2.6 , rather than identifying these distinct classes, and supplies the bounded infinite-energy examples asked for in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.2. Proof Proposition 16.21.1 treats the wells. At $C=0$, separation on $(-1,1)$ gives precisely the heteroclinics already classified. At $C=-1/4$, the identity forces $f'=0$ and $W(f)=1/4$, so $f=0$. For $-1/4<C<0$, there is a unique $a\in (0,1)$ with $W(a)=-C$, since $W$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$. Factoring $2(W(f)-W(a))$ gives the displayed expression. On the permitted range $(-1,1)$ this is nonnegative exactly when $|f|\leq a$. The separated time integral from $-a$ to $a$ is finite: both endpoint zeros are simple. Starting at $(f,f')=(0,\sqrt{2(W(0)-W(a))})$, the solution reaches $a$, turns because $f''=a^3-a<0$, reaches $-a$ and turns again. Reflection at the extrema and ODE uniqueness produce a smooth periodic solution. The conserved orbit contains every possible nonconstant datum at this energy, proving uniqueness up to its phase and reversal. Its energy over a period is positive, so summing disjoint periods gives infinite total energy. The constant zero has the positive constant energy density $1/4$. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.3 (The fundamental period is strictly increasing) . BF7D7DE9DC38 For amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ the least period is \[  T(a)=4\sqrt2\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{d\theta }{\sqrt{\, 2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )\, }}.  \] It is smooth and strictly increasing, with $\lim _{a\downarrow 0}T(a)=2\pi $ and $\lim _{a\uparrow 1}T(a)=+\infty $. For $a\geq 1/2$ it satisfies $T(a)\leq C(1+|\log (1-a^2)|)$. Proof One quarter-period is the time from $0$ to $a$. In its separated integral substitute $f=a\sin \theta $; the factor $a\cos \theta $ cancels and yields the formula. This orbit is strictly monotone between successive extrema, so the resulting full return is the least period. On any compact amplitude subinterval the denominator stays positive. Differentiating under the integral gives \[  T'(a)=4\sqrt2\, a\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{1+\sin ^2\theta }{[2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )]^{3/2}}\, d\theta >0.  \] Dominated convergence at zero gives $2\pi $. At one, the integrand increases to $1/\cos \theta $, whose integral diverges, proving the other limit by monotone convergence. Write the squared denominator as $2(1-a^2)+a^2\cos ^2\theta $. For $a\geq 1/2$ and $r=\pi /2-\theta $, use $\cos \theta =\sin r\geq 2r/\pi $. The integral is bounded by a constant times $\int _0^{\pi /2}((1-a^2)+r^2)^{-1/2}dr$. Its elementary antiderivative gives the logarithmic upper bound. $\square$ Example 16.21.4 (Small oscillations and a single long-period layer) . 257BC8D7226F Normalize the increasing zero of the periodic profile by $f_ a(0)=0$ and $f_ a'(0)>0$. Then \[  a^{-1}f_ a(t)\longrightarrow \sin t\quad (a\downarrow 0),\qquad f_ a(t)\longrightarrow q(t)\quad (a\uparrow 1)  \] in $C^\infty $ on every compact interval. Each long-period solution contains both an increasing and a decreasing transition; the second moves outside every fixed interval under this normalization. Proof The initial derivative is $f_ a'(0)=a\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Thus $v_ a=f_ a/a$ solves $v_ a''=a^2v_ a^3-v_ a$ with $v_ a(0)=0$ and $v_ a'(0)=\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Since $|v_ a|\leq 1$, the integral form of this ODE and Gronwall's inequality give convergence with first derivatives to the solution of $v''=-v$, $v(0)=0$, $v'(0)=1$. The equation and successive differentiations give every higher derivative. This limit is $\sin t$. At the other endpoint the initial data converge to $(0,1/\sqrt2)$ for the unchanged equation $f''=f^3-f$. The same continuous-dependence argument, using $|f_ a|\leq 1$, yields the heteroclinic $q$ on compact intervals. Its decreasing zero occurs at $T(a)/2$, which diverges by Proposition 16.21.3 . This explains why local convergence to one layer is compatible with a second transition in every full period. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.5 (Energy of one periodic cell) . 29FB8961950E Let $\mathcal E(a)=\int _0^{T(a)}((f_ a')^2/2+W(f_ a))dt$. Then \[  \mathcal E(a)=4\int _0^ a\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}\, ds+W(a)T(a), \qquad \mathcal E'(a)=W(a)T'(a)>0.  \] Its endpoint limits are $\pi /2$ at $a=0$ and $2c_ W$ at $a=1$. Proof The Hamiltonian says that the energy density is $(f_ a')^2+W(a)$. Substitution of the profile value on each quarter-period therefore gives the first formula. Write the first term as $J(a)$. The integrand vanishes at its upper endpoint, and its parameter derivative has only an integrable inverse-square-root singularity there. Differentiation, justified either by the substitution $s=a\sin \theta $ or by truncation followed by that bound, yields \[  J'(a)=-4W'(a)\int _0^ a\frac{ds}{\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}} =-W'(a)T(a).  \] The derivative of $J+WT$ is consequently $WT'$, proving strict increase. At zero $J\to 0$, $W(a)\to 1/4$, and $T\to 2\pi $. At one the integrand of $J$, extended by zero from $[0,a]$ to $[0,1]$, is bounded by $\sqrt{2W(s)}$ and converges to it. Hence $J\to 4\int _0^1\sqrt{2W}=2c_ W$. Finally $W(a)=(1-a^2)^2/4$ times the logarithmic period bound tends to zero. This proves the second limit without confusing a full period with one transition. $\square$ Example 16.21.6 (All nonconstant phases on a circle) . 9C4D3AAD2ECB On a circle of length $\ell $, the equation $\varepsilon ^2u''=u^3-u$ has a nonconstant solution with exactly $m$ full oscillations precisely when \[  m\in \mathbb N,\qquad 2\pi m\varepsilon <\ell .  \] Its amplitude is the unique $a\in (0,1)$ solving $T(a)=\ell /(m\varepsilon )$, and it is unique up to translation and reversal. At equality no nonconstant solution of that oscillation number exists. Proof Lift a solution periodically to the line and rescale its independent variable by $\varepsilon $. The bounded classification excludes heteroclinics and leaves exactly the periodic profiles. Their least period in the physical coordinate is $\varepsilon T(a)$, so fitting $m$ complete periods is equivalent to the displayed equation. Proposition 16.21.3 maps $(0,1)$ strictly increasingly onto $(2\pi ,\infty )$, proving existence and uniqueness exactly under the strict inequality. At the endpoint the amplitude would be zero, giving the constant zero rather than a new periodic profile. $\square$ Example 16.21.7 (An explicit negative eigenfunction in every periodic cell) . 6F88FAC155AE For a periodic profile of amplitude $a$, set \[  d_ a=\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2},\qquad b_ a=\frac{2+d_ a}{3},\qquad v_ a(t)=b_ a-f_ a(t)^2.  \] Then $v_ a>0$ is periodic and \[  \left(-\frac{d^2}{dt^2}+3f_ a^2-1\right)v_ a =\lambda _ a v_ a,\qquad \lambda _ a=1-d_ a<0.  \] On a circle comprising one or any integer number of periods, $\lambda _ a$ is the least Rayleigh quotient, attained only by multiples of $v_ a$. Moreover $\lambda _ a=-\tfrac 32(1-a^2)^2+O((1-a^2)^4)$ as $a\uparrow 1$. Proof Put $B=a^2(2-a^2)$. The Hamiltonian gives $(f_ a')^2=f_ a^4/2-f_ a^2+B/2$, whence $(f_ a^2)''=3f_ a^4-4f_ a^2+B$. Consequently, for a constant $b$, \[  \left(-D^2+3f_ a^2-1\right)(f_ a^2-b) =(3-3b)f_ a^2+b-B.  \] It is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $3-3b$ precisely when $3b^2-4b+B=0$. For any periodic $H^1$ test $\phi $, expansion and integration by parts around the circle give \[  Q_ f(\phi )-\lambda _ a\int \phi ^2 =\int v_ a^2\left|(\phi /v_ a)'\right|^2.  \] There is no endpoint term because the functions and coefficients are periodic. This proves the least-quotient assertion and its equality characterization without a spectral completeness theorem. Taylor expansion of $\sqrt{1+3(1-a^2)^2}$ gives the final estimate. The negative direction becomes small in a long cell, but it remains negative at every finite amplitude. $\square$ Proposition 16.21.8 (Periodic profiles have infinite index on the line) . 49D79826FC5E Every nonconstant periodic entire profile has infinite Morse index for compactly supported variations. Its extension $u(y,t)=f_ a(t)$ to every $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $d\geq 1$, also has infinite index. Here infinite index means that the quadratic form is negative definite on compactly supported test subspaces of arbitrarily large finite dimension. Proof Example 16.21.7 supplies a positive bounded periodic eigenfunction $v_ a$ with negative eigenvalue $\lambda _ a$. For a nonzero compact smooth cutoff $\chi $, the same integration by parts on the line gives \[  Q_ f(v_ a\chi (t/R)) =\lambda _ a\int v_ a^2\chi (t/R)^2+ R^{-2}\int v_ a^2\chi '(t/R)^2<0  \] for large $R$: the first term is bounded above by a negative constant times $R$, while the second is $O(R^{-1})$. Thus there is a compactly supported smooth negative test $\phi $. This also gives a concrete alternative to the endpoint-pairing proof of instability in Lemma 12.6.9 . Translate $\phi $ by sufficiently separated integer multiples of $T(a)$. The potential is periodic, each form value is the same negative number, and disjoint supports eliminate all cross terms. Their span has negative definite form, with arbitrarily large dimension. In higher dimension test with $\phi (t)\eta (y/R)$ for a fixed nonzero compact smooth $\eta $. Dividing by $\int \eta (y/R)^2$ leaves $Q_ f(\phi )+R^{-2}C_\eta \int \phi ^2$, which is negative for large $R$. Separate copies by integer periods in $t$ to obtain the same arbitrarily large negative subspaces. title: Proposition 16.21.1 (Every bounded entire profile stays between the wells)
search_title: Every bounded entire profile stays between the wells
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Proposition 16.21.1 (Every bounded entire profile stays between the wells) . 828FD329FEDF If $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ is bounded and solves $f''=f^3-f$, then $|f|\leq 1$. If it takes the value $+1$ or $-1$, it is that constant. For its Hamiltonian $C=(f')^2/2-W(f)$ one has $-1/4\leq C\leq 0$. Proof Suppose $f(t_0)=b>1$. Reverse time if necessary so that $f'(t_0)\geq 0$. As long as $f\geq b$, its second derivative is at least $b^3-b>0$. Integration shows that it remains above $b$ with increasing derivative for every later time, contradicting boundedness. Apply the same argument to $-f$ to exclude values below $-1$. At a well, a nonzero derivative would cross outside the allowed range; with zero derivative, ODE uniqueness gives the constant solution. Since $W(f)\leq 1/4$, the Hamiltonian is at least $-1/4$. If it were positive, the identity $(f')^2=2(W(f)+C)\geq 2C$ would make $f'$ nonvanishing with constant sign and magnitude bounded below on the line. That again contradicts boundedness. This proves both endpoints of the permitted range without assuming that a global maximum is attained. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.21.2 (Classification of bounded entire profiles)
search_title: Classification of bounded entire profiles
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Theorem 16.21.2 (Classification of bounded entire profiles) . C7DBCCB764C2 Every bounded entire solution is a constant in $\{ -1,0,1\} $, a translated and possibly reversed heteroclinic, or a periodic profile with amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ oscillating between $-a$ and $a$. For each amplitude there is, up to translation and reversal, exactly one such periodic solution. It satisfies \[  (f')^2=\frac12(a^2-f^2)(2-a^2-f^2),\qquad C=-W(a).  \] The periodic profiles and the zero constant have infinite total energy on the line. This extends the finite-energy classification of Theorem 12.2.6 , rather than identifying these distinct classes, and supplies the bounded infinite-energy examples asked for in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 2.2. Proof Proposition 16.21.1 treats the wells. At $C=0$, separation on $(-1,1)$ gives precisely the heteroclinics already classified. At $C=-1/4$, the identity forces $f'=0$ and $W(f)=1/4$, so $f=0$. For $-1/4<C<0$, there is a unique $a\in (0,1)$ with $W(a)=-C$, since $W$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$. Factoring $2(W(f)-W(a))$ gives the displayed expression. On the permitted range $(-1,1)$ this is nonnegative exactly when $|f|\leq a$. The separated time integral from $-a$ to $a$ is finite: both endpoint zeros are simple. Starting at $(f,f')=(0,\sqrt{2(W(0)-W(a))})$, the solution reaches $a$, turns because $f''=a^3-a<0$, reaches $-a$ and turns again. Reflection at the extrema and ODE uniqueness produce a smooth periodic solution. The conserved orbit contains every possible nonconstant datum at this energy, proving uniqueness up to its phase and reversal. Its energy over a period is positive, so summing disjoint periods gives infinite total energy. The constant zero has the positive constant energy density $1/4$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.21.3 (The fundamental period is strictly increasing)
search_title: The fundamental period is strictly increasing
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Proposition 16.21.3 (The fundamental period is strictly increasing) . BF7D7DE9DC38 For amplitude $a\in (0,1)$ the least period is \[  T(a)=4\sqrt2\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{d\theta }{\sqrt{\, 2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )\, }}.  \] It is smooth and strictly increasing, with $\lim _{a\downarrow 0}T(a)=2\pi $ and $\lim _{a\uparrow 1}T(a)=+\infty $. For $a\geq 1/2$ it satisfies $T(a)\leq C(1+|\log (1-a^2)|)$. Proof One quarter-period is the time from $0$ to $a$. In its separated integral substitute $f=a\sin \theta $; the factor $a\cos \theta $ cancels and yields the formula. This orbit is strictly monotone between successive extrema, so the resulting full return is the least period. On any compact amplitude subinterval the denominator stays positive. Differentiating under the integral gives \[  T'(a)=4\sqrt2\, a\int _0^{\pi /2} \frac{1+\sin ^2\theta }{[2-a^2(1+\sin ^2\theta )]^{3/2}}\, d\theta >0.  \] Dominated convergence at zero gives $2\pi $. At one, the integrand increases to $1/\cos \theta $, whose integral diverges, proving the other limit by monotone convergence. Write the squared denominator as $2(1-a^2)+a^2\cos ^2\theta $. For $a\geq 1/2$ and $r=\pi /2-\theta $, use $\cos \theta =\sin r\geq 2r/\pi $. The integral is bounded by a constant times $\int _0^{\pi /2}((1-a^2)+r^2)^{-1/2}dr$. Its elementary antiderivative gives the logarithmic upper bound. $\square$

title: Example 16.21.4 (Small oscillations and a single long-period layer)
search_title: Small oscillations and a single long-period layer
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Example 16.21.4 (Small oscillations and a single long-period layer) . 257BC8D7226F Normalize the increasing zero of the periodic profile by $f_ a(0)=0$ and $f_ a'(0)>0$. Then \[  a^{-1}f_ a(t)\longrightarrow \sin t\quad (a\downarrow 0),\qquad f_ a(t)\longrightarrow q(t)\quad (a\uparrow 1)  \] in $C^\infty $ on every compact interval. Each long-period solution contains both an increasing and a decreasing transition; the second moves outside every fixed interval under this normalization. Proof The initial derivative is $f_ a'(0)=a\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Thus $v_ a=f_ a/a$ solves $v_ a''=a^2v_ a^3-v_ a$ with $v_ a(0)=0$ and $v_ a'(0)=\sqrt{1-a^2/2}$. Since $|v_ a|\leq 1$, the integral form of this ODE and Gronwall's inequality give convergence with first derivatives to the solution of $v''=-v$, $v(0)=0$, $v'(0)=1$. The equation and successive differentiations give every higher derivative. This limit is $\sin t$. At the other endpoint the initial data converge to $(0,1/\sqrt2)$ for the unchanged equation $f''=f^3-f$. The same continuous-dependence argument, using $|f_ a|\leq 1$, yields the heteroclinic $q$ on compact intervals. Its decreasing zero occurs at $T(a)/2$, which diverges by Proposition 16.21.3 . This explains why local convergence to one layer is compatible with a second transition in every full period. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.21.5 (Energy of one periodic cell)
search_title: Energy of one periodic cell
section: 16.21 Periodic phases and the long-period transition limit
text: Proposition 16.21.5 (Energy of one periodic cell) . 29FB8961950E Let $\mathcal E(a)=\int _0^{T(a)}((f_ a')^2/2+W(f_ a))dt$. Then \[  \mathcal E(a)=4\int _0^ a\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}\, ds+W(a)T(a), \qquad \mathcal E'(a)=W(a)T'(a)>0.  \] Its endpoint limits are $\pi /2$ at $a=0$ and $2c_ W$ at $a=1$. Proof The Hamiltonian says that the energy density is $(f_ a')^2+W(a)$. Substitution of the profile value on each quarter-period therefore gives the first formula. Write the first term as $J(a)$. The integrand vanishes at its upper endpoint, and its parameter derivative has only an integrable inverse-square-root singularity there. Differentiation, justified either by the substitution $s=a\sin \theta $ or by truncation followed by that bound, yields \[  J'(a)=-4W'(a)\int _0^ a\frac{ds}{\sqrt{2(W(s)-W(a))}} =-W'(a)T(a).  \] The derivative of $J+WT$ is consequently $WT'$, proving strict increase. At zero $J\to 0$, $W(a)\to 1/4$, and $T\to 2\pi $. At one the integrand of $J$, extended by zero from $[0,a]$ to $[0,1]$, is bounded by $\sqrt{2W(s)}$ and converges to it. Hence $J\to 4\int _0^1\sqrt{2W}=2c_ W$. Finally $W(a)=(1-a^2)^2/4$ times the logarithmic period bound tends to zero. This proves the second limit without confusing a full period with one transition. $\square$

text: Example 16.21.6 (All nonconstant phases on a circle) . 9C4D3AAD2ECB On a circle of length $\ell $, the equation $\varepsilon ^2u''=u^3-u$ has a nonconstant solution with exactly $m$ full oscillations precisely when \[  m\in \mathbb N,\qquad 2\pi m\varepsilon <\ell .  \] Its amplitude is the unique $a\in (0,1)$ solving $T(a)=\ell /(m\varepsilon )$, and it is unique up to translation and reversal. title: 16.22 Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
search_title: Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
section: 16.22 Exact phase-layer energies and geometric limits
text: These examples refine the smooth-interface recovery calculation from [ ChAC ] , Section 3.1, and the periodic ODE examples from Section 16.21 . They distinguish a particular competitor's energy from the existence or minimality of a critical point. The potential, $q$, $\psi $ and $c_ W$ retain their normalization from Definition 12.1.1 . Example 16.22.1 (Vertical graph layers retain an area excess) . CB8ACA2FE3D2 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be bounded and open, and $h\in C^2(\Omega )\cap W^{1,\infty }(\Omega )$. On $\Omega \times \mathbb R$ put $u_\varepsilon (y,z)=q((z-h(y))/\varepsilon )$. On this unbounded cylinder, energy and discrepancy mean the integrals of the local densities; the function is locally Sobolev but need not be globally in $L^2$. Then, for every $\varepsilon >0$, \[  E_\varepsilon (u_\varepsilon ;\Omega \times \mathbb R) =c_ W\int _\Omega \left(1+\frac{|Dh|^2}{2}\right)dy, \qquad \xi _\varepsilon ^{u_\varepsilon }(\Omega \times \mathbb R) =\frac{c_ W}{2}\int _\Omega |Dh|^2dy.  \] The excess over $c_ W$ times the graph area is exactly \[  \frac{c_ W}{2}\int _\Omega \left(\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}-1\right)^2dy.  \] In particular this unnormalized vertical profile is generally not a recovery sequence for the graph perimeter. Proof Write $t=(z-h(y))/\varepsilon $. Then $|Du_\varepsilon |^2=\varepsilon ^{-2}\psi (t)^2(1+|Dh|^2)$ and $W(q(t))=\psi (t)^2/2$. The energy density is therefore $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (t)^2(1+|Dh|^2/2)$ and the discrepancy density is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (t)^2|Dh|^2/2$. Integrate in $z$, using $dz=\varepsilon \, dt$ and $\int \psi ^2=c_ W$, to obtain both identities. The graph area is $\int _\Omega \sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ by the area formula. The elementary identity $1+s/2-\sqrt{1+s}=(\sqrt{1+s}-1)^2/2$ proves the excess formula. It vanishes precisely when $Dh=0$ almost everywhere; the error does not disappear merely by taking a thinner transition layer. $\square$ Example 16.22.2 (The residual detects the same normalization error) . F91CC32ACDDD For the preceding layer, \[  \varepsilon ^2\Delta u_\varepsilon -W'(u_\varepsilon ) =q''(t)|Dh|^2-\varepsilon \psi (t)\Delta h.  \] If this is identically zero for all $(y,z)$, then $Dh=0$, so $h$ is constant on every connected component. When $h(y)=b\cdot y+c$, the correctly normalized tilted-plane solution is instead \[  \widetilde u_\varepsilon (y,z) =q\left(\frac{z-b\cdot y-c}{\varepsilon \sqrt{1+|b|^2}}\right).  \] Its energy per base area is $c_ W\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$ and its discrepancy vanishes. Proof Twice differentiating the composition gives $\varepsilon ^2\Delta u=q''(t)(1+|Dh|^2)-\varepsilon \psi (t)\Delta h$. Subtract $W'(q)=q''$ to obtain the residual. Divide by $\psi >0$ at a fixed $y$: the factor $q''(t)/\psi (t)=-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ varies with $z$, whereas $Dh$ and $\Delta h$ do not. The identity for all $z$ forces $|Dh|^2=0$. For an affine graph the normalized argument is signed Euclidean distance divided by $\varepsilon $, so the planar-interface calculation of Proposition 12.4.1 applies. Direct integration in $z$ gives the stated energy factor $\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$. The unit norm of the distance gradient gives equipartition pointwise. $\square$ Proposition 16.22.3 (The second-order energy of a distance layer in three-space) . DEB92BC85E40 Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth compact embedded two-sided surface without boundary, and choose an injective symmetric tube $F(y,z)=y+z\nu (y)$, $|z|<\rho $, as in Lemma 12.10.1 . For $u_\varepsilon (F(y,z))=q(z/\varepsilon )$ define \[  m_2=\int _{\mathbb R}t^2\psi (t)^2dt\in (0,\infty ).  \] The energy on this tube satisfies \[  E_\varepsilon (u_\varepsilon ;\operatorname {Tube}_\rho (\Sigma )) =c_ W\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma ) +\varepsilon ^2m_2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu +O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }).  \] There is no linear term in $\varepsilon $. Proof The normal coordinate has unit gradient. Hence the energy density times the volume ratio is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (z/\varepsilon )^2(1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2)$. Change variables $z=\varepsilon t$. On the symmetric interval the term $t\psi (t)^2$ is odd, so its integral is exactly zero. The remaining terms give the exact finite-interval formula \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }\psi ^2dt +\varepsilon ^2\left(\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu \right) \int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }t^2\psi ^2dt.  \] The exponential decay $\psi ^2\leq Ce^{-2\sqrt2|t|}$ makes $m_2$ positive and finite. The omitted zeroth moment is $O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon })$. The second-moment tail, multiplied by $\varepsilon ^2$, is bounded by $C(\rho ^2+\varepsilon \rho +\varepsilon ^2)e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }$ and has the same stated order for fixed $\rho $. This proves the formula. It is an expansion for the specified layer on the tube; extending the function to an ambient domain requires a separate tail estimate such as the one in Theorem 12.4.3 . $\square$ Example 16.22.4 (Spherical and toroidal corrections) . C3A0BCB3BC29 For a round sphere of radius $R$, the second-order term in Proposition 16.22.3 is $4\pi m_2\varepsilon ^2$, independent of $R$. For every circular ring torus it is zero. This correction is governed by total Gauss curvature, whereas the Willmore energy of the same ring tori is positive and varies with the radius ratio. Proof On the sphere, $K_\Sigma =R^{-2}$ and its area is $4\pi R^2$, so $\int K_\Sigma =4\pi $. For a ring torus the already computed identity in Example 16.18.3 gives $\int K_\Sigma =0$. Insert these values in the tube formula. The ring-torus energy in Theorem 16.18.2 is $\pi ^2R^2/(r\sqrt{R^2-r^2})$. Thus no identification of the tube correction with the Willmore energy is justified by this example; the two curvature integrals are different. $\square$ Example 16.22.5 (An exact periodic solution converges to two interfaces) . E2F3056BDF26 Fix a circle of length $\ell $. For $0<\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$ choose $a_\varepsilon $ by $T(a_\varepsilon )=\ell /\varepsilon $ and set $u_\varepsilon (x)=f_{a_\varepsilon }(x/\varepsilon )$, normalized by the increasing zero at $x=0$. These are exact critical points, and \[  u_\varepsilon \longrightarrow \begin{cases}  +1,& 0<x<\ell /2,\\  -1,& \ell /2<x<\ell \end{cases} \quad \text{in every finite }L^ p(S^1_\ell ).  \] Their energy measures converge weakly to $c_ W(\delta _0+\delta _{\ell /2})$, and their total energy tends to $2c_ W$. Proof The period equation implies $a_\varepsilon \to 1$. For any fixed $b\in (0,1)$, the time for $f_ a$ to rise from zero to $b$ converges, as $a\to 1$, to $\int _0^ b(2W(s))^{-1/2}ds<\infty $. On the positive half-period the profile stays above $b$ except within this uniformly bounded time of either zero, by reflection about its maximum. Multiplication by $\varepsilon $ shows that $u_\varepsilon \to 1$ uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,\ell /2)$. The symmetry $f_ a(t+T(a)/2)=-f_ a(t)$ handles the negative half. Boundedness by one then gives every finite $L^ p$ convergence. Change variables $x=\varepsilon t$ in the energy: the total is exactly $\mathcal E(a_\varepsilon )\to 2c_ W$ by Proposition 16.21.5 . Around either zero, for every fixed $L$ the rescaled profiles converge smoothly to a heteroclinic on $[-L,L]$. Their energy on the physical interval of radius $\varepsilon L$ therefore tends to $\int _{-L}^ L\psi ^2$. Sending $L\to \infty $ shows that every fixed neighborhood of either zero carries limiting energy at least $c_ W$. Since the total limit is exactly their sum, energy outside any disjoint pair of such neighborhoods tends to zero. For a continuous test function, replace it on each small neighborhood by its value at the center and use uniform continuity. The resulting error tends to zero as the neighborhoods shrink, proving the stated weak convergence. This limit has two perimeter points of multiplicity one, even though each approximating critical point is unstable. $\square$

When $h(y)=b\cdot y+c$, the correctly normalized tilted-plane solution is instead \[  \widetilde u_\varepsilon (y,z) =q\left(\frac{z-b\cdot y-c}{\varepsilon \sqrt{1+|b|^2}}\right).  \] Its energy per base area is $c_ W\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$ and its discrepancy vanishes. Proof Twice differentiating the composition gives $\varepsilon ^2\Delta u=q''(t)(1+|Dh|^2)-\varepsilon \psi (t)\Delta h$. Subtract $W'(q)=q''$ to obtain the residual. Divide by $\psi >0$ at a fixed $y$: the factor $q''(t)/\psi (t)=-\sqrt2\tanh (t/\sqrt2)$ varies with $z$, whereas $Dh$ and $\Delta h$ do not. The identity for all $z$ forces $|Dh|^2=0$. For an affine graph the normalized argument is signed Euclidean distance divided by $\varepsilon $, so the planar-interface calculation of Proposition 12.4.1 applies. Direct integration in $z$ gives the stated energy factor $\sqrt{1+|b|^2}$. The unit norm of the distance gradient gives equipartition pointwise. $\square$

text: Proposition 16.22.3 (The second-order energy of a distance layer in three-space) . DEB92BC85E40 Let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb R^3$ be a smooth compact embedded two-sided surface without boundary, and choose an injective symmetric tube $F(y,z)=y+z\nu (y)$, $|z|<\rho $, as in Lemma 12.10.1 . For $u_\varepsilon (F(y,z))=q(z/\varepsilon )$ define \[  m_2=\int _{\mathbb R}t^2\psi (t)^2dt\in (0,\infty ).  \] The energy on this tube satisfies \[  E_\varepsilon (u_\varepsilon ;\operatorname {Tube}_\rho (\Sigma )) =c_ W\operatorname {Area}(\Sigma ) +\varepsilon ^2m_2\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu +O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }).  \] There is no linear term in $\varepsilon $. Proof The normal coordinate has unit gradient. Hence the energy density times the volume ratio is $\varepsilon ^{-1}\psi (z/\varepsilon )^2(1+Hz+K_\Sigma z^2)$. Change variables $z=\varepsilon t$. On the symmetric interval the term $t\psi (t)^2$ is odd, so its integral is exactly zero. The remaining terms give the exact finite-interval formula \[  \operatorname {Area}(\Sigma )\int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }\psi ^2dt +\varepsilon ^2\left(\int _\Sigma K_\Sigma \, d\mu \right) \int _{-\rho /\varepsilon }^{\rho /\varepsilon }t^2\psi ^2dt.  \] The exponential decay $\psi ^2\leq Ce^{-2\sqrt2|t|}$ makes $m_2$ positive and finite. The omitted zeroth moment is $O(e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon })$. The second-moment tail, multiplied by $\varepsilon ^2$, is bounded by $C(\rho ^2+\varepsilon \rho +\varepsilon ^2)e^{-2\sqrt2\rho /\varepsilon }$ and has the same stated order for fixed $\rho $. This proves the formula. It is an expansion for the specified layer on the tube; extending the function to an ambient domain requires a separate tail estimate such as the one in Theorem 12.4.3 . $\square$

title: Example 16.22.4 (Spherical and toroidal corrections)

text: Example 16.22.4 (Spherical and toroidal corrections) . C3A0BCB3BC29 For a round sphere of radius $R$, the second-order term in Proposition 16.22.3 is $4\pi m_2\varepsilon ^2$, independent of $R$. For every circular ring torus it is zero. This correction is governed by total Gauss curvature, whereas the Willmore energy of the same ring tori is positive and varies with the radius ratio. Proof On the sphere, $K_\Sigma =R^{-2}$ and its area is $4\pi R^2$, so $\int K_\Sigma =4\pi $. For a ring torus the already computed identity in Example 16.18.3 gives $\int K_\Sigma =0$. Insert these values in the tube formula. The ring-torus energy in Theorem 16.18.2 is $\pi ^2R^2/(r\sqrt{R^2-r^2})$. Thus no identification of the tube correction with the Willmore energy is justified by this example; the two curvature integrals are different. $\square$

text: Example 16.22.5 (An exact periodic solution converges to two interfaces) . E2F3056BDF26 Fix a circle of length $\ell $. For $0<\varepsilon <\ell /(2\pi )$ choose $a_\varepsilon $ by $T(a_\varepsilon )=\ell /\varepsilon $ and set $u_\varepsilon (x)=f_{a_\varepsilon }(x/\varepsilon )$, normalized by the increasing zero at $x=0$. These are exact critical points, and \[  u_\varepsilon \longrightarrow \begin{cases}  +1,& 0<x<\ell /2,\\  -1,& \ell /2<x<\ell \end{cases} \quad \text{in every finite }L^ p(S^1_\ell ).  \] Their energy measures converge weakly to $c_ W(\delta _0+\delta _{\ell /2})$, and their total energy tends to $2c_ W$. Proof The period equation implies $a_\varepsilon \to 1$. For any fixed $b\in (0,1)$, the time for $f_ a$ to rise from zero to $b$ converges, as $a\to 1$, to $\int _0^ b(2W(s))^{-1/2}ds<\infty $. On the positive half-period the profile stays above $b$ except within this uniformly bounded time of either zero, by reflection about its maximum. Multiplication by $\varepsilon $ shows that $u_\varepsilon \to 1$ uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,\ell /2)$. The symmetry $f_ a(t+T(a)/2)=-f_ a(t)$ handles the negative half. Boundedness by one then gives every finite $L^ p$ convergence. Change variables $x=\varepsilon t$ in the energy: the total is exactly $\mathcal E(a_\varepsilon )\to 2c_ W$ by Proposition 16.21.5 . Around either zero, for every fixed $L$ the rescaled profiles converge smoothly to a heteroclinic on $[-L,L]$. Their energy on the physical interval of radius $\varepsilon L$ therefore tends to $\int _{-L}^ L\psi ^2$. Sending $L\to \infty $ shows that every fixed neighborhood of either zero carries limiting energy at least $c_ W$. Since the total limit is exactly their sum, energy outside any disjoint pair of such neighborhoods tends to zero. For a continuous test function, replace it on each small neighborhood by its value at the center and use uniform continuity. The resulting error tends to zero as the neighborhoods shrink, proving the stated weak convergence. This limit has two perimeter points of multiplicity one, even though each approximating critical point is unstable. $\square$

section: 7.18 Sobolev compactness on closed manifolds
text:
The mollification argument used for BV compactness in Theorem 4.2.7 also gives the $L^2$ compactness needed for fixed-parameter elliptic problems. The translation-and-smoothing method parallels [ Sim18 ] , Chapter 2, Theorem 2.6; the phase-field application is the compactness step in [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4. We give the $H^1$ version explicitly. Lemma 7.18.1 (The quadratic translation estimate) . 14BA3E3305C8 For $f\in H^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ and $h\in \mathbb R^ n$, \[  \| f(\, \cdot +h)-f\| _{L^2}\leq |h|\, \| Df\| _{L^2}.  \] If $ho _\delta $ is a nonnegative smooth mollifier of integral one supported in $B_\delta $, then $\| ho _\delta *f-f\| _2\leq \delta \| Df\| _2$. Proof For smooth $f$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $f(x+h)-f(x)=\int _0^1 Df(x+sh)\cdot h\, ds$. Square, apply Cauchy–Schwarz in $s$, and integrate in $x$; translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives the first estimate. For $H^1$ functions apply the calculation to their smooth mollifications and pass to the limit in $L^2$ for the functions and their weak derivatives. Approximation by mollifiers follows from translation continuity in $L^2$; it does not require any compactness theorem. Finally average the first estimate against $ho _\delta (h)$ and use the triangle inequality for the $L^2$ integral to obtain the second. $\square$ Theorem 7.18.2 (Strong L2 compactness on a closed manifold) . F7C78AA7EF28 On a smooth closed Riemannian manifold $(M^ n,g)$, every bounded sequence in $H^1(M)$ has a strongly $L^2(M)$ convergent subsequence. The same is true for an $H^1(\mathbb R^ n)$ bounded sequence whose members are supported in one fixed compact set. This is the compact embedding used in the fixed-parameter problem of [ ChAC ] , Exercise 4.4. Proof First take the Euclidean sequence with common compact support $K$. For fixed $\delta >0$, its convolutions have support in $K+\overline B_\delta $ and uniform bounds on values and first derivatives: \[  \| ho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| ho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2, \qquad \| Dho _\delta *f_ j\| _\infty \leq \| Dho _\delta \| _2\| f_ j\| _2.  \] Arzela–Ascoli makes this family precompact uniformly on the common compact set, hence in $L^2$. Lemma 7.18.1 bounds the $L^2$ distance from each original function to its convolution by $C\delta $. For each tolerance choose $\delta $ small and then a finite net for the convolutions. The same net, with the uniformly small smoothing error added, is a finite net for the original sequence. Total boundedness and completeness of $L^2$ yield a convergent subsequence. On $M$, choose finitely many coordinate charts and a smooth partition of unity with each cutoff supported compactly in its chart. The coordinate representations of the cutoff functions times $f_ j$, extended by zero, have a common compact support and uniform Euclidean $H^1$ bounds. This follows from the product rule and bounded comparability of the coordinate metric and volume density on the compact supports; zero extension creates no boundary jump there. Apply the Euclidean result in each chart and take a subsequence common to this finite collection. Since the cutoffs sum to one and their volume densities are uniformly comparable, the resulting sequence is Cauchy in $L^2(M)$. This proves the compactness statement without imposing a bound on the values of $f_ j$. $\square$ Corollary 7.18.3 (A positive Poincare constant on a connected closed manifold) . 92C2144D9701 If $M$ is additionally nonempty, connected and positive-dimensional, then \[  \lambda _1=\inf _{\substack {v\in H^1(M),\  \int _ Mv=0\ v
e 0}}  rac{\int _ M|
abla v|^2}{\int _ Mv^2}>0.  \] Consequently $\lambda _1\int _ M|f- ar f|^2\leq \int _ M|
abla f|^2$ for every $f\in H^1(M)$, where $ ar f$ is its average. Proof If the infimum were zero, choose mean-zero $v_ j$ of $L^2$ norm one with $\| 
abla v_ j\| _2	o 0$. Theorem 7.18.2 supplies a strongly $L^2$ convergent subsequence. Distributional testing in each chart shows that the limit has zero weak gradient. Lemma 6.5.1 makes it constant locally, and connectedness propagates that constant over the manifold. Its mean is zero, so it is zero, contradicting the limiting $L^2$ norm one. The inequality is then the Rayleigh definition applied to $f- ar f$. On a disconnected manifold, separate constants on different components show why a single global mean-zero condition would not suffice. $\square$
